vignette:
Eduardo, a 55-year-old Navy officer of Latin American descent, had spent decades on the water, a career built on precision and command. The trauma that now defined his life happened not at sea, but on a humanitarian mission in a coastal city that became a war zone. He and his crew were tasked with extracting civilians from a district that had come under sudden, heavy artillery fire. In the chaos, a shell struck a building they were using as a staging point. Eduardo was knocked unconscious by the blast. When he came to, he saw a young woman, a local interpreter he’d been working with for weeks, pinned under rubble. He tried to lift the beam, but it was too heavy. He had to leave her to save the rest of the team. He still hears her voice calling his name over the radio static, and sees the red dust settling on her outstretched hand. The memory comes back with a visceral, full-sensory reality—the smell of cordite and wet concrete, the percussive shockwave in his chest, the taste of grit in his mouth. He can feel the exact strain in his arms as he tried to lift that beam. Other times, he can recount the entire event in a flat, dispassionate tone, as if it happened to a stranger, leaving him feeling hollow and numb afterward.

Eduardo was certain that his actions during those minutes revealed a fundamental, unchangeable truth about himself: he was a weak person. This belief had hardened into a fixed idea. He was convinced he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, and he felt a crushing, personal failure for not protecting the people under his command. This sense of weakness and failure directly fed the intrusive quality of the memory. When he remembered the event, he did not just see the scene; he saw himself as the man who failed, and the guilt was so intense it felt like a physical pressure in his chest. The memory, in turn, reinforced his negative appraisals. Every time the image of the interpreter’s face flashed into his mind—often triggered by the sound of a helicopter’s rotors or the sight of a pile of construction debris—he was forced to relive his inaction. The memory itself was the primary, punishing evidence that he was, indeed, weak. He had come to believe that if he were a stronger person, he would have found a way, and the fact that he hadn’t was proof he was worthless.

In the months that followed, Eduardo began to avoid his usual routines. He requested desk duty, claiming a need for administrative oversight, which his superiors granted out of respect for his years of service. He stopped attending the informal gatherings at the base gym, where the loud clang of weights and the sharp, sudden shouts of younger officers reminded him too much of the chaos of that day. At home with his partner, he grew quiet and withdrawn, often sitting in the dark in the living room after she had gone to bed, listening to the radio static on a low band, as if trying to hear a voice that would never come again. The clinical picture had become a tightening loop: the belief that he was weak made him hypervigilant to any sign of hesitation in himself, which then triggered the full memory of the event, which in turn confirmed his belief. He had begun to monitor his own heartbeat, afraid that any spike in anxiety was a sign that he was losing control, which he interpreted as further proof of his weakness. This cycle had eroded his confidence to the point where he struggled to make even minor decisions at work, second-guessing every order he gave.

What finally brought Eduardo to seek help was a moment of acute crisis. While driving past a construction site, the sound of a jackhammer—a percussive, rhythmic pounding—triggered a full sensory reliving. He pulled over, shaking, and saw the interpreter’s face in the reflection of the windshield. He realized he could not keep driving away from it. He was terrified that if he did not get help, he would eventually do something to harm himself, or that his partner would leave him because he had become a ghost in his own home. He hoped, with a fragile and deeply buried optimism, that someone could help him forgive himself—or at least, help him stop feeling like a stranger in his own life.

Ayesha was a 28-year-old South Asian woman who came to treatment after months of living as if her body had never really left the room where she had been tortured. During her first recounting, she described being held down, hearing men moving around her, and learning with terrifying certainty that ordinary sounds could turn into danger without warning. Since then, she had found herself suddenly feeling and acting as if it were happening again: the pressure in her chest, the sharp startle at a footstep, the instant flood of terror when a door slammed. What frightened her most was how quickly her mind could be pulled back into that scene. She would be standing in her tailoring shop, measuring fabric for a customer, and a passing shout in the hallway could make her freeze as though the men were just outside the room.

That sense of danger had become the organizing fact of her days. Ayesha said she scanned exits as soon as she entered any room or building, not because she wanted to, but because she felt she needed to know where she could run if something went wrong. In her shop, she positioned herself near the doorway and noticed every movement in the street outside. In clinic waiting rooms, she sat rigidly, eyes moving from one door to another, counting people, memorizing paths, watching for anyone who might come in behind her. She was superalert and watchful on guard, and the effort of keeping herself prepared left her exhausted by evening. Even at home with her husband, she listened for unexpected sounds and slept lightly, as if her body had learned that rest made her vulnerable.

Over time, this constant sense of threat shaped what she allowed herself to do. Ayesha had come to believe that if she let her guard down, she would be caught unprepared again. That belief pushed her toward a narrow, protective routine: she avoided emotional stress, especially arguments, frightening stories, or anything that stirred strong feelings, because she feared that once her emotions rose, the memories would become harder to hold back. She also avoided relaxing because it felt dangerous to her, almost like inviting something bad to happen while she was not paying attention. If her husband suggested that she sit with tea on the balcony after dinner, she would refuse and instead keep busy folding clothes or checking locks, telling herself that staying active helped her stay safe. The calmer she tried to become, the more exposed she felt, so she worked to keep herself tense and occupied.

That same fear had kept her from seeking medical care and psychological help for a long time. After the torture, she had not gone to a doctor for the lingering pain in her body, and later she delayed coming for therapy because she worried that talking about what happened would make the images more vivid. She said she did not trust the relief that other people offered, because the moments when she felt briefly at ease had often been the moments when a flashback arrived without warning. In her mind, symptoms and danger had become linked: a wave of memory, a rush of fear, then the need to pull back from people, from emotion, from stillness itself. Her husband noticed that she had grown more distant and that even small social gatherings left her depleted, but Ayesha preferred to stay on the edge of the room rather than risk feeling overwhelmed.

By the time she finally sought help, the pattern had narrowed her life. At work she turned down larger tailoring orders that would require her to spend long hours with clients, because crowded appointments made her hyperaware and scanning. She had begun leaving the shop earlier than before, not wanting to be there after dark when the street outside felt less predictable. She was distressed by how much energy it took to remain on guard, and by how little room was left in her life for ease or closeness. What brought her in at last was the fear that she was becoming permanently trapped in this state, unable to trust her own body or let herself rest. She hoped treatment might help her feel safe enough to stop watching every doorway, but she was equally afraid that if she lowered her guard, the memories would return with the same force as before.

Lin was forty-nine, divorced, and working the IT help desk at a community college in the San Gabriel Valley. She had served a single tour in Afghanistan fifteen years ago as a communications specialist. The forward operating base where she was stationed had been hit by a mortar attack on a hot, dusty afternoon. She remembered the shriek of the incoming round, the sudden pressure, then the fire that caught a fuel truck parked near the comms tent. The smell of burning diesel and plastic filled the air, thick and acrid, as she helped drag a wounded soldier toward the landing zone where a medevac helicopter was descending, rotors thudding low and loud. That sound—the rhythmic chop of blades—and that burnt smell had never left her.

Now, back in civilian life, those same triggers found her in ordinary places. A faint whiff of something burning in the office kitchen—someone's burnt toast, a malfunctioning server fan—could make her hands shake and her heart pound before she even knew what was happening. When a maintenance helicopter flew low over the campus, she would freeze at her desk, her body tensing as though the walls might collapse. The workplace itself had become a trigger: the hum of computers, the fluorescent lights, the way colleagues would suddenly appear at her cubicle. Each surprise approach felt like a potential threat. She had begun to feel threatened by strangers even in neutral situations—a student asking for directions, a delivery person at the front desk. Her physical reactions were immediate: rapid breathing, a hot flush, the urge to bolt. She found herself checking behind her constantly, scanning the hallway before she left the office.

The feeling of being threatened drove her into rigid patterns. To escape that raw, jumpy state, she started avoiding any situation that might stir strong emotions—she stopped watching the news, declined invitations to crowded gatherings, and kept conversations at work surface-level. She also refused to talk about the deployment with anyone; when a well-meaning coworker once asked about her military service, she changed the subject and then excused herself to the restroom. That same hypervigilance, however, also sharpened her awareness of triggers: the more on edge she felt, the more she noticed every helicopter sound in the distance, every odd smell, every unexpected footstep behind her. Her threat system was constantly feeding on itself.

The avoidance and self-silencing only made things worse. By not talking about the event, she never gave her memories a chance to soften; the burnt smell and helicopter sound stayed as vivid and terrifying as they had been that afternoon. At times the intrusive thoughts became so unbearable that she hurt herself physically—digging her nails into her palm or pressing the sharp edge of a paperclip into her forearm—because the pain was something she could control, a momentary focus that drowned out the flashback. But that very act of self-harm brought the trauma back to the forefront of her mind, looping her into a fresh wave of threat perception. After she hurt herself, she would feel even more exposed and unsafe, scanning the parking lot on her way home as if someone were watching.

What finally brought Lin to a clinic was a specific incident two weeks ago. A student had left a bag of burnt popcorn in the office microwave, and the smell had filled the entire IT suite. She had a full panic attack—hyperventilating, disoriented, convinced she smelled diesel—and ended up hiding in the supply closet for twenty minutes. Her supervisor, concerned, suggested she take leave. Lin now sat in the therapist’s office because she was afraid of losing her job, and she was even more afraid that the images from that base would never leave her. She hoped, hesitantly, that talking about it would not make it worse. She was tired of checking behind her, tired of the pain in her hands, tired of feeling like a stranger in her own life.

**Vignette: Miriam**

Miriam is a 66-year-old Guatemalan-born woman who has worked as a literary editor for nearly three decades, first in Mexico City and now in a small publishing house in Chicago where she has lived since her late thirties. She is soft-spoken and precise with language in the way that people who have spent a lifetime caring about words tend to be. She chooses what she says carefully, and she pauses often, as though she is editing herself in real time.

She grew up during the height of Guatemala's civil conflict. In 1981, when she was twenty-two and newly married, the violence reached her mid-sized city in a way it had not before. One afternoon, returning from the market with her younger sister, she witnessed the killing of several civilians in the street — men from her neighborhood, people she recognized — carried out by paramilitary forces in broad daylight. She and her sister pressed themselves against a wall and did not move. Her sister was trembling so violently that Miriam held her by the shoulders and told her to look at her face, only her face. She does not remember how long they stood there. What she remembers is the smell — something metallic and thick — and the quality of the light, which she describes as very flat and very wrong. Within months, she and her then-husband fled the country.

For years, she functioned. She built a career she is proud of, raised a son largely on her own after her divorce in the mid-nineties, and immersed herself in literature with a devotion that was, she now understands, partly protective. Books kept her at a safe distance from her own interior life. She rarely spoke about Guatemala, even to close friends, and when the topic arose she would redirect the conversation with practiced ease.

The difficulties that brought her to therapy began approximately two years ago, after she accepted an editorial project — a novel set during a Latin American civil conflict. Reading the manuscript in her apartment, alone at her desk, she found herself unable to continue past the third chapter. Her hands were shaking. She was not sure, at first, what was happening to her. She closed the laptop and sat on the floor of her kitchen for an hour. That night she could not sleep, and when she did drift off briefly she woke from a dream that was not quite a dream — more like a return, vivid and physical, to that street in 1981.

Since then, sleep has been unreliable. She wakes between two and four in the morning with her heart pounding, though she often cannot identify a specific nightmare, only a residue of dread that takes hours to lift. During the day she finds herself scanning her surroundings in ways she didn't used to — noting exits in restaurants, startling at sudden sounds on the street, feeling inexplicably unsafe in crowds. She has declined several social invitations and has become, she says with some embarrassment, "a person who prefers to stay home."

Her work has suffered in ways that distress her deeply. She cannot return to the manuscript she abandoned, and she finds that certain passages in other texts — descriptions of violence, of helplessness, even of particular kinds of light — pull her out of her editorial focus and into something she struggles to name. She describes it as being dragged underwater. She surfaces, but it takes time, and she feels ashamed of what she perceives as a professional failure.

She speaks about her sister, who still lives in Guatemala City, with particular tenderness and a guilt she has carried quietly for decades — the guilt of having left, of having built a life elsewhere. She does not fully connect this guilt to the afternoon they stood against that wall together, but the connection surfaces in the way her voice changes when she speaks of her sister, dropping lower, as though she is trying not to be heard.

She describes herself as a private person. She says she has never talked about this before, not really. She seems both relieved and frightened to be doing so now.

# Rosa's Story

Rosa Delgado had been a combat engineer for twenty-eight years when the IED detonated beneath the Humvee. She was forty-seven then, leading a route clearance mission through the Helmand Province in July 2014. The blast came without warning—a flash of orange that consumed her entire field of vision, then heat so intense it seemed to melt the air itself. The concussion threw her against the reinforced door panel, and for a moment she couldn't hear anything but a high-pitched ringing. Then came the screaming. One of her soldiers was on fire, rolling in the dirt, and she was already moving toward him, her training overriding the chaos in her nervous system. She got him to cover, got the tourniquet on another casualty whose leg ended below the knee, and only much later—after the evacuation helicopters had lifted away and the base medic told her she'd done everything right—did she notice the blistering on her own left forearm where the heat had caught her skin.

The physical wounds healed. The burn scars faded to a pale, thin line. But something in Rosa's body had not returned to baseline. By the time she was medically cleared to return stateside in 2015, her nervous system had become a sentinel, permanently vigilant for the next catastrophe. She was promoted to a training role at Fort Leonard Wood, where she oversaw demolition exercises and explosive safety protocols. It should have been manageable—controlled environments, no combat—but the work itself had become a minefield. When recruits detonated charges during live-fire drills, the flash and concussive wave would hijack her immediately. The sudden sight of flame or the specific temperature of heat radiating from an explosion would trigger the full memory without warning: the orange consuming everything, the screaming, the weight of her soldier's body as she dragged him. The memory itself was fragmented and chaotic—she could not tell a coherent story of those moments, even to herself. What she remembered came in sensory shards: the specific high-pitched tone of the ringing in her ears, the smell of scorched metal and flesh, the feeling of helplessness despite her training. Those auditory echoes would replay in her head for hours afterward, the phantom ringing so vivid she'd find herself checking if anyone else could hear it.

By 2018, Rosa had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with her. Other engineers could witness controlled detonations without their hands trembling. Other soldiers could move past combat without their bodies turning into coiled springs. What happened to her was deeply unfair—she had done everything right that day, had saved lives, and yet she was the one left shattered. No investigation had changed anything. No accountability had come. She was certain the world was a dangerous place, that threats were everywhere, that her body's constant state of alert was the only thing keeping her alive. These beliefs began to shape every choice she made. She started avoiding anything that could be stressful—first the live-fire drills, then the training facility itself, then the base commissary where the fluorescent lights and crowds felt unpredictable. She volunteered for administrative work instead, though it meant a lateral move and the loss of the role she had built. At home, she numbed her feelings with discipline and distance, moving through evenings with her husband Miguel like someone underwater. She couldn't articulate to him why she flinched at the sound of the grill igniting on their back patio, why she had begun to constantly scan their neighborhood for signs of threat—the way a car slowed on their street, the unusual silence of an evening with no traffic noise. That silence especially terrified her. It felt like the held breath before catastrophe.

The avoidance and emotional numbing created their own spiral. By withdrawing from stressful situations, Rosa reinforced her belief that the world was dangerous and that she was incapable of managing it. Her hypervigilance—that constant scanning of her surroundings—kept her threat system perpetually activated. Her body remained tense and ready to react to danger that never came, leaving her exhausted and unable to concentrate at work. She found herself ruminating on the unfairness of it all, which deepened her conviction that something was broken inside her. The numbing she used to manage her emotions only isolated her further from Miguel, who grew increasingly frustrated with her distance. Six months ago, her supervisor had gently suggested she consider a medical evaluation. Rosa had resisted for weeks, certain that admitting she needed help would confirm her deepest fear: that she was defective, that the trauma had fundamentally altered who she was as a person. But last month, when she realized she had spent an entire weekend in her garage, unable to enter the house because the kitchen window faced the neighbors' property where someone had been burning brush, she finally called the Veterans Affairs clinic. She is fifty-four now, and what she fears most is that the damage is permanent, that she will spend the rest of her life trapped in this hyperalert state, unable to be present with her husband or find meaning in the work that once defined her. What she hopes for, though she barely allows herself to articulate it, is that somehow the fragmented pieces of that day might finally cohere into a story she can tell and then, perhaps, begin to put down.

Mai was thirty-eight years old, a welder on a commercial construction crew, when a beam she was cutting free from a temporary support slipped and struck a colleague in the leg, severing an artery. The colleague survived, but Mai’s memory of those few seconds never settled into a complete story—she could taste metal as if it were still on her tongue, but the moment the beam fell and the screaming began was a blur of broken images, and the guilt that flooded her when the memory returned felt as fresh as it had in the emergency room.

In the weeks that followed, Mai found herself avoiding the crew’s lunchroom and taking her breaks alone. Whenever the taste of metal rose unexpectedly—at her workbench, or when she bit into a sandwich—her heart would hammer and her palms would go cold, making it impossible to focus on the next weld. She had begun to notice that even a clang of steel or the hiss of an acetylene torch could bring back that same incomplete, guilt-laden flash, and her body would react before she could stop it: sweating, a sickening jolt, her concentration shattered for the rest of the shift. This persistent sense of danger — that her body was on edge even when nothing was happening — kept the accident close in her mind, as if she needed to keep replaying it to stay ahead of whatever might go wrong next. At night, sleep came only in fitful stretches; she would lie awake with her chest tight, the incomplete picture playing on a loop, certain she was missing something she should have done differently.

The more she tried to push the memory away—by staying busy, by refusing to let her mind drift back—the more it seemed to ambush her at random moments. One afternoon, while walking past the warehouse where the accident happened, the metallic taste hit her so sharply that she had to lean against a wall, gasping. That evening she berated herself for still not being able to piece together exactly what went wrong, and the self-blame rumination carried her into another sleepless night. She had come to believe that the guilt meant she was fundamentally careless, and that belief made every trip to the job site feel like a test she might fail again.

Mai’s avoidance spread: she started arriving late to work so she would miss the morning safety briefing, and she stopped joining her coworkers for after-shift drinks or weekend barbecues. Friendships frayed; people stopped inviting her. The loneliness only deepened the rumination, and the more she dwelled on her mistake, the more her memory of the event seemed to shrink to a single flash—the taste, the sound, the guilt—while the moments before and after stayed inaccessible. When she finally sought help, it was because the physical reactivity had become so severe that she had walked off the job site twice in one week, and her foreman had warned her that if she couldn’t keep her concentration, she would be moved to a different crew—or let go. What frightened Mai most was the possibility that she would never be able to recall the full truth of what happened, and that without it, the guilt would never leave her alone.

Lina, a 20-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and married soldier, has been grappling with the aftermath of an assault that left her feeling disconnected from both herself and her community. The traumatic event itself occurred in the barracks where she was stationed. One night, as she was working late on a report, a fellow soldier broke into her room, assaulting her despite her pleas for him to stop. Lina has vivid visual memories of this event — images that replay like a video in her mind. However, these memories often feel alien, as if they belong to someone else rather than herself. The extremity of the assault makes it hard for her to believe she was actually involved. The memory of this traumatic night keeps intruding on Lina’s daily life. She finds herself constantly redirecting her thoughts to other things or trying to make sense of what happened by overanalysing every detail, which only intensifies the memories’ vividness and frequency. These intrusive recollections have led Lina to engage in maladaptive strategies like overeating as a way to distract herself from the distressing images. Lina’s belief that somebody else would have intervened to stop the assault has deeply impacted her sense of self-worth and competence, leading to feelings of guilt and inadequacy. This negative appraisal makes it harder for her to cope with everyday situations, pushing her towards further maladaptive behaviors such as overeating or trying to drown out the memories by constantly thinking about something else. Over time, these coping mechanisms have led Lina to experience a growing sense of disconnection from herself and her community. The more she turns to food and redirection as ways to cope, the less she feels like she can connect with others in meaningful ways. She is certain that the person she has become since the assault is unrecognizable to her, contributing to an even deeper sense of isolation. The alienation from her culture and community has also grown as Lina withdraws into herself. Her once strong connection to her South Eastern Asian heritage now feels distant and tenuous, further exacerbating her negative appraisals about her own worth and ability to cope with the trauma she experienced. Lina’s daily life as a soldier is now fraught with triggers that remind her of the assault. The barracks where it happened are constantly in her mind, making it difficult for her to perform her duties without being overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts and memories. Her overanalysing has only made these images more vivid and distressing, creating a cycle that feels almost impossible to break. The combination of her maladaptive coping strategies and the persistence of traumatic memories has left Lina feeling increasingly disconnected from herself and others. She is most afraid of never recovering her sense of self and losing all connection to her community. What finally brought her to seek help was the realization that she could no longer function effectively in her role as a soldier, nor find peace within herself. Lina hopes for a way to reconnect with her true self and find healthier ways to manage her distressing memories without feeling like she is living in isolation from those around her. She wants to reclaim a sense of control over her life and feel like the person she was before the assault once again.

Meet Kai, a 63-year-old widowed construction worker from Oceania. He's been struggling to cope with the memories of physical abuse he suffered at the hands of his late wife. The trauma has left an indelible mark on his life, and it's only recently that he's begun to realize the extent of its impact. It started when Kai would see specific body parts – a wrist, a shoulder – that reminded him of the way his wife used to grab or push him during their arguments. These visual triggers would transport him back to those moments, making him feel like he was reliving the abuse all over again. As he recalls, "I'd be working on a site, and I'd see a guy with a similar build to my wife's, and suddenly I'm right back there, feeling helpless." Talking about the event or being around people related to it would also set him off, making him feel like he was losing control. To cope with these feelings, Kai developed some maladaptive strategies. He started carrying large amounts of cash on him at all times, impulsively spending money on things he didn't need just to distract himself from the memories. "It's silly, I know," he says, "but when I'm feeling anxious or scared, buying something new makes me feel like I've got some control back." He also became obsessed with staying near exits whenever he was in a room or building, always scanning for potential escape routes. This habit even extended to his construction work, where he'd position himself near the site's entrance just in case. But these strategies didn't alleviate Kai's sense of threat; if anything, they seemed to heighten it. He started waking up multiple times during the night to check whether he was safe, and ordinary sounds would make him jump or startle. "I'll be lying there, and suddenly I'll hear a creak or a groan, and I'm convinced someone's breaking in," he admits. This constant state of hypervigilance left him feeling drained and on edge. As Kai struggled to manage these symptoms, his negative appraisals began to solidify. He started believing that he was weak, that he couldn't rely on himself to get through tough situations. "I keep thinking about all the times I didn't stand up for myself during those arguments," he says, shaking his head. "It's like I'm reliving my own failure over and over." This emotional numbness has also left him feeling disconnected from the world around him – like he's just going through the motions. Kai's maladaptive strategies only seemed to reinforce these negative appraisals. His compulsive spending, for example, made him feel guilty and ashamed, further solidifying his sense of weakness. And when he avoided conflict or confrontation, it only confirmed to himself that he was indeed unable to rely on himself. Despite the exhausting cycle of triggers, maladaptive strategies, and negative appraisals, Kai is finally seeking help. The recent loss of a close friend has left him feeling isolated and alone, and he's begun to realize that his coping mechanisms are no longer sustainable. "I just want to feel like myself again," he says, looking down at his hands. "I don't know if I can ever go back to who I was before all this happened, but I have to try."

Thao Nguyen was forty-two when the fever spiked so violently that the floor beneath her seemed to tilt, pulling her into a sudden, life-threatening illness that left her gasping on a hospital gurney. She had come to believe the experience was so extreme that it threatened to rewrite her reality. In the months that followed, the antiseptic sting of hospital disinfectant settled into her memory like a permanent marker. Now, whenever she passes a pharmacy or catches the sharp scent of a cleaning solution on the subway, her breath catches. The cold temperature of the ICU lingered in her bones; even the brisk, air-conditioned corridors of her logistics firm make her shiver, and she learned to keep a heavy wool cardigan draped over her shoulders as a quiet shield. When she first saw the IV needle being prepared during her stay, the sight had felt like a breach, and now that same visual cue—a syringe in a colleague’s hand, a blood pressure cuff inflating on a vendor—makes her step back. Thao manages project timelines for a mid-sized firm, a role that demands precision and presence. Yet her days are marked by a careful retreat. She tries to erase the memory of the event by keeping her schedule full, her mind occupied with Gantt charts and team stand-ups. When a lull opens during her morning review meetings, she feels a sudden, wordless dread wash over her, unmoored from any specific picture, as though her body is still bracing for the crisis to return. During a recent quarterly review, the office HVAC cycled on, blasting a stream of cold air across her desk. She felt the familiar shiver climb her spine, and without a word, she reached for a thermal mug and shifted her chair away from the vent, a small retreat that mirrored her wider avoidance. She watches her own thoughts closely during these moments, constantly monitoring her mental space for signs of going crazy. Her husband notices how she avoids the office nurse’s routine visits, how she schedules physical examinations with meticulous care, sometimes delaying them until the symptoms are manageable. She does not go to hospitals unless absolutely necessary, and the sight of an ambulance parked outside her corporate building sends her to the side entrance instead of the main lobby. The story of her illness often feels impossible to reconcile with the woman she is today. Thao sometimes laughs at her own recollections, certain that the severity she lived through cannot be entirely true, that the medical team must have overstated how close she came to the edge. Yet certain moments cut through the fog with startling sharpness: the exact cadence of the respiratory therapist’s voice, the sudden stillness of the cardiac monitor when her rhythm stuttered, the way the cold air rushed over her face as the gurney rolled into the emergency bay. The rest of the experience remains half-formed, blurred at the edges, but the certainty of those clear fragments anchors her awareness. She had come to believe that her life has been destroyed by the trauma, that the steady arc of her years had snapped. She is certain she failed in her most important role in life, both for the projects she leads and for the household she shares with her husband. She holds the conviction that her body has been permanently damaged by what happened, that the vulnerability she felt during the crisis has not passed but settled into her muscles and lungs. Now, at forty-two, Thao sits in a therapist’s office for the first time, her cardigan pulled tight. A PCL5 score of sixty-seven is just a number on a chart, but it reflects the quiet accumulation of her days: the way she monitors the temperature of the room, the way she notes every unfamiliar scent, the way she holds her breath when the clinician reaches for a pen or a clipboard. She has come to believe that the world outside her office doors no longer feels safe. What she hopes for is not a return to how things were, but a way to carry the weight without letting it dictate her steps. What frightened her most is that the cold, the scent, the sight of medical tools will once again pull her under, and that she will have to choose between watching her body and living her life.

# Marcus

Marcus was twenty-five when he first came to the clinic on a Tuesday afternoon, his supervisor at the downtown hotel having finally insisted he speak to someone after he'd called out sick for the third time in two weeks. He sat in the waiting room in his housekeeping uniform—navy polo, name tag slightly crooked—and his leg bounced steadily against the linoleum floor. When he spoke, his voice was steady but his hands moved constantly, fingers picking at the hem of his shirt.

The trauma had begun when Marcus was seven. His father's boyfriend, Derek, moved into their apartment in late autumn. By winter, what had seemed like occasional roughness—a hard grip on the arm, a shove into the hallway—had become systematic. One night in January, Marcus had wet the bed. Derek's response was to drag him from under the covers, strip the sheets, and force Marcus's face down against the bare plastic mattress—the kind with a peculiar synthetic smell and a slick, grainy texture that Marcus could still feel against his cheek and forehead when he closed his eyes. The man held him there in the dark, pressing down, while Marcus couldn't breathe properly and didn't know if it would end. It did, eventually, but the pattern continued in different forms until Marcus was eleven and his mother finally left with him. By then, something fundamental had shifted in how Marcus understood the world.

Now, eighteen years later, Marcus lived alone in a studio apartment but never stayed there after dark. He would arrive home from his shift at the hotel around three in the afternoon, complete whatever tasks he needed to complete, and then leave again—to the twenty-four-hour diner, to a friend's place, to anywhere that had light and other people. When he did sleep, it was usually on his couch with the television on, the volume low but constant, because silence and darkness still felt like a trap closing around him. He had come to believe that he was marked—that something about what had happened to him was visible on his skin, that people looking at him could somehow see the shape of his humiliation. He felt, most of the time, like a thing rather than a person, as though the substance of who he was had been replaced by something hollow and used.

The nightmares had started a few years ago, intensifying in the past six months. They came almost every night—the memory of that mattress, the pressure, the dark, the feeling of being held down. But they weren't just dreams; they were vivid replays that felt completely real, with the texture against his skin, the smell, the inability to move. Sometimes he would wake up gasping, convinced for several seconds that he was still there, still being held. Other times the memory would surface during the day—triggered by a child crying in one of the hotel hallways, or by the particular weave of a rough blanket he encountered while changing beds—and the emotion would hit him so suddenly and with such force that he would have to step into a supply closet and wait for it to pass, his whole body shaking.

What had finally driven Marcus to call the clinic was a shift change at work. He'd been assigned to the night housekeeping rotation, which meant arriving at the hotel at ten p.m. The first two nights, he'd experienced what felt like constant panic—hyperaware of every shadow, every sound, his body flooding with adrenaline at the slightest movement. On the third night, a guest's child had cried from behind a closed door as Marcus was cleaning the hallway. He'd abandoned his cart, clocked out, and left the building. He hadn't returned. His supervisor had called him the next morning, and Marcus had found himself unable to explain. How could he say that the dark was dangerous, that he couldn't trust anyone, that being alone with another person—even a supervisor trying to help—made his chest tight with a fear he couldn't name?

He sat across from the therapist now, still in his work uniform, and admitted quietly that he didn't know how to live like this anymore. He was afraid of the night. He was afraid of being seen. He was afraid of what would happen if he stopped running.

James is a 54-year-old civil servant who has dedicated his life to public service, working tirelessly in a local government office. For more than two decades, he has enjoyed a stable career that has allowed him to build a comfortable life. However, his world has been turned upside down since the trauma he endured three years ago, which he still grapples with daily.

It all began with a seemingly innocuous argument with his partner, Mark. James recalls the night vividly, the way tension filled the air as they exchanged words that felt sharper than knives. The disagreement escalated quickly, and before he knew it, Mark’s anger erupted. James had never seen this side of him before. It was as if a switch had flipped, revealing a darkness that had lain dormant. The physical assault that followed left lasting scars, both on his body and in his mind. He remembers the cold, unyielding floor beneath him as he curled into a ball, desperately trying to shield himself from the fury aimed at him. 

In the weeks that followed, James tried to return to his normal life. He went to work, where he was known as a diligent employee, always willing to lend a helping hand. But the familiar hum of the office now felt like a cacophony of noise, each sound jarring against his frayed nerves. He often found himself lost in thought, staring blankly at his computer screen, unable to focus on the tasks at hand. His colleagues noticed the change — the way he flinched at sudden movements or how he withdrew during casual conversations. 

James has always valued his independence, but after the incident, he felt an overwhelming sense of vulnerability. Simple tasks like grocery shopping became monumental challenges. He would stand in the grocery aisle, frozen, as memories of that night flooded back. The bright fluorescent lights overhead felt harsh and unforgiving, and he began to avoid crowded places, fearing they would trigger memories of the chaos he had endured. His world shrank, and he became a ghost in his own life, drifting from one day to the next.

Evenings are the hardest. The stillness of his home often amplifies his thoughts. James can still hear the echoes of Mark’s voice, the anger laced in every word. He finds himself replaying that night over and over, searching for signs he might have missed, wondering if there was anything he could have done differently. Sleep eludes him; when he finally does drift off, he is met with nightmares that leave him drenched in sweat, waking him up gasping for air. He lies awake, staring at the ceiling, grappling with a haunting silence that feels like a weight on his chest.

His relationship with Mark has been complex ever since the incident. They attempted to work through it, but the trust has eroded, replaced by a persistent fear. James finds himself questioning everything Mark says or does, constantly on edge. He notices the way his heart races when Mark’s phone buzzes or when he comes home late. The anxiety gnaws at him, making it difficult to engage with Mark in a meaningful way. They often sit in silence, a chasm growing between them that neither knows how to bridge.

James finds solace in his work, throwing himself into projects to distract from his internal turmoil. He becomes a champion for mental health initiatives at the office, advocating for support systems for colleagues. It’s as if he is trying to heal himself through helping others, though he often feels like a fraud. The passion he once felt for his career now mingles with a deep-seated fear that he won’t be able to maintain his composure in front of his peers.

As he navigates his day-to-day life, James grapples with the shadows of his past. He yearns for the strength to reclaim his life, to feel safe and whole again. He knows that healing is a journey, but each day feels like an uphill battle. In moments of quiet reflection, he holds onto hope — a flicker of light that one day, he may find peace within himself again.

Each time he withdrew, the world outside felt more threatening, reinforcing his belief that he needed to keep his distance to remain safe, which only deepened his isolation and sense of vulnerability. This withdrawal from others only deepened his sense of threat, as he convinced himself that he could not handle any unexpected situations or confrontations, further isolating him in his distress. The more he engaged in these behaviors, the more he felt the weight of evidence stacking up against him, convincing him that his inability to cope without them was a clear sign of his fragility. Each time he gambled, he was left with a sense of guilt that only reinforced his negative beliefs about himself, leading him to conclude that he was weak and incapable of facing the memories without resorting to these strategies. The more he avoided confronting these memories, the more intense they became, reinforcing his belief that he was powerless to change his situation and that the past would always haunt him. Marianne had been working for years as a hotel manager when the police violence that now dominated her inner life took place. It had happened in a public setting, in a moment that should have felt ordinary and safe, and what stayed with her most was not only the force of it but the helplessness of being surrounded by people and yet feeling completely unprotected. In the aftermath, she found herself replaying every detail with a clarity that felt cruel: the faces, the voices, the exact arrangement of the room and the sequence of what happened next. Even now, when she spoke about it, she would often slow down as if she were looking at the scene directly in front of her, because the memory remained so clear and detailed that it seemed less like something from the past than something preserved intact inside her.

At first, Marianne assumed that the shock would fade with time, but instead she began to notice that thoughts of the event were arriving uninvited. She could be in the middle of a workday at the hotel, checking reservations or speaking with a guest, when an unwanted thought would break in and pull her back to that day without warning. Certain moments in her surroundings could do it instantly: the sight of a uniform at the lobby entrance, a sudden burst of raised voices near the front desk, or being pressed shoulder to shoulder in a crowded corridor during a busy check-in period. In those moments, she would feel as though the whole memory had come back at once, not as a vague recollection but as a complete return of the terror she had felt then. She described it as being “right back there,” with the same jolt in her body and the same certainty that something dreadful was about to happen again. The anniversary of the event was especially hard for her. As that date approached each year, she became tense and watchful, and she would find herself bracing for the day long before it arrived, as if the calendar itself were enough to open the door to the memory.

Marianne’s work, which had once given her a strong sense of purpose, became more difficult in quiet but significant ways. Because the hotel lobby, banquet rooms, and nearby public spaces could be crowded, she began to alter the way she moved through her own workplace. She stayed at the edges of groups, cut conversations short when the lobby filled, and avoided standing in the busiest parts of the entrance area for long. These changes were not dramatic enough for others to notice at first, but over time they narrowed how she managed her days and made her feel less like the capable person she had been before. After her husband died, she had already been carrying grief, and the trauma added a second layer to her sense of loss. She came to believe that the people and institutions that should have protected her had let her down, and this belief hardened whenever she thought back to how powerless she had been in that moment and how little safety she had received afterward.

What distressed Marianne most was the way the event seemed to have altered her own sense of self. She said she did not know herself anymore in the way she once had. Before the trauma, she had seen herself as composed, practical, and able to handle difficult situations; now she felt unfamiliar to herself, as if part of her had been broken off or taken away. She was also certain that she had permanently changed for the worse. This was not said casually but with the weary conviction of someone who had been living with the same conclusion for a long time. Remembering the event brought back not only the vivid details but the same terror she had felt at the time, and that terror still seemed to carry the authority of proof to her: proof that the world was not safe, and proof that she was no longer the person she had been before it happened.

By the time she sought help, Marianne had become tired of arranging her life around the possibility of being suddenly overwhelmed by the memory. She was still working, but more cautiously and with less confidence, especially in crowded settings that used to feel manageable. She came to therapy because the unwanted thoughts, the yearly worsening around the anniversary, and the way ordinary surroundings could instantly flood her with the full memory were no longer something she wanted to continue enduring alone. What she hoped for was not to forget what happened, because she knew she could not, but to feel less at the mercy of it. What frightened her most was the possibility that this changed version of herself would be permanent.

Sade, a 35-year-old African-American woman, had always found joy in her work as a tutor, nurturing the minds of her young students. However, after the trauma she endured three months ago, that joy felt like a distant memory. Sade had been attacked in her neighborhood during a late-night walk home. The details of the event loomed large in her mind, creating a vivid and unsettling tapestry of fear and confusion. Each time she tried to recall the events, she felt as if she were watching someone else’s life unfold, a sense of alienation enveloping her as the memory felt detached and disjointed from her reality. The terror she experienced during the attack would surge back, making her stomach churn with nausea, a physical reminder of the emotional scars she carried. Each time these memories intruded, they reaffirmed her belief that she was irreparably broken, leading her to avoid situations where she might confront her pain.

Since the assault, Sade had developed acute sensitivity to certain triggers, particularly the sound of children crying. Each cry reminded her of her own vulnerability during the attack, leading her to think that she was destined to feel broken and unsafe forever. With each reminder of her vulnerability, Sade found herself spiraling deeper into the belief that she would always be vulnerable, which reinforced her conviction that safety was an unattainable dream. Each time she heard a child cry, it led her to think that she was forever broken, reinforcing her belief that she would never experience safety or joy again. The sound would echo in her mind, and with it came the unshakeable thought that she was permanently damaged, incapable of feeling whole again. This belief that she was damaged deepened her need to isolate herself, as she reasoned that being around others would only expose her fragility and bring more pain. The more she convinced herself that she was fragile and irreparably damaged, the more she felt that withdrawing from others was not just a choice, but the only sensible strategy to avoid further pain and humiliation. Each cry made her think, with growing certainty, that she would never escape this feeling of brokenness, reinforcing the belief that safety was a distant memory for her. It might seem innocuous to others, but for her, the wails of a child pierced through her thoughts, reminiscent of her own helplessness. When a student cried in her tutoring sessions, a wave of dread washed over her, reinforcing her belief that she had been irreparably damaged. Sade could not help but think that she was forever altered, a shadow of her former self. This belief solidified her decision to withdraw from social interactions, as she felt that being around others would only serve as a painful reminder of her perceived limitations. She had come to believe that she would never regain her previous sense of safety or joy, leading her to avoid situations that might spark happiness or hope, fearing that such feelings were now out of reach.

In her mind, the thought of facing the world became increasingly daunting. She believed that if she couldn’t even face her friends, it was a clear indication that she was weak and unable to cope with life’s challenges, reinforcing her decision to withdraw. Sade frequently found herself ruminating about the attack, wrestling with self-blame that felt almost instinctive. Every time she replayed the event in her mind, the self-blame grew stronger, leading her to feel that the attack was a reflection of her own inadequacies, deepening a sense of worthlessness. She would replay the events over and over, wondering what she could have done differently, convinced that the attack was somehow her fault. This habit of self-blame only deepened her feelings of inadequacy and despair, making it harder for her to cope with everyday challenges. Each time she faced even the slightest upset, Sade felt overwhelmed, gripped by the belief that she lacked the resilience to handle life’s inevitable stresses.

Sade's memory of the assault was fragmented and chaotic. This disorganization made it difficult for her to process her feelings, leading her to believe that engaging with those memories would only exacerbate her emotional turmoil and drive her further into avoidance. The chaotic nature of her memories led her to avoid discussing the trauma altogether, as she feared that confronting them would only deepen her emotional distress and prove her belief that she was unmanageable. Each time she attempted to recall the event, the disarray of her memories pushed her to avoid any discussion about it, fearing that delving deeper would overwhelm her with emotions she felt ill-equipped to handle. This disjointed recollection made it difficult for her to process her feelings, leading her to avoid discussing the event and contributing to her feelings of isolation. The fragmented memories would surface unexpectedly, leaving her grappling with the belief that she couldn’t handle the emotions tied to the trauma, further solidifying her need to withdraw. Each time she avoided discussing the event, it left the memories untouched, making them feel more potent and unmanageable, which only fueled her desire to stay silent. Some moments were clear, while others faded into a fog she couldn’t penetrate. This inconsistency fueled her sense of helplessness, making her avoid discussing the event with others. She struggled to articulate her experiences, believing that if she delved into the details, she would be unable to manage the emotional fallout. This thought avoidance only served to entrench her feelings of isolation, as she found herself withdrawing from friends and family who wanted to support her. The fear of being reminded of the assault kept her from engaging in conversations, leading her to miss gatherings and avoid people altogether. Her instinct to avoid social interactions not only deepened her isolation but also transformed every missed opportunity into a painful reminder of her perceived inadequacy — she felt that if she couldn't handle being around others, it confirmed her belief that she was weak. This strategy of avoidance itself became a constant reminder of her perceived fragility, as she began to believe that if she could not even face her friends, there must be something inherently weak about her. Every time she employed avoidance strategies to cope, it confirmed her growing belief that she was more fragile than those around her, solidifying her negative self-image and pushing her deeper into isolation.

The impact of these maladaptive strategies began to compound over time. With every strategy she employed to cope, she grew more convinced that she was fragile, creating a negative feedback loop where her actions reinforced her negative self-perception. Each time she employed these strategies, she felt a quiet confirmation that she was unable to cope without them, leading her to conclude that she was more fragile than others around her. As Sade avoided reminders of her trauma, the memories seemed to loom larger in her mind, almost like a shadow that followed her relentlessly. This suppression of memories had paradoxically kept them fresh and vivid, creating a cycle where avoidance fed the intensity of her recollections. The more she shut down her feelings and thoughts surrounding the trauma, the more vivid and intrusive the memories became, almost as if her avoidance was feeding them. The more she tried to suppress her thoughts, the more they surfaced, intertwining with her daily life and experiences. Each time she turned away from her memories or avoided confronting her feelings, she inadvertently kept the memories alive, allowing them to intensify and shape her daily experiences in ways that felt increasingly inescapable. This cycle of avoidance only reinforced her belief that she was fragile; each time she turned away from a trigger, it felt like proof that she was unable to cope with the world around her. Each time she felt a flicker of hope or happiness, she quickly shut it down, convinced that such feelings were fleeting and would only lead to disappointment. The cycle felt inescapable, with her negative appraisals reinforcing her maladaptive behaviors, which then fed back into her memories.

Now, as Sade sat in her therapist's office for the first time, she felt a mélange of fear and hope. She understood that her avoidance had created a barrier, not just to the memories, but to the possibility of healing, leaving her feeling trapped in a cycle of fear and despair. She was terrified of confronting the memories that haunted her but recognized that something had to change. Her relationship had begun to suffer as her partner struggled to understand her emotional distance. Withdrawing from her partner became a way to shield herself from the pain, yet she couldn’t shake the belief that her inability to connect was a sign of her weakness. Sade knew she needed help to reclaim her life, to break free from the grip of her trauma and the beliefs that had formed in its wake. Yet she remained paralyzed by the thought that confronting her trauma could unravel her further, reinforcing the idea that she was incapable of handling the emotional weight of her memories. She feared that if she did not confront her memories and the negative beliefs so tightly woven into her reality, she might remain trapped in this relentless cycle forever. What frightened her most was the possibility that she might never find peace, but deep down, she held a small flicker of hope that perhaps, with support, she could begin to navigate her path toward healing. Each time the painful memories intruded, they only reinforced her negative self-assessment, leading her to think that if she couldn't handle her own thoughts, there must be something inherently wrong with her.

Carl had spent most of his life in his small, quiet town in northern Ohio, a place where he felt a sense of normalcy and routine. At 76, he held a steady job as a cashier, a role that had given him purpose after the loss of his wife two years prior. However, beneath the surface of his daily interactions, Carl was wrestling with an unseen burden that had begun to isolate him from the world. The traumatic memories of his youth during the war had started to resurface with alarming intensity, leaving him trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance.

The haunting memories began to seep back into his life, triggered by the simplest of things. A few months ago, while waiting for a bus, a loud honk from a passing car made Carl’s heart race. Instantly, he was transported back to the chaos of the war zone where he had survived bombings and gunfire. The visceral images of destruction and fear flashed before him like a film reel, leaving him feeling as if he were reliving the terror once again. The world had become a dangerous place in his mind, and he found himself increasingly hypervigilant. He watched those around him closely, looking for signs of potential harm, convinced that danger lurked just beneath the surface of everyday life.

Carl had come to believe that the world was no longer a safe place, a notion that seemed to solidify with each passing day. He often pushed away any positive feelings that dared to surface, fearing they would be swiftly followed by loss or tragedy. To him, happiness felt like a fleeting dream, something that could vanish at any moment. Whenever he felt a moment of joy—a laugh shared with a customer or a smile from a neighbor—he would clench his teeth and force the feeling away, telling himself that it was safer to remain detached. It was as if he had built an emotional wall around himself, convinced that vulnerability could lead to further pain.

Driving, once a simple task, became an insurmountable challenge for Carl. The thought of being behind the wheel sent shivers down his spine. He could no longer bear the idea of losing control, of being trapped in a vehicle should the chaos of his past resurface. Instead, he opted for long walks to work, avoiding the bus and any situation that might require him to drive or be a passenger. This self-imposed isolation began to affect his relationships; friends grew concerned as he declined invitations to outings and social gatherings. They didn’t understand the constant battle he was waging against his own mind, and slowly, the distance between them widened.

At night, the struggle continued. Carl’s bed, which once offered comfort, transformed into a battleground of restless thoughts and memories. Sleep eluded him as he forced himself to remain alert, convinced that he needed to be vigilant against unseen dangers. The dark brought with it a flood of emotionless recollections, where the events of the war played out like a detached documentary. He could recall the sights and sounds, but without feeling, as if someone else had lived through that horror. Yet, in the quiet moments of solitude, the vivid images would invade his mind, dragging him back to the fear and helplessness he had felt so many years ago.

As the weeks turned into months, Carl’s mental state deteriorated. He started to feel he was no longer capable of engaging with the world as he once had. The war had stolen not only his sense of safety but also his confidence in himself. He felt like a mere shadow of the man he used to be, a man defined by his work, his relationships, and his passion for life. With each passing day, he struggled more with thoughts of inadequacy and a profound sense of loss—not just of his wife, but of the life he once knew.

Finally, one evening, as he sat alone in his living room, the weight of his fears became unbearable. The isolation, the hypervigilance, the relentless memories—they had all culminated in a realization that he could no longer manage this alone. The thought of reaching out for help filled him with trepidation; what if they didn't understand? What if he was too far gone? Yet, in that moment of despair, hope flickered faintly. Carl decided it was time to seek help, a chance to reclaim the life he feared he had lost forever. What frightened him most was the uncertainty of this new journey—could he find a way to navigate a world that felt so perilous? Or would he remain trapped in the echoes of his past?

Marcus was thirty-nine when he walked into the clinic, though the way he carried himself—shoulders rounded, eyes that seemed to look past rather than at you—made him appear older. He had come because his ex-wife had finally stopped answering his calls, and his supervisor had given him a written warning about missing work. Both developments felt inevitable to Marcus, like dominoes he had watched falling but could not catch. What he wanted to understand, though he couldn't quite articulate it, was why the ground beneath his life had become so unstable.

Seven years earlier, Marcus had been working on a residential renovation crew in Trenton when the accident happened. It was a Tuesday in late September, the kind of clear morning that felt like nothing bad could occur. He and three other men were framing out the second floor of a colonial-style home. Marcus was on the ground, cutting lumber, when he heard the shout—a sound of surprise rather than pain at first. He looked up to see his friend and crew chief, David, falling backward off the scaffolding. The image burned itself into Marcus's mind in fragments: David's arms windmilling, the terrible geometry of his body striking the concrete foundation, the specific smell of dust and blood and something else Marcus couldn't name but could taste on his tongue—copper mixed with something acidic, something he later realized was his own fear. The sound David made when he landed was not a scream but a wet, final silence. Marcus had stood there, hands still gripping the saw, unable to move, unable to stop what had already stopped.

David died three days later in the hospital. The investigation found that someone had failed to secure the scaffolding properly. Marcus had checked it that morning—he was always careful—but not thoroughly enough. That was the thought that had lived in his chest ever since: he could have caught it. He could have stopped it. But he hadn't, because he was not the kind of person who stopped bad things. The world, he had come to understand, was not a place where competence or vigilance mattered. Bad things happened, and you stood there helpless, and then you lived with it. When he was around loud noises on the job site—the sudden bang of a nail gun, the crash of dropped materials—his entire body would go rigid, his breath catching in his chest as if the sound itself might be a harbinger of another fall. He had come to dread the unpredictability of construction sites, the way danger could announce itself without warning, the way a single moment of inattention could reshape the world.

For the first two years after David's death, Marcus had drunk heavily. When the drinking stopped working—when it no longer dulled the sensory flashes that arrived without warning—he had found other ways to absent himself. He began gambling, first online, then at the casino in Atlantic City. The rush of placing a bet, the possibility of a win, the total absorption of his attention—these things worked better than alcohol. They gave him permission to not be present in his body, to not feel the weight of his own inadequacy. He would drive to Atlantic City on his days off and lose money he didn't have, and in those hours at the table, he was not the man who had failed to save his friend. He had also come to avoid certain places entirely. He no longer went to the grocery store where he used to shop with Jennifer—the smell of raw meat in the butcher section would hit him without warning, that same copper-iron tang that had coated his mouth the day David fell, and he would have to leave, his hands shaking, his heart racing as if the accident were happening again in real time. He had stopped attending the annual crew reunion, stopped going to the bar where the guys gathered on Friday nights. He told himself it was easier this way, that seeing them only reminded him of what he had failed to prevent, but the truth was more complicated: he was afraid that if he saw them, if he had to speak about David or pretend that everything was normal, something in him would break open in a way he could not control.

At work, Marcus had become someone his crew barely recognized. He had always been steady, patient with younger workers, someone who could defuse tension with a joke. Now he moved through job sites in a kind of controlled fury that he never allowed himself to express. When a subcontractor made a mistake, or when someone on his crew cut a corner, Marcus would feel the rage rise in his throat like bile, and he would swallow it down. He would excuse himself, walk to his truck, sit in the cab with his hands gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles went white. To let that anger out felt dangerous to him—if he started, he believed, he would not be able to stop. And if he lost control, he might hurt someone, and then he would be the kind of man who broke things, the kind of man who made things worse. So he kept it sealed inside, a pressure that never released. The memory of David's fall came without warning and with complete sensory vividness. A smell—dust after rain, or sometimes the particular copper-iron scent of raw meat at a grocery store—would transport Marcus instantly back to that moment. He could taste it again, that acidic-metallic compound that coated his mouth. He would see the image: David's body, the angle of his fall, the terrible stillness. These were not thoughts that Marcus could reason with or dismiss. They were pictures that played without his permission, and they came with a certainty that he was powerless to prevent the next catastrophe, that he was fundamentally inadequate to the task of keeping people safe.

When these memories arrived, Marcus would sometimes deliberately try to leave his body, to dissociate, to create distance between himself and the sensation. He had learned to do this—to mentally step outside himself, to watch himself from a remove, to blank out the sensory details. It worked sometimes. Other times, he would end up at the casino instead, or sitting in his truck for hours, unable to account for the time. His ex-wife, Jennifer, had tried for three years to reach him. She had suggested therapy, medication, anything. But Marcus had come to believe that there was nothing to fix, nothing to understand—only a truth he had learned: that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that he was inadequate to protect anything or anyone, and that the best he could do was try not to hurt anyone else while he waited for the next inevitable disaster. When Jennifer finally left, it had felt like confirmation rather than surprise. Now, sitting in the clinic, Marcus was not sure what he wanted. He was certain that talking about what happened would not change the fact of it. He was certain that he could not stop bad things from happening. But something had shifted. His supervisor's warning had been the final weight on a scale that had been tipping for years. He had come because he had nowhere else to go, and because somewhere beneath the conviction of his own helplessness, there was a small, terrified part of him that wondered if he was wrong.

Linh Tran is a 24-year-old Vietnamese American woman who works as an urban planner for a mid-sized municipal agency, a role that requires her to attend public meetings, collaborate with colleagues, and present proposals to community stakeholders. She sought psychological support after a routine workplace health screening left her unable to return to the office for three days — an absence she attributed to a stomach bug but which she privately understood as something she could not yet name.

Linh grew up in a household shaped by her maternal grandmother's authority. Her grandmother, who had raised her following her parents' separation, was unpredictable and physically severe. Punishment was not occasional; it was woven into the fabric of daily life, administered without warning and without explanation. What Linh remembers most vividly — though even this memory arrives in pieces — is the quality of being watched before it happened. Her grandmother's gaze would fix on her, and Linh would feel herself become something smaller than a person, an object awaiting handling. The strikes often came when Linh was already unwell — once, memorably, while she was nauseated and bent over the bathroom sink. The smell of that room, the fluorescent light, the sensation of her own body failing her while her grandmother's hand came down — these details do not arrive to her as a coherent narrative. More often they arrive as a wave of rage with no image attached, or as a surge of nausea that seems to have no physical origin.

By the time Linh left for college, she had developed a set of habits she thought of simply as being careful. She agreed readily with others, rarely expressed preferences, and arranged her life to avoid situations that felt unpredictable. She told herself this was maturity. It was only in her early twenties, as the demands of her professional life expanded, that the careful architecture she had built began to show its costs.

At work, Linh is required to attend community planning sessions in city hall conference rooms — large, fluorescent-lit spaces where she often finds herself at the front of the room, visible to a crowd. Being seen in this way, particularly when she cannot predict who is watching or what their faces mean, produces a vigilance she cannot suppress. A colleague shifting suddenly in a chair, a supervisor turning quickly toward her — these movements register in her body before her mind can assess them, and she finds herself unable to hold the thread of what she was saying. Her difficulty concentrating during these moments has led her supervisor to note, with some concern, that her presentations have become less assured. Linh has interpreted this feedback as confirmation of something she has long suspected: that she is fundamentally weak, that others can see it, and that it is only a matter of time before this is made fully visible.

Outside of a small number of settings — her apartment, a particular coffee shop two blocks from her office — Linh does not feel safe. She has declined two invitations to colleagues' gatherings in the past four months, each time offering a plausible excuse. When a close friend recently asked her directly whether something had happened in her childhood, Linh ended the conversation and did not contact her friend for two weeks. The idea that someone might name the event, might refer to it, felt like an intrusion she was not equipped to survive.

The workplace health screening that finally brought her to treatment involved a nurse practitioner conducting a brief physical examination. The clinical setting, the overhead light, the sensation of being observed and handled, and a wave of nausea during the blood draw converged in a way Linh had not anticipated. She sat in the parking lot afterward for forty minutes. She has not been able to stop thinking, in the weeks since, about how different everything might have been — her confidence, her relationships, her sense of herself as a person rather than an object — if her childhood had been otherwise.

What Linh most fears, entering therapy, is that speaking about what happened will confirm that it has permanently marked her. What she most hopes is that someone will agree, without requiring her to justify it, that what was done to her was genuinely wrong.

Roberto Garcia is a 54-year-old business owner who came to therapy at his wife’s insistence, though he himself would say he is fine—just tired, a little on edge. He still owns the small grocery store in the East Los Angeles neighborhood he built from nothing twenty years ago, but he no longer enjoys the work. He describes himself as a man who “got too close to something he shouldn’t have seen.” That something happened during his twenties, when he volunteered with an aid organization in a Central American war zone. One afternoon at a checkpoint, a truck backfired two feet from him, and the soldier beside him was shot through the chest before the echo faded. Roberto was sprayed with blood and knocked to the ground by the man’s body. He still remembers the heat of the bullet fragment that grazed his arm, and the way the soldier’s eyes went slack.

For years after, Roberto threw himself into work and family, telling himself he had been lucky. But the old chaos started seeping in about three years ago, not as a memory but as a feeling that something was wrong. He began carrying a compact pistol in his store apron—just in case—and found himself scanning every customer who stepped too close to the counter. At first it felt like vigilance; now it feels like dread. A single loud noise—a car backfire, a dropped crate—stops his breath and sends his hand to the grip hidden under his apron. The instant his fingers wrap around the weapon, his mind goes into overdrive: he replays the checkpoint, the shot, the soldier’s blood, and he starts asking himself why he survived when that man did not. He goes over that question again and again, sometimes for hours after closing, sitting alone in the back office with the pistol on the desk in front of him.

The weapon itself has become a trigger. Because he carries it, Roberto is hyperaware of every potential threat: a customer reaching into a jacket, a teenager laughing too loud in the candy aisle. That laugh especially rattles him—he feels confused by the sound, almost angry that anyone can be happy in a world where such things happen. Positive emotions in others strike him as naïve or dangerous, and he has started snapping at his wife when she tells a joke at dinner. He picks arguments with her, with customers, with the delivery driver—anything to feel the sharp spike of adrenaline that drowns out the rumination for a few minutes. “I start a fight,” he said flatly, “just to stop thinking.” But the fights always circle back. After a shouting match with a customer about a mistaken price, Roberto stood trembling in the aisle, the gun heavy against his ribs, and he understood that he had created the very proximity—the heated face-to-face closeness—that now triggered his panic. He had walked right into the zone.

The cycle has cost him. His wife now sleeps in the guest room; two of his regular customers have stopped coming. Last month, during a small celebration for his employee’s birthday, someone popped a balloon and Roberto dropped to the floor, knocking over a display. The shame afterwards was unbearable, and he locked himself in the office and pulled out his pistol, not to hurt himself, but just to hold it—a habit that now feels like the only reliable thing in his life.

The last straw came when his twelve-year-old nephew ran up to hug him in the store parking lot and Roberto shoved him away before he realized what he was doing. He saw the boy’s face crumple, and that night he told his wife he would see someone. What Roberto is most afraid of now is that he will push everyone away and be left alone with the question he cannot stop asking: “Why did I survive?” But part of him, the part that still picks the lock on the gun safe each morning, is not sure he wants to find out.

Kwame was an 18-year-old African American police officer who had come for help after years of feeling as if his own body and mind were always braced for something to go wrong. He grew up in a home where his father’s violence toward his mother was a recurring part of childhood, and one evening in particular had stayed lodged in him with painful clarity: the raised voice from the kitchen, the sudden crash of something hitting the wall, his mother backing into the corner, and his own small body frozen nearby, unable to move or make it stop. When he remembered that night, it did not return as a full story but as a few sharp pictures, each one vivid and separate, and he could feel himself back in the same position he had been in then, shoulders hunched, chest tight, as if his body were replaying the scene before his mind could catch up. What he felt most when the memory came was overwhelming grief.
