She had failed to protect him. Every time the memory surfaced, these appraisals grew sharper, and every time she blamed herself, the memory returned more vividly, as if her guilt were a summons.

The avoidance, she believed, kept her safe. But it also made the world smaller. Her husband began to find her standing in the middle of rooms, staring at nothing, her hands trembling. She stopped going to the neighborhood where the bodega had been, then stopped taking the subway altogether, then stopped leaving the studio except for necessities. One afternoon, a delivery man knocked too hard on her door, and she felt the cold February air on her skin again, the full memory crashing through her—the bodega, the gunshot, Carlos’s eyes. She had locked herself in the bathroom and wept. The lack of control over her own mind terrified her more than anything else. That evening, she told her husband she needed to see someone. What frightened her most was the thought that she would carry that February night inside her forever, that it would keep pulling her back until there was nothing left of the woman who had once designed dresses for women who danced.

Linda is a 68-year-old retired American woman who came to treatment more than a year after the sudden death of a loved one, a loss that had divided her life into a clear before and after. She had been married for decades and, before the death, much of her routine had been built around family gatherings, familiar neighbors, and a circle of long-standing social contacts she and her husband regularly saw. The death itself had been abrupt and overwhelming, the kind of moment that left her with the unshakable sense that something catastrophic had happened on her watch. In the first retellings, what stood out was not only grief but a fixed conviction: she should have protected the person who died, and she had failed. She returned to that thought repeatedly, as if there might still be some way to undo it by examining it from every angle. She had come to believe that this failure said something final about her.

In the weeks that followed, Linda did not describe herself as falling apart outwardly. Instead, she began organizing her days with relentless activity. Although retired, she kept herself in constant motion, filling hours with chores, errands, projects around the house, and anything else that would keep her from sitting still. If there was laundry to fold, a closet to reorganize, paperwork to sort, she did it immediately. She told herself it was better to stay productive than to let herself think. Her husband noticed that she rarely paused, even late in the evening. On the surface it looked like competence, but Linda knew it was something more urgent. The moment the house became quiet, her whole body seemed to tighten. Even when she knew she was at home and safe, she could not relax. She sat on the edge of chairs, held tension in her shoulders and jaw, and startled easily at small disturbances. She described herself as feeling constantly braced, as if danger might break in again without warning.

As time passed, the world around her became divided into places and people she could still tolerate and those she could not. The hardest encounters were with people she had socialized with before the death. Running into old friends, or even imagining those conversations, felt unbearable because they belonged to the life before everything changed. She avoided gatherings she once would have attended automatically. When neighbors invited her and her husband over, she found reasons not to go. If she saw familiar names on her phone, she let the calls go unanswered. It was not that she had stopped caring about people; rather, seeing them sharpened the sense that she was now separate from everyone else. She felt isolated and set apart, as though others still lived in the ordinary world while she had somehow been exiled from it. Over time she began to think, with increasing certainty, that she no longer belonged anywhere.

Retirement, which had once offered freedom and structure on her own terms, became the setting for this narrowing life. Without a workplace to require contact, it became easier to avoid people altogether. Her days were spent mostly at home, moving from one task to another, rarely allowing any stillness. The consequence was that her world grew smaller. Friends stopped asking as often. Her husband, though present and concerned, could not reach her in the same way, and she knew he felt the loss of their shared social life. Linda felt ashamed of that too, but shame sat alongside fear, anger, and guilt in a mass of strong emotion she could not sort through. At times she felt horrified by how quickly life had changed; at others she was angry that everyone else seemed able to continue. Most persistent was guilt. What frightened her most was the possibility that the death had revealed a truth about her—that when it mattered, she had not protected the person she loved.

By the time she sought help, Linda was exhausted by the effort it took to keep going in this way. She was still busy from morning to night, still turning away from social contact, still living in a body that would not stand down. She came in because she could see how constricted her life had become and because she missed the version of herself who could be with other people without feeling estranged. At the same time, she was afraid of what might happen if she stopped keeping busy, afraid of being fully alone with the guilt she carried, and afraid that talking about the death would confirm what she already believed—that she had failed in the one way that mattered most. What she hoped for, though she said it cautiously, was some way to feel less cut off from the world and less condemned by her own mind.

Thomas Vance was seventy thousand feet above the desert when the right engine catastrophically failed. The subsequent explosion tore through the fuselage, and the violent deceleration sent his vision swimming with a nauseating dizziness that left him feeling utterly ill. He wrestled the aircraft through the final descent, the metallic cracks of the landing gear embedding themselves in his nervous system. When he finally walked away from the crumpled fuselage, the world no longer felt like a domain of calculated precision; it felt fundamentally treacherous. Over the next several months, the memory of that descent did not fade but recalibrated his senses. Whenever he heard a car backfire or a heavy door slam at the flight line, the familiar wave of dizziness would return, accompanied by a visceral feeling of being physically unwell. These sensory shocks immediately locked his shoulders tight and sent his entire body into a state of constant readiness to react. He found himself scanning every briefing room and aircraft hangar for threats, his eyes darting to shadows and every sudden shift in posture triggering a violent flinch. Thomas began to interpret these reactions not as normal stress responses, but as proof that his own mind was fracturing. He felt completely dead inside, a hollowed-out shell where his former confidence used to reside, and he became certain that the rigid laws of safety and control he had once trusted were completely shattered. Fearing another physical collapse, Thomas adopted rigid routines to stabilize himself. He stopped attending squadron socials or weekend trips, telling himself he simply lacked the energy, when the truth was he was giving up all pleasant activities to conserve control. He began strictly rationing his meals, measuring every portion, because regulating his stomach felt like the only way to prevent another bout of dizziness. This relentless self-policing, however, only deepened his conviction that he was fundamentally broken. He viewed his own reactions as evidence that he could not trust his own body to keep him safe, and he avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations as if they were death sentences. The stricter he became about these restrictions, the more certain he became that he was irreparably damaged. In turn, this profound sense of internal and external threat kept his attention permanently fixed on danger. The moment he noticed a drop in the barometer or heard a distant thud, his body would immediately flood with tension, and his startle response would fire before his conscious mind could even process the sound. Thomas knew he was in a trap. The very act of isolation convinced him that the world was inherently dangerous, which only made him more watchful and more prone to dizziness at the slightest provocation. Now, at fifty-six, Thomas sits in a ground operations office, the hum of the ventilation system feeling unnervingly like an engine turning over. The weight of his own vigilance has grown unbearable, and the strain on his marriage has reached a breaking point; his wife no longer knows how to reach him without triggering a startle response. He has finally walked into a clinic, not because he expects a quick fix, but because he is terrified that one more explosion of sound, one more dizzy spell, will cost him his family or his license entirely. He hopes, quietly, to learn how to stand still in his own life again.

Robert, a 62-year-old potter living in a small New England town, had spent thirty years coaxing beauty from clay. He and his wife, Margaret, raised two children, and their son, Daniel, had grown into a quiet, gentle man who loved working alongside his father in the studio. On a clear Tuesday afternoon two years ago, Daniel died of a sudden cardiac arrest while at work. The call came to Robert at the wheel of his truck; by the time he reached the hospital, his son was gone. There was no warning, no illness to prepare for—just a gap where Daniel’s voice used to be.

In the weeks that followed, Robert found himself moving through the house as though walking through invisible walls. He stopped going into Daniel’s room, stopping even to glance at the closed door. When Margaret left a photograph of Daniel on the kitchen counter, Robert quietly slid it into a drawer without saying a word. He began to notice that any object, any sound, any scent that carried even a trace of Daniel—the smell of wood shavings from the studio, the creak of the porch swing where Daniel used to sit—sent a cold spike through his chest. So he began to eliminate them. He moved the swing to the shed. He bought new brushes for his pottery, discarding the old set Daniel had given him for his birthday. He stopped listening to the radio station they had both enjoyed. He didn't explain these choices to Margaret; he simply made them, one by one, and hoped the silence would protect him.

What startled Robert most was what happened when something good came his way. A friend stopped by with a glazed bowl he had finished, full of praise. Robert felt a warm surge in his chest—and instantly shut it down. He turned away, muttered something about needing to clean his tools, and walked out of the room. Positive emotions had become treacherous, as though feeling even a flicker of contentment meant forgetting Daniel. He had come to believe that if he let himself feel happy, he would be punished, or worse, that the happiness would somehow erase his grief. So he refused every invitation, every opportunity for joy. Margaret suggested a weekend trip to the coast; Robert said no without explanation. The thought of planning anything—a dinner date, a doctor’s appointment, a retirement party—filled him with a low, persistent dread. He stopped making any plans at all, living day to day in a gray, uncommitted present. He told himself it was simpler that way, though it was not simpler. It was just less dangerous.

The studio, once his sanctuary, became a place of avoidance. He could not touch the clay without seeing Daniel’s hands pressing into it. He could not sit at the wheel without hearing Daniel’s laugh from the stool beside him. Within months, Robert had stopped working entirely. The wheel sat still, the kiln cold. Margaret had to take on extra hours at the library to cover the lost income, a fact that Robert knew but could not bring himself to address. He spent his days in the back room of the house, reading old magazines, feeding the woodstove, waiting for the hours to pass. Conversations with Margaret grew shorter. He knew she was hurting too, but talking about Daniel felt like pulling the scab off a wound that had not yet healed. So he said nothing.

It was Margaret who finally insisted, six months ago, that he see someone. She had found him staring at a cracked mug in the kitchen—a mug Daniel had made as a teenager—and without a word, Robert had thrown it in the trash. She wept, and for the first time he could not turn away. He agreed to come to this office because he had run out of ways to keep the world at a distance, and because the emptiness he had built around himself had begun to feel more terrifying than the grief it was meant to contain. He is afraid of what will happen if he lets himself feel—afraid the grief will swallow him whole—but he is also, in a small corner of his chest that he barely acknowledges, hoping that something else might still be possible.

She is 76 now, still married, still carrying herself with the careful, measured composure that served her well for decades in radiology. People who meet her later in life often see only a polished professional woman with a steady voice and quick intelligence, someone who has spent a career reading images, finding structure in uncertainty. What they do not see at first is how much of her internal life is still organized around a war she survived as a young civilian, and how much of her present-day world is arranged to keep that past from breaking through.

She remembers the beginning with an almost photographic clarity. She is living in a city that has started to change shape under war, where ordinary routines are gradually overtaken by the sound of distant explosions, by checkpoints, by the instinct to listen before speaking. At first she continues working, telling herself that life must go on, that patients still need answers, that her own fear can be postponed. As the violence draws closer, she becomes skilled at moving through danger without looking like she is doing so. She learns which streets to avoid, how to keep her face calm when her body is braced for impact, how to continue speaking in the middle of fear.

The event that stays with her is not one single image but a sequence of moments that seemed to split the world open. She is caught in the wrong place as shelling begins, and the sounds are so sudden and overwhelming that her body reacts before her mind can understand. She drops low, covers herself, and feels with a sick certainty that the people around her are just as vulnerable as she is. There is dust, screaming, the sharp smell of smoke, and a horrifying sense that time has become unstable. In the days that follow, she keeps functioning because there is nothing else to do. She helps where she can. She checks on others. She counts the living. She does not yet realize that the memory is already settling into her nervous system like a permanent alarm.

Afterward, even when she is safe, her body does not believe it. For years she lives with the expectation that danger can return without warning. Loud noises make her flinch before she can stop herself. Sudden bangs in her neighborhood, the backfire of a car, fireworks on a holiday all send a jolt through her chest. She becomes hyperaware of exits, windows, and the position of her chair in a room. She prefers to sit where she can see the door. She scans faces for signs of trouble. In crowded places she feels a rising tension that has less to do with the present than with a memory her body seems to remember better than her mind.

As a radiologist, she has spent most of her adult life in a profession that rewards attention to detail and calm under pressure. The work fits her in many ways; she likes order, precision, the discipline of reading what is hidden. But the same skill that makes her good at her work also keeps her tied to vigilance. She notices everything. At times she struggles with concentration when reminders of the war intrude unexpectedly. A smell, a sound, a headline on the news can pull her out of the present and into a place she does not want to revisit. She describes those moments as if the past does not merely come to mind but arrives in her body, complete with the same tightening in her stomach, the same shallow breathing, the same sense that she must act immediately to survive.

Sleep has never fully returned to her. She falls asleep reluctantly and often wakes in the dark with her heart racing, unable to shake the feeling that something is wrong. When she dreams, the war is not always literal, but it is always nearby. She wakes disoriented, sometimes frightened to discover that her hands are clenched. At times she avoids going over the details of what happened because once she starts, she fears she will not be able to stop. She has learned to seal away parts of the story for long stretches, but the cost of that containment is a kind of quiet exhaustion. There are days when she feels emotionally distant from others, including her husband, as if some part of her remains behind glass. She loves him and depends on him, yet there are layers of experience she has rarely been able to share fully.

Now, in her later years, the memories have become less raw but no less present. Retirement has not brought the relief she expected; instead, with fewer distractions, she notices how much space the past still takes up. She remains proud of her resilience, and there is a dignity in the way she has built a life around what she endured. Still, she speaks of living with a persistent sense of being on guard, as though peace is something temporary and fragile. Even in safety, she listens for danger. Even in quiet, part of her waits for the next blast.

Thomas had spent most of his life in the quiet rhythm of a civil service office, answering letters, filing reports, and rarely finding himself alone in a room with a man. The trauma that shattered that rhythm began one autumn evening when his long‑time partner, a woman with a volatile temper, grabbed him by the arm and slammed him against the kitchen wall. The physical force left bruises that darkened the inside of his ribs, and the emotional pain left a deep sense of helplessness. In that instant, Thomas felt a loss of control that would echo in every corridor of his future days. The sound of his partner’s voice, the smell of sweat, the taste of metallic blood—these sensations were seared into his mind in a single, terrifying flash. The loss of control he felt during that night became the first trigger that pulled Thomas into a defensive loop. Whenever he sensed a male presence in a closed space—be it a conference room or a narrow hallway—his mind rushed to the memory of being overpowered. This trigger drove him to adopt a constant socializing strategy: he would fill his day with brief conversations, small tasks, and the presence of other people so that he was never alone with his thoughts. At the same time, Thomas detaches from the memory itself, telling himself he is “too tired to think about it” whenever the recollection threatens to surface. By keeping people around him, he hopes the familiarity of voices will stave off the feeling of helplessness, but the effort to remain in a crowd also creates a sense that he is always on guard, further entrenching his perception of loss of control. The triggers also sharpened the memory itself. The next morning, as he walked through the office stairwell, the echo of the partner’s harsh whisper made his ears flood with a taste he could still feel—an iron tang that clung to his tongue. When he stared at the black ink on a page, the scene unfolded behind his eyes like a photographic snapshot: the kitchen, the walls, the motion of his hands. These vivid images came with such clarity that they made it difficult for Thomas to deliberately recall the event. The more he tried to pull the memory into conscious thought, the harder it became, and the more it seemed to dissolve into a distant, almost dream‑like image. When the memory surfaced in this vivid, almost automatic way, it in turn re‑ignited the same triggers. The taste of blood that flooded his mouth whenever he imagined the attack turned the otherwise ordinary fluorescent lighting of the office into a threatening glare. Even the hum of the copy machine seemed to echo the hiss of a knife. Each time the memory returned, Thomas’s fear of a male presence sharpened, and his belief that he had lost control resurfaced, setting the stage for his next defensive maneuver. Detaching from the memory, his most frequent maladaptive strategy, fed back into the memory in a subtle but powerful way. Because Thomas habitually told himself to “move on,” he had become skilled at pulling the memory out of conscious recall. Yet, in moments of forced social interaction—when he was forced to talk to a colleague about a project—his mind would leap to the event, as if the conversation served as a cue for the memory to reappear. The constant need to be surrounded by people, combined with the deliberate avoidance of being alone, made it almost impossible for him to process the memory in a healthy, reflective way. The strategies themselves became triggers. The more Thomas kept himself surrounded, the more he felt a sense of alienation, as if he were living in a cage of people who could not understand his terror. The constant socializing created a pressure to conform, making him feel as though he had no control over his own narrative. Detaching from the memory made him feel out of sync with his own life; he could not explain to anyone why he was so uneasy around men in a single office. These feelings of detachment and alienation fed back into his perception of loss of control, forming a reinforcing loop that tightened with each passing day. In the present, Thomas is a civil servant who often finds himself in meetings with senior male officers. He has begun to avoid conference rooms by arriving late or leaving early, which has caused colleagues to question his reliability. His constant need to be in the presence of others has begun to impair his performance: deadlines slip because he spends too much time on small talk, and the memory of the abuse flares when he hears a man's voice in a quiet hallway. The cycle has grown tighter, and the isolation that once kept him safe now feels like a threat. Thomas has finally decided to seek help because he fears that, if he does not break this pattern, he will lose his job and the only steady anchor he has left. What he hopes most is to learn a way to face the male presence in the office without the flood of vivid taste and photographic recall, and to regain a sense of control that has eluded him since that night.

Meet Giovanni, a 68-year-old European-American politician who has spent his life in the public eye. It's been two years since the life-threatening car accident that changed everything. Giovanni remembers the crash like a series of snapshots – each moment frozen in time. He recalls the sound of screeching tires, the feeling of weightlessness as his car spun out of control, and the searing pain as metal crumpled around him. The smell of alcohol still makes Giovanni uncomfortable; it was the other driver's intoxication that caused the accident. Whenever he catches a whiff of booze, he's instantly transported back to that fateful night. The image of cars mangled in accidents now fills his mind, making it hard for him to shake off the feeling of unease. These triggers set off a chain reaction in Giovanni's mind – he starts dwelling on what he could've done differently, replaying the accident in his head, and wondering if he's somehow to blame. Giovanni has become increasingly withdrawn since the accident. He avoids driving or being a passenger in vehicles, fearing another crash will happen at any moment. His self-blame rumination is all-consuming; he can't help but repeatedly blame himself for what happened, even though the other driver was clearly at fault. This maladaptive strategy only serves to reinforce his negative appraisals – Giovanni has come to believe that the accident occurred because of some inherent flaw in his character. As a result, Giovanni feels like he's constantly on edge, waiting for the next shoe to drop. He wakes up during the night to check if everything is okay, and unusual silence makes him feel like something ominous is lurking just out of sight. His difficulty concentrating has become a major issue – he can't focus on his work as a politician, and his relationships with colleagues and loved ones are starting to suffer. Giovanni's memories of the accident remain fragmented and difficult to put into words. When he tries to explain what happened, he gets stuck, unable to finish the story. The physical pain from that night still lingers, too – whenever the memory returns, Giovanni feels a sharp pang in his body. His negative appraisals have become a self-reinforcing cycle; he's convinced that others can see the accident written all over him, like some sort of invisible scar. As time passes, these maladaptive strategies only seem to intensify Giovanni's symptoms. He becomes more and more vigilant, always on the lookout for potential threats. This hypervigilance makes it hard for him to relax – even in the comfort of his own home, surrounded by loved ones. His wife has started noticing changes in him, too; she describes how he'll suddenly freeze up when driving or walking down the street. Giovanni knows something needs to change. He's starting to feel like he's losing himself to these negative appraisals and maladaptive strategies. The constant threat of danger has become overwhelming – it's as if his brain is constantly screaming at him to be on guard. His memories of the accident continue to haunt him, a constant reminder that he's somehow flawed. Giovanni has finally sought help because he can't shake off the feeling that he's trapped in this never-ending cycle of fear and self-doubt. He hopes therapy will give him tools to manage his symptoms and rebuild his sense of identity – one that isn't defined by the accident or his perceived shortcomings.

Eleanor Vance grew up in a quiet New England house where the air always seemed to hold its breath. Her caregiver’s moods were a shifting landscape; one moment he would read to her by the fireplace, the next he would snap over a misplaced book or an unanswered question. She remembered the afternoon he struck her after she spilled tea on the rug, his sudden lunge freezing her in the hallway. What terrified her most was not just the violence, but the way he would promise to make it right before turning cold again. Years later, standing alone with a male contractor in her kitchen, or attending a friend’s funeral in a quiet cemetery, the ground felt just as unstable. The uncertainty of how he would react, the solemn weight of grief, and the isolation with another man all carried the same invisible threat: that trust could vanish in an instant, leaving her exposed. As Eleanor matured, the house’s unpredictability rewired her nervous system. When a colleague raised his voice during a deadline review, or when a sudden knock came at her door, her body would brace before her mind could even register the context. She spent years trying to quiet the constant low hum of watchfulness, yet every new ambiguity in her schedule felt like a spark in a dry field. Encountering these moments pulled the past into sharp relief. The scene of the rug, his belt, and her own frozen posture surfaced with the clarity of slides projected onto her retinas, even when she found herself staring at a spreadsheet, unable to find words to explain why her chest tightened so suddenly. Confronted with these relentless reminders, Eleanor began to convince herself that she was fundamentally powerless to steer her own life, and that she would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. Over the decades, these internal shifts calcified into habits that reshaped her daily life. Working as a QA engineer required her to scrutinize systems for flaws, a task that mirrored her relentless search for safety. Yet her insistence on avoiding unscheduled meetings with male supervisors and her refusal to navigate cemeteries without a companion slowly isolated her at work. When she caught herself holding her breath during a vendor call, or when her shoulders locked at a partner’s quick shift in posture, the physical alarm never ceased to fuel her core beliefs. Each time her nerves flared without cause, Eleanor interpreted it as proof that the world remained fundamentally dangerous and that she would never be able to prevent harm from reaching her again. The memories of that childhood helplessness would not fade; instead, they would deepen her conviction that she had betrayed herself by surviving passively. She would sit in her study, certain that she would never forgive herself for the years she lost, and the shame of that inaction would instantly make the prospect of stepping outside feel like walking into a trap. For years, Eleanor managed her life by strictly controlling her environment, yet the more she restricted her movements, the heavier the invisible weight grew. When her husband gently suggested they attend his sister’s memorial service, her throat closed around the word yes. She had come to believe that any lapse in vigilance would invite the same helplessness she had known as a child, and that the memories of the abuse would only grow more vivid, leaving her emotionally hollow before the shock returned. The constant state of guard, the photographic intrusions, and the crushing belief that she was fundamentally unrescued wove together into a seamless circuit. She would wake at three in the morning, heart hammering, convinced that her body’s readiness for violence was the only evidence that danger was still waiting. This relentless feedback kept her trapped in the aftermath, until the sheer exhaustion of carrying the shame finally compelled her to sit across from a therapist. She did not know if she would ever forgive herself for the years she lost to fear, but she was hoping, against every instinct, to learn how to trust the ground beneath her feet again.

Mai was seventy-one when she finally agreed to speak in detail about what had happened, though the event itself still arrived in her mind with the force of something immediate. She had been living in the United States for decades, working as a lawyer, and had built a life that was orderly, demanding, and public. The assault occurred when she was alone and not expecting danger, and what stayed with her most was not only the violence itself but the humiliating way it was accompanied by the experience of being looked at sexually, as if she had been reduced to an object in someone else’s gaze. In the aftermath, she found that ordinary sounds could throw her back into the same tightened, alarmed state. A sudden noise behind her, a voice that sounded too close, or related sounds that resembled the sensory edges of the assault could make her shoulders jerk and her attention snap toward the source before she had fully registered what she was hearing. The reaction was bodily and instant, and she would feel her own heart pounding so hard that it seemed to fill her entire chest.

In the weeks that followed, Mai noticed that she no longer trusted her body in the way she once had. She had been the kind of person who relied on competence and composure, but now she was unsettled by the sudden surge of her own heartbeat, by the fear that her body could tip her into panic without warning, or that it might betray her in some other, less predictable way. She described this in practical terms, saying that when her heart raced she could not convince herself that she was safe, because the sensation itself felt like proof that something was wrong. At work, where she was still engaged with legal matters, she became acutely aware of time passing in meetings, on phone calls, and while waiting for documents or replies. If something took longer than expected, she immediately assumed something bad was happening. A delayed response from a client, a late arrival, or an unanswered call was enough to put her on edge, scanning through possibilities she knew were not always reasonable but could not dismiss. She had come to believe that she had to be on guard all the time, because danger could appear without warning and because waiting, for her, had become almost intolerable.

As the months went on, Mai also noticed how differently night felt from day. During daylight she could still move through her routines, but after dark she had much less sense of ease, and she found it harder to feel safe at night. The dimness of evening, the quiet of the house, and any unexpected sound in the dark seemed to enlarge her sense of vulnerability. She and her husband had shared their home for years, yet even there she remained watchful after sunset, listening longer than she used to before settling into bed, and being reluctant to relax fully once the house grew still. She had also become increasingly aware of the way other people’s looks affected her. If she sensed she was being looked at sexually, even briefly, she experienced an immediate tightening and discomfort that made her want to withdraw. What might once have been brushed off as a passing stare now felt loaded and exposing, as though being seen in that way carried the possibility of danger and humiliation.

Mai spoke about these experiences with a mixture of restraint and clear distress. She described having strong negative feelings that were hard to contain: fear, horror, anger, and shame all seemed to exist close together, and she did not experience them as fleeting. They could rise in ordinary moments, leaving her feeling suddenly flooded and unsettled, especially when one of her triggers appeared or when she was left alone with her thoughts. Over time, she had come to see the world as a dangerous place, and this conviction sat alongside her wish to continue functioning as she always had. As a lawyer, she had spent her life assessing risks and managing details, but now the everyday world felt less predictable and less trustworthy. She remained married and continued to carry herself with dignity, yet those close to her could see that she was more guarded, more alert to what might go wrong, and less able to dismiss the sense that she needed to watch everything around her.

What finally brought Mai to seek help was the accumulation of these moments: the pounding heart that startled her, the silences that made her imagine something bad was happening, the unease that settled over evenings, and the way reminders in public could make her feel exposed or unsafe. She did not want her life to keep narrowing around vigilance and fear. More than anything, she hoped to feel at home in her own body again, to move through day and night without constantly bracing for threat, and to reclaim some sense that the world could still contain ordinary safety.

Leila is a 45-year-old Middle Eastern woman who has been working as an auditor for over two decades. Her life took a dramatic turn several years ago when she was involved in a combat incident during her deployment to Iraq. The traumatic event she experienced has left lasting scars, both emotional and psychological. On that fateful day, Leila and her unit were ambushed by enemy forces in a remote desert region. The explosions rang out suddenly, and the ground shook violently as shrapnel and debris flew through the air. She remembers flashes of gunfire and the acrid smell of smoke mixed with cologne from one of her fellow soldiers who had been struck down. Leila managed to survive but the memory of that day remains fragmented and incomplete. There are parts of what happened she simply cannot recall, no matter how hard she tries. Since returning home, Leila has found herself waking up in cold sweats from nightmares, reliving those terrifying moments over and over again. The scent of a certain cologne can instantly transport her back to that traumatic event, filling her with intense fear and anxiety. Even the sound of an explosion or a loud bang triggers vivid flashbacks and overwhelming panic. Leila’s coping mechanisms have become increasingly rigid and restrictive. She often thinks about how life would be different if she had never been in that combat situation, engaging in counterfactual thinking as a way to cope with her distress. Open spaces where she feels vulnerable are particularly difficult for her; she now avoids such places entirely. Instead of feeling safe outdoors, Leila is constantly scanning her surroundings, looking behind her, and planning escape routes wherever she goes. Leila's sense of safety has shrunk significantly since the traumatic event. She only feels secure in a very limited number of places, mostly within the confines of her home or familiar buildings where she works as an auditor. Even then, she constantly checks to ensure that no one is following her and meticulously plans potential escape routes before feeling comfortable. The memories of the combat incident are fragmented and disjointed. Leila feels like she is only remembering parts of what happened, with significant gaps in her recollection. This incompleteness adds to her distress, as she struggles to piece together a coherent narrative from the disconnected fragments that surface unpredictably. Leila's negative appraisals about herself have also taken root since the trauma. She believes she should have been able to protect others and feels guilty for failing to do so. Additionally, Leila has come to see the event as somehow tied to her personal character, leading her to blame herself for what happened. Her body’s ongoing reactions of fear and hypervigilance further reinforce her belief that she is still in danger, even though she knows rationally that she is safe. Over time, these avoidance behaviors have strained Leila's relationships and impacted her work as an auditor. She has become increasingly isolated, avoiding social gatherings and professional networking events where open spaces or unfamiliar faces might trigger her anxiety. The constant need to check her surroundings and plan escape routes has also made it difficult for her to focus on her job tasks. What finally brought Leila to seek help was a particularly intense bout of nightmares followed by a debilitating panic attack at work, which forced her to take an extended leave of absence. She is most afraid that she will never truly feel safe again and that the trauma will continue to define who she is. However, she also hopes that with professional support, she can regain some sense of control over her life and learn strategies to manage her symptoms effectively. Leila’s journey towards healing involves confronting these fears step-by-step, understanding the fragmented nature of her memories, and gradually expanding her safe zones while reducing avoidance behaviors. Through therapy, Leila aims to process her trauma more fully and reclaim a greater sense of security in her daily life.

Mateo had always prided himself on the steadiness of his hands. For forty years as a surgeon, they had been his gift, moving with a calm, practiced precision that belied the life-or-death stakes beneath them. Now, at sixty-two, he found himself staring at them as if they belonged to a stranger, a fine tremor running through his fingers that had nothing to do with age. The shaking had started six months ago, on the day his son Daniel had been driving him home from the hospital. It was a Tuesday, the rain so heavy it blurred the world into a watercolour of grey and red tail-lights. They were talking about Daniel’s upcoming wedding when the screech of tires tore through the conversation. Mateo remembers the impact not as a single event, but as a series of brutal, sensory fragments: the sickening lurch of the car spinning, the explosive crack of the airbag deploying, and the rough, synthetic burn of its fabric scraping against his cheek.

In the weeks that followed, that moment refused to stay in the past. The memory would ambush him, not as a hazy recollection, but with a terrifying vividness that felt more real than the present moment. He would be scrubbing in for a procedure, the slightly coarse texture of the disposable gown under his fingers suddenly becoming the airbag against his skin, and the memory would slam into his mind. He’d see the spiderweb of shattered glass, smell the acrid chemical propellant, feel the crushing weight on his chest. It would force its way in, uninvited and overwhelming, and he would have to shove it back down before it could reach the worst part—the sight of Daniel, slumped and still against the steering wheel. He never let the memory get that far; he was certain that if he did, the horror would swallow him whole.

His life began to shrink, contracting around the effort to keep the memory at bay. The first thing to go was driving with his son. When Daniel would call, Mateo’s heart would hammer against his ribs, and he’d let the phone ring out, the sound of his son’s voice now a direct line to the accident. He told his wife it was better if they just met at restaurants, avoiding the intimacy of a shared car. Then he gave up his weekend tennis matches, the physical strain of lunging for a ball feeling too much like the body-wracking panic of the crash. The joy drained from his days. He stopped reading, stopped listening to music, stopped doing anything that required a quiet mind, because a quiet mind was an open invitation for the memory to intrude. He spent his evenings in a state of deliberate distraction, flipping through television channels, trying to outrun his own thoughts.

The world, once his domain, was now a landscape of hidden threats. A news report showing twisted metal on a highway shoulder would leave him breathless and sweating. At work, where he’d once found purpose, he now felt a constant, humming anxiety. During a recent cholecystectomy, his hand had frozen over the patient. The memory had surged—the airbag, the smell, the sudden, violent stop—and for a full five seconds, the operating theatre had vanished. He could only hear the frantic beat of his own heart. His assistant had to murmur his name twice before the present snapped back into focus. He managed to finish the surgery, but the incident terrified him. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally broken, that the calm, competent man he had been was gone forever, replaced by this fragile, frightened shell.

It was his wife, Elena, who finally insisted he seek help. She found him one evening standing stiffly in the living room, his face pale, after a car backfired on their street. "I can't watch you disappear, Mateo," she had said, her voice soft but firm. "You are still here, but you are not with me." He is here now because he knows she is right. He is terrified of losing his career, the one part of his identity he thought was unshakable. But what frightens him most is the growing distance he feels from the people he loves, a chasm carved out by a single, terrible moment that he cannot seem to leave behind.

Jacob, a 34-year-old school counselor, had always been someone who thrived on helping others, but his life took a devastating turn when an accident changed everything. During a school field trip, he had been responsible for supervising a group of children when one of them, distracted by a game, collided with a metal fence. Jacob's hasty reaction to pull the child back resulted in a serious injury, leaving him paralyzed by guilt. The aftermath of that day haunted him relentlessly; he could still hear the echoes of the child's cries and see the look of sheer terror on their face. These vivid memories would often flood back with a jolt whenever he encountered certain triggers, such as seeing children playing in the park or hearing an ambulance siren, instantly transporting him to the scene of the accident. Each time he encountered reminders of that event, from the smell of antiseptic lingering in medical offices to the distant sirens of police cars, sharp waves of anxiety would wash over him, triggering a cascade of distressing thoughts and memories. In those moments, Jacob found himself increasingly drawn to filling his time with work tasks, believing that if he stayed busy, he could escape the grip of those overwhelming feelings that threatened to pull him under. In those moments, Jacob instinctively sought to fill his time with meetings and tasks at work, believing that staying busy would shield him from the overwhelming guilt and anxiety that surged at the thought of the accident. But this constant busyness only led to more triggers; he would find himself avoiding certain topics in meetings, fearing that any mention of safety protocols would remind him of the child's injury, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy. In the months that followed, Jacob found himself employing various coping strategies to keep his mind occupied, avoiding any moments of stillness that might allow the horrific memory to surface. He would stay busy at work, filling his days with meetings and responsibilities, yet even in those moments, he could feel the faint tug of his trauma. However, this avoidance strategy only kept the memories of the accident fresh and vivid in his mind, as he found that the more he tried to ignore them, the more they seemed to resurface with even greater intensity. The busy schedule he maintained seemed to be a necessary shield against the emotional turmoil, but it only served to reinforce his belief that he was fragile and incapable of coping. Each time Jacob leaned on his coping mechanisms, he felt a deepening conviction that he could not handle life's challenges without them, which further entrenched his sense of fragility and inadequacy. The scent of antiseptic would take him back to the hospital where the child was treated, and he'd feel the panic rise in his chest. The panic triggered by these reminders often led Jacob to keep himself constantly busy at work, filling his days with meetings and responsibilities to avoid confronting the memories that threatened to surface. However, this constant busyness also served to reinforce his belief that he was fragile and incapable of coping, as he found himself relying on distractions rather than confronting his feelings head-on. As memories flooded his mind, he sometimes felt as if the event was happening all over again, the guilt and shame consuming him anew. It was as if he had been thrust back into that moment, unable to find the words to articulate the depth of his sorrow and regret. Jacob's self-doubt morphed into an ever-present shadow, making him question his ability to make the right decisions. This deep-seated belief that he had made a grave mistake led him to avoid challenging situations, convinced that he would only prove his inadequacy again. His negative appraisals became self-fulfilling prophecies, as he rationalized that steering clear of difficult conversations was essential to avoid reaffirming his belief that he was unworthy of success and respect. Each time he chose to sidestep a difficult conversation or a decision, he felt a surge of guilt that confirmed his negative self-image, intensifying his fear of further failure. Each time he chose to avoid taking initiative, it reinforced his internal narrative that he was unworthy and incapable, solidifying his sense of failure in his own mind. His conviction that he was unworthy of making decisions often led him to avoid taking initiative, as he feared that any misstep would only reinforce his sense of failure. He felt as though his life had been irrevocably destroyed by that single moment of misjudgment. This pervasive sense of blame—believing that he had caused the injury because of his actions—only served to intensify his avoidance of the memories and situations associated with the accident. As he navigated his daily life, even the most innocuous encounters—a call from a parent or a discussion about student safety—would trigger a wave of anxiety, reminding him of his perceived failure and reinforcing his need to withdraw. He avoided places where he might run into police officers or area hospitals, as their presence could easily trigger another wave of guilt and anxiety. This avoidance created a pattern where the very act of steering clear of these reminders only broadened his landscape of fear, as he felt increasingly trapped by the reminders he had constructed around himself. This avoidance became a map of his fear, with every location he bypassed reinforcing his belief that the world was filled with reminders of his failure and that confronting them was too dangerous to consider. With each place he avoided, he felt a growing sense of fragility, as though needing to escape these reminders confirmed that he was incapable of facing the reality of his past. He was terrified of the judgment he might face, both from the authorities and from himself, reinforcing a cycle of avoidance that left him feeling increasingly isolated. In his mind, each avoidance behavior became a testament to his belief that he was incapable of handling the scrutiny that would inevitably come if he were to confront his trauma. This fear of judgment turned even innocuous interactions, like a parent’s inquiry about a child’s safety, into triggers for anxiety, making him retreat further into himself. In the throes of his trauma, Jacob’s sleep became a battleground. Each night, he lay awake, caught between the need to remain vigilant and the overwhelming fatigue that settled in. The fear of those memories rising to the surface only intensified his sense of threat, making sleep feel like a dangerous gamble that could transport him back to the scene of the accident at any moment. Each time he opted to stay awake instead of allowing himself to relax, it only served to heighten his perception of danger, as he had never allowed himself the chance to discover that his memories could be managed rather than overwhelming. The fear of falling asleep was palpable; he worried that if he closed his eyes, the memories would come rushing back with full force, accompanied by the visceral sensations of horror and despair. Each time those memories emerged, they carried with them a sense of immediate danger, as if the trauma were still unfolding, amplifying his fear and keeping him in a constant state of vigilance. He would lie awake at night, convincing himself that if he just stayed alert, he could protect himself from reliving the trauma, but this only deepened his exhaustion and sense of dread, strengthening his belief that he was trapped in a terrifying cycle. Each time he was reminded of the accident, the threat felt immediate and physical, leading him to stay awake, believing that vigilance was the only way to protect himself from reliving the trauma. As he struggled to drift into sleep, he was haunted by a relentless replay of the accident, which not only served as a reminder of his failure but also magnified his emotional turmoil. The effort to suppress these memories only seemed to strengthen their hold on him, as if his avoidance was a signal to his mind that the threat of reliving that day was still very real. In trying to keep his trauma at bay, Jacob inadvertently reinforced the notion that his memories were too dangerous to confront, deepening his fear of facing them head-on. The more he tried to push the memories away, the more they loomed large in his mind, reinforcing his belief that he was eternally trapped in a cycle of pain and failure. The sense of physical reactivity became a constant companion, with his heart racing and palms clammy whenever he was reminded of that fateful day. In his attempts to escape the grip of his memories, Jacob had fallen into a pattern of mental distraction—filling his mind with trivial concerns to stave off the pain that lingered beneath the surface. This strategy, however, only perpetuated his negative appraisals. Each time he successfully distracted himself, he felt a fleeting sense of relief, but it was always followed by a deeper sense of self-blame and the nagging thought that he was simply delaying the inevitable confrontation with his trauma. He was aware that his methods were not solving anything; yet, the fear of facing the full weight of his past kept him ensnared in this cycle of avoidance. This cycle only deepened his negative appraisals, making him believe that his inability to confront his trauma confirmed he was fragile and incapable of moving past it. Eventually, Jacob realized that he could no longer live in this state of turmoil. His relationships began to suffer, particularly with his wife, who felt the emotional distance growing between them. This distancing was fueled by his belief that he was unworthy of love and support, leading him to avoid discussing his feelings and fears, which only exacerbated the misunderstandings between them. The guilt and shame kept him from being present, leading to arguments and misunderstandings that deepened his isolation. While he had tried to shield his loved ones from his pain, he found that the very act of avoidance had alienated him from their support. His reluctance to engage in open conversations about his feelings only deepened his isolation, as he began to internalize the idea that he was unworthy of their love and understanding. This pattern of avoidance further entrenched his belief that he was incapable of handling the emotional weight of his trauma, leading him to feel even more inadequate and alone. These intense feelings would often lead him to engage in avoidance strategies, as he rationalized that steering clear of conversations about the accident or the child would prevent him from experiencing the depth of those emotions again. Ultimately, it was the painful realization that he was not only struggling to help himself but also failing to be the partner and counselor he aspired to be that pushed Jacob to seek help. He recognized that his pattern of avoidance had begun to define his life, and he feared that each act of evasion was a confirmation of his belief that he was unfit for both love and responsibility. He feared that his continued avoidance and reliance on distractions would only solidify the notion that he was less capable than others, and he desperately wanted to break free from this cycle before it consumed him entirely. Each act of avoidance seemed to confirm his fragile self-image, as if his inability to confront his trauma was evidence that he truly was incapable of handling his emotions. He feared that if he didn’t act soon, he would be trapped in this cycle of guilt and shame forever, losing not just himself but also the connection to those he loved. He hoped to regain a sense of peace and reconnect with those he loved, fearing that if he didn’t act soon, he might lose everything he once held dear. Every moment spent avoiding his feelings felt like a step toward isolation, reinforcing his belief that he was unworthy of support and connection from those he cared about. Each time he avoided discussing his feelings or the accident, he felt a growing sense of inadequacy, as if his inability to confront his trauma confirmed that he was less capable than others.

Ali is a 34-year-old Middle Eastern man married to his high school sweetheart, Leila. He works as a publisher in New York City and has been struggling with intrusive thoughts and feelings since a traumatic event that occurred six months ago. On a sunny afternoon, while walking home from work, Ali witnessed an armed assailant brutally attack Leila near their apartment building. Though she survived, the physical and psychological toll on both of them was immense. The trauma left deep scars in Ali’s mind. He now experiences fragmented memories of the event that come to him as disconnected pieces rather than a coherent narrative. Often, he hears voices in his head, echoing the terrifying sounds from that day—screams and the metallic clatter of weapons. These auditory intrusions are particularly vivid when he feels very tired or exhausted, which happens frequently since the attack due to his disrupted sleep patterns. Ali’s triggers have become potent reminders of that harrowing day. The vulnerability associated with being naked is a constant fear for him; he worries about Leila’s safety whenever she goes out alone and feels an overwhelming sense of responsibility to protect her. Public transport, especially riding the bus, has become unbearable due to his heightened anxiety. He fears crowded spaces where potential threats are harder to predict. His threat monitoring behaviors are pervasive. Ali constantly studies people's faces and body language for signs of danger, always on edge, scanning environments for any potential weapons or dangerous objects. This hyper-vigilance extends to his avoidance of unfamiliar places; he feels a profound sense of unease in new settings where assessing the level of risk is challenging. These behaviors have taken a toll on Ali’s life and work. His daily commute has become a source of immense stress, leading him to frequently arrive at the office exhausted. This fatigue often impacts his productivity and focus during meetings. He has also started avoiding social gatherings that require traveling or being in unfamiliar locations. Over time, this avoidance has strained his relationships with colleagues and friends who no longer understand why he is so withdrawn. Ali’s interactions with Leila have been profoundly affected as well. While he wants to support her recovery, his own anxiety often leads him to overcompensate by monitoring every aspect of her life, which can feel suffocating for her. The constant replaying of the traumatic event in his mind makes it difficult for Ali to engage fully with their daily lives or plan for the future. What finally brought Ali to seek help was a realization that these symptoms were worsening and affecting both his professional and personal relationships. He is most afraid of losing control, of being unable to protect Leila or maintain his role as a supportive husband and colleague. Yet, he also harbors hope that with the right support, he can regain some semblance of normalcy in his life. Ali’s journey towards healing is one of acknowledging the profound impact of trauma on his daily existence and recognizing the need for professional guidance to navigate these challenges.

**Vignette: Te Ao — Age 75**

Te Ao grew up on a small island in French Polynesia, the youngest of six children in a family that measured time by tides and seasons. They came to New Zealand in their thirties, built a career in financial analysis, raised a family, and buried a spouse. At seventy-five, they still go into the office three days a week — a point of pride, a reason to get dressed, a structure that keeps the days from blurring into one another. Their colleagues know them as meticulous, composed, and quietly formidable. What they do not know is what happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening, when Te Ao was raped by a man they had trusted — a neighbor of twelve years who had helped carry groceries and attended their spouse's funeral.

The attack happened in Te Ao's own kitchen, in the house they have lived in for over two decades. It lasted less than twenty minutes. It has not stopped since.

In the weeks that followed, Te Ao told no one. Shame is not quite the right word for what they carried — it was more like a contamination, a sense that the house, the kitchen, the body they had inhabited for seventy-five years had all become foreign territory. They scrubbed the floor tiles until the grout turned white. They stopped cooking. They began eating crackers and tinned fish at their desk, finding reasons to stay at the office until dark rather than return home before the streetlights came on.

Sleep, when it comes at all, comes badly. Te Ao wakes at two or three in the morning with their heart hammering, certain that someone is in the house. They check the locks — sometimes three or four times — before sitting in the hallway with the lights on, unable to explain to themselves why the bedroom feels more dangerous than the corridor. The dreams are not always explicit. Sometimes it is simply the smell of his aftershave, arriving without context, and they wake gasping with a grief that has no clean edges.

At work, Te Ao functions. The spreadsheets are precise, the risk assessments thorough. But there are moments — a colleague standing too close, a hand placed briefly on their shoulder, a man laughing too loudly in the break room — when something seizes in their chest and the numbers on the screen stop making sense. They have learned to excuse themselves to the bathroom, to run cold water over their wrists, to wait for the sensation to pass. They have become expert at managing what is visible.

What is harder to manage is the flatness. Te Ao describes looking at photographs of their late spouse and feeling nothing — not grief, not warmth, just a kind of grey distance, as though the person in the photographs lived someone else's life. They used to call their eldest daughter every Sunday. Now the calls come less frequently, and when they do, Te Ao finds themselves saying they are fine, they are tired, they are busy — the words arriving automatically, a rehearsed performance of a person still intact.

There is a particular quality to the hypervigilance that Te Ao finds hardest to articulate. It is not fear exactly, they say. It is more like a permanent readiness, a body that has decided the world requires constant monitoring. They scan every room they enter. They sit with their back to walls. On the bus, they count the exits. They have stopped attending the community group at the marae they have belonged to for thirty years, finding the proximity of other bodies unbearable in ways they cannot justify to themselves or anyone else.

What brought Te Ao to therapy was not the sleeplessness or the hypervigilance or even the dreams. It was a moment at their desk last month when they realized they could not remember what it felt like to want anything — not a meal, not a conversation, not a morning. They stared at the quarterly report in front of them and thought, with a clarity that frightened them: *I used to be someone who was here.*

Clarence, at 79, carried the echoes of a childhood memory that had never truly settled. He was just a boy, perhaps seven or eight, when the world fractured around him. He remembered the thick, humid air of a summer evening, the scent of overgrown honeysuckle heavy in the air, mixed with something sharp and acrid – cheap whiskey. He’d been playing near the old, ramshackle shed in their backyard, partially hidden by a thicket of wild bushes, when the shouting started. His parents’ voices, usually a comforting backdrop, turned harsh, punctuated by the clatter of something breaking inside the house. Then, a sharp, guttural cry, followed by a violent *thud* that shook the very ground under his small feet. The memory then blurred, a frantic scramble of fear and confusion, culminating in the deafening *SLAM* of the back door, a sound that reverberated through his bones, sealing the terror inside him.

For decades, the memory of that evening remained an elusive, shape-shifting thing. When Clarence tried to deliberately recall the full sequence, the details seemed to slip away, leaving him with disconnected, fragmented pieces that never quite formed a coherent picture. Yet, the emotional intensity of the event could return with a sudden, overwhelming force, a wave of raw fear and helplessness washing over him without any accompanying image or clear recollection of what had truly happened.

These feelings were often sparked by specific sensory cues. The smell of alcohol, even a faint whiff from a colleague’s breath or a cleaning product, could send a shiver down his spine, bringing with it that old, suffocating dread. Auditory triggers were particularly potent in his work as a warehouse worker. The sudden, jarring clang of a metal loading dock door slamming shut, or the sharp crack of a pallet falling, could instantly transport him back, his heart pounding in his chest, a cold sweat breaking out on his brow. Even being in a natural environment, particularly one with overgrown foliage or a certain quiet stillness reminiscent of that backyard, could make him feel profoundly uneasy, a sense of impending danger lurking just beyond his sight.

To cope with these surges of distress, Clarence had developed a deeply ingrained set of strategies. He found solace in the numbing comfort of alcohol, a habit that had grown stronger over the years, a way to quiet the internal clamour. He often had a small flask in his locker, reaching for it after a particularly jarring incident at work, or simply to take the edge off the evening. He also found that conflict, strangely, could be a potent distraction. He’d often pick arguments with co-workers about inventory discrepancies or the best way to stack boxes, creating a minor drama that kept his mind occupied, diverting it from the deeper, more unsettling feelings. He’d even find himself instigating debates at the local community center, anything to keep the conversational pot stirred.

Perhaps the most significant change in Clarence’s life was his relentless pursuit of company. He simply could not bear to be alone with his thoughts. After his shift at the warehouse, he’d linger, chatting with younger colleagues, offering unsolicited advice, or insisting on helping with tasks that weren’t his. If he wasn’t at work, he was at the senior center, playing cards, or calling friends, sometimes late into the night. His ex-wife had often complained about his inability to just "be present" and his constant need for external stimulation, a dynamic that ultimately contributed to their divorce years ago. He had come to believe that if he allowed himself a moment of quiet solitude, the fragmented memories would coalesce into something unbearable, something that would finally break him.

Recently, however, the strategies felt less effective. The hangovers were worse, the arguments more draining, and even surrounded by people, a profound loneliness began to seep in. A particularly strong trigger at the warehouse—a large metal door slamming shut just as a new shipment of sanitiser, reeking of alcohol, was unloaded—had left him trembling and disoriented for the better part of an hour. It was a wake-up call. He was tired, bone-weary of the constant vigilance, the endless seeking of distraction. What frightened him most was the thought of facing the full, unvarnished truth of that childhood day, but what terrified him more was the prospect of living out his remaining years perpetually running from it. It was this creeping exhaustion and the fear of a lonely, haunted old age that finally led Clarence to seek help, hoping there was still a way to find some peace.

Rohan, a 26-year-old editor, found himself at a crossroads, his once vibrant life with his wife now shadowed by an pervasive sense of dread that had steadily tightened its grip since an incident with the police several months prior. He had been walking home late one evening, lost in thought after a long day at the publishing house, when he was suddenly cornered and roughly apprehended by officers who mistook him for a suspect in a nearby altercation. Pushed hard against a cold, grimy brick wall, his arms twisted behind his back, Rohan remembered the biting chill seeping into his skin. A female officer, her voice sharp and dismissive, had interrogated him, her presence dominating the terrifying encounter. He recalled feeling an eerie detachment, as if watching the scene unfold from a distance, completely powerless. He was held for hours in a small, frigid room, the stale air thick with the faint metallic scent of disinfectant, before being released without charge, the experience leaving an indelible mark.

In the months that followed, Rohan’s world began to shrink. The specific temperature on his skin, even a slight chill in his air-conditioned office, could send a jolt of alarm through him, instantly reminding him of the cold wall and the cell. These tactile triggers, often innocuous, would often plunge him into a profound self-doubt, where he would ruminate on how his reactions since the event showed that he was a lousy coper, unable to handle even minor discomfort without spiraling. Similarly, being alone with women, particularly in quiet or confined spaces like a meeting room with a female colleague, became a potent trigger, bringing back the intimidating presence of the officer. This, too, fed his growing conviction that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that danger lurked in every corner.

His escalating negative appraisals profoundly affected his inner world. Because he had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore, his mind would invariably drift to the traumatic memory, not as a fleeting thought but as an immersive experience. When these memories came to mind, he would feel his body was in the same position as when the frightening event occurred, a visceral reenactment that left him gasping for breath and drenched in sweat. This physical reliving of the trauma, combined with an overwhelming grief on recall, only served to strengthen his appraisal that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. The sheer weight of the memory, bringing with it the grief and the unsettling feeling of his body being constrained, often confirmed his deepest fears about the futility of his existence.

This cycle was self-reinforcing. His deep-seated belief that nothing good could happen to him anymore made him hypervigilant, constantly scanning his environment, unconsciously seeking confirmation of his fears. This meant he was exquisitely sensitive to potential triggers, like the faintest drop in temperature in his office or the presence of a lone female colleague, which would then confirm his negative appraisals. When he thought about the frightening event, he would sometimes experience olfactory recall, catching a phantom whiff of the metallic disinfectant he smelt in the holding room. The sudden, vivid sensory experience of this memory made him acutely aware of any similar smells in his environment, turning them into potent triggers that would instantly transport him back to the trauma.

Rohan’s work as an editor, which once brought him immense satisfaction, now felt like a constant battle. He found himself avoiding collaborative projects, especially those requiring one-on-one meetings with female authors or colleagues, damaging his professional reputation. His detachment, initially a coping mechanism during the trauma, now resurfaced as a dissociative feeling whenever he was stressed or triggered, making him feel unreal and further isolating him from his wife and his once-cherished routines. The constant internal struggle, the belief that he was a lousy coper and that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, had eroded his enthusiasm, making him a shadow of his former self. It was this creeping despair, the feeling of a life slowly draining of color and purpose, that finally compelled Rohan to seek help, hoping to reclaim some semblance of the future he once envisioned.

She is 31, a South Eastern Asian woman who works as a journalist, and when she tells the story now, she does it the way she has learned to do many difficult things in her job: in sequence, with details, as if getting the facts right might somehow contain what happened. Before her life split into before and after, she is married, busy, and often tired in the ordinary way. She and her younger brother text almost every day. He sends her voice notes full of jokes, links to strange local news stories, and reminders that she works too hard. Even after her divorce, when her life feels less anchored, he is the person she still calls without thinking.

The call about his death comes on a weekday while she is at the newsroom, editing a piece under deadline. A relative’s number flashes on her phone, and she ignores it at first, then answers on the third try with irritation already in her voice. She remembers the sound that comes through the line before she understands the words: screaming, confusion, someone saying there has been an accident, someone else saying he is gone. She keeps asking, “What hospital?” because her mind cannot make room for death until she has ruled out rescue. She hears herself speaking sharply, almost professionally, demanding names, times, locations. Later she feels ashamed of that tone, but at the time it is the only way she can remain upright.

In the first days after, she moves as if assigned a role she must perform. She books travel, speaks to police, answers relatives, helps arrange the funeral. People praise her for being strong. She hates hearing it. At night she sees images she never witnessed: her brother alone, frightened, calling for help. She tries to replace them with real memories of him, but the imagined final moments intrude with a force that feels violent. She sleeps in fragments, waking with her heart pounding, disoriented and soaked in sweat. Sometimes she jolts awake hearing her phone ring, only to realize the room is silent.

When she returns to work, she expects routine to steady her. Instead, journalism becomes another place where grief ambushes her. Sirens in the street make her freeze at her desk. Breaking-news alerts send a shock through her body before she even reads them. She is assigned a story about a fatal road accident and feels her throat close while interviewing a witness. She keeps her notebook open and her face composed, but afterward she locks herself in the bathroom and vomits. From then on, she starts swapping assignments whenever she can, pretending she is overloaded or already committed. She tells colleagues she is focusing on political reporting now, but privately she is trying to avoid any mention of sudden death, hospitals, emergency responders, mourning families.

Outside work, her world narrows. She stops answering friends who say she needs to get out of the apartment. She cannot bear the bright, casual cruelty of normal conversation. If someone complains about a sibling, she goes cold and distant. Family gatherings become unbearable because every meal carries the shape of his absence. She watches her mother’s face for signs of fresh collapse and feels responsible for holding everyone together, yet she resents them too, especially when they ask her to retell what officials said. She has memorized every fact around his death and returns to them compulsively, reading old messages, checking timelines, scrolling through photographs late into the night until dawn light enters the room.

Her divorce, once a painful but manageable loss, now takes on a different meaning. She begins to think everyone leaves suddenly, either by choice or by force. She no longer trusts good moments. If she laughs with a colleague over coffee, a thought arrives immediately after: this can disappear in a second. She startles when people touch her unexpectedly. She sits near exits in restaurants and scans crowds without deciding to. On public transport she studies strangers’ faces, bracing for bad news that has not yet happened. She says she feels “on assignment” all the time, as though some part of her is permanently gathering evidence against safety.

There are stretches when she feels almost nothing. She speaks, writes, files stories, pays bills, and answers emails with mechanical competence, then goes home and sits in the dark scrolling through her brother’s old voice notes. She has not deleted his number. Sometimes she opens the chat window just to see his name at the top of the screen. She still expects, in some irrational corner of herself, that a new message will arrive.

Now, months later, she looks composed to most people. She is productive enough to pass at work and articulate enough to explain what happened. But her life is organized around avoidance, vigilance, and the exhausting effort to outrun images that return uninvited. She says the world no longer feels tragic in a philosophical sense; it feels actively unsafe, intimate in its danger. The hardest part, she says, is that she used to believe that if she paid close attention, she could understand events and tell them clearly. Her brother’s death has broken that faith. She is left with facts, and none of them make him less gone.

The first time Tariq realized he was being watched, it happened on a Tuesday evening outside the bus stop near his apartment. He had just stepped out of a late shift at the design studio, his canvas bag heavy with sketchbooks and a prototype tablet. A silver sedan had idled too long at the curb, its windows fogged despite the crisp air. He told himself it was nothing until the next week, when he found his studio locker slightly ajar, his personal charger missing, and a single folded note tucked inside that read, I know how you work. From that moment, the ordinary rhythm of his days fractured. He began replaying the weeks before it happened, searching for the exact moment his own behavior had invited the intrusion. He was certain the event happened because of the way he acted, convinced that if he had not posted his project milestones on his public portfolio or replied to that initial message from a stranger’s account, the whole thing would have stopped. The guilt settled in his chest like a stone; he blamed himself for the way he acted, parsing every past choice as a mistake that had left him exposed. By month two, Tariq’s apartment had become a series of mental checkpoints. He checked the deadbolt three times before bed, not out of habit, but because he had come to believe the world was a dangerous place where safety could vanish without warning. He told himself he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, and that logic dictated every movement. When a delivery driver in a navy jacket walked past his window, Tariq’s breath would catch, his hand instinctively tightening around his coffee mug. The memory of the silver sedan still surfaced unbidden whenever a car idled nearby, his vision tunneling just enough to make him step back from the door. He stopped taking the route he used before, taking longer paths through well-lit corridors just to avoid the blind corners. Friends noticed the distance, but Tariq didn’t explain that his fear wasn’t about them—it was about the unpredictable way threats always seemed to arrive from places he thought were safe. His job as a UX designer, once a source of creative flow, became a landscape of quiet avoidance. He worked in an open-plan studio on the fourth floor, surrounded by glass walls and shared screens. During a late-week critique, when a colleague tapped him on the shoulder to show a wireframe, Tariq flinched so hard his keyboard clacked loudly across the desk. He had started leaving his phone on airplane mode during work hours, dismissing calls with quick texts. What frightened him most was the thought that his digital trail could still be visible, that every screen share or cloud upload might be leaving another door open.
