She notices her husband growing frustrated at her avoidance of evening conversations, her projects slipping behind schedule, and her own anxiety becoming a constant companion. She fears that if she does not break this loop, she will become permanently trapped in a state where she feels alone and unrecognizable, a stranger to the architect she once was. She hopes to regain control over her thoughts, to quiet the false alarms, and to find a way to let the memory of the night fade into the background rather than dominate her present life.

John, a 69-year-old widowed financial analyst, had always been a man of routine and precision. His life was marked by stability until the day his wife, Mary, passed away suddenly from a heart attack. The memory of that fateful evening remained seared in his mind—a vivid snapshot of the ambulance sirens wailing into the night, the paramedics rushing in and out of their home, and the finality of the hospital's sterile walls as they confirmed her passing. In the months following Mary’s death, John found himself increasingly triggered by loss themes. Simple conversations at work about retirement plans or family events would send his mind spiraling back to that night. The sight of a funeral procession on the way to his office or the mention of a colleague's recent bereavement would suddenly bring the memory flooding back. These intrusive thoughts were not just memories; they were visceral, bringing with them a wave of intense negative emotions—fear, horror, and an overwhelming sense of guilt for not being able to save her. Each trigger seemed to amplify his physical reactivity, causing his heart to race and his hands to tremble as if he were reliving the trauma. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, John began to numb himself emotionally. He threw himself into work, staying late at the office and avoiding any social gatherings that might remind him of Mary. When a coworker suggested they visit a local cemetery on a Sunday afternoon to pay respects to a mutual friend’s loved one, John declined, citing an urgent project deadline. The thought of being in a place associated with loss was too much to bear. He also found himself suppressing thoughts of the trauma, often catching himself mid-thought and quickly redirecting his mind to work-related tasks. John’s emotional numbing and avoidance behaviors only served to heighten his sensitivity to triggers. By avoiding grief reminders, he inadvertently created an environment where even the smallest cues could set off a chain reaction. A casual mention of a lost pet in a news article or a passing comment about someone moving away would send him into a spiral of negative emotions. The more he tried to suppress these thoughts, the stronger they became, leading to increased irritability and angry outbursts at home and work. One particularly difficult day, John’s manager approached him with concerns about his recent performance. The stress of constantly managing triggers and suppressing thoughts had taken its toll, affecting his concentration and decision-making skills. This feedback was a turning point for John. Realizing that his maladaptive strategies were not only failing to alleviate his suffering but also impacting his professional life, he finally decided to seek help. John’s current state is one of deep ambivalence. On one hand, he is afraid that therapy will force him to confront the very memories and emotions he has been trying so hard to avoid. On the other hand, he is desperate for a way to break the cycle of triggers, negative emotions, and maladaptive coping mechanisms that have dominated his life since Mary’s passing. He hopes that with professional support, he can find a path forward—one where the memory of his beloved wife does not continue to overshadow every aspect of his daily existence.

Gerald Mast, a 73-year-old divorced journalist of Canadian-American descent, presented for an intake assessment with a PCL-5 score of 74, indicating severe posttraumatic stress. Gerald spent the better part of four decades covering industrial and environmental disasters across North America, and it was during the coverage of a catastrophic chemical plant explosion in the Gulf Coast region — one he witnessed at close range — that his current difficulties began. He had been embedded with an emergency response team when a secondary detonation tore through a processing unit without warning. The concussive force, the acrid chemical taste that coated his mouth and throat for hours afterward, and the sight of bodies and wreckage captured in his own camera's viewfinder before the lens shattered — these sensory fragments became the fault lines of what followed. The explosion's defining quality was its absolute unpredictability: no alarm, no escalation, simply ordinary industrial noise and then annihilation.

In the months that followed, Gerald found that the world had reorganised itself around potential detonations. Unpredictable situations — a car backfiring, a fire drill at the newspaper office, a colleague appearing suddenly in a doorway — sent him into a state of hyperscanning that he could not consciously override. He began listening for sounds of entry at his apartment door each night, cataloguing the weight of objects on nearby tables, noting in restaurants and newsrooms alike which items could be wielded as weapons. He could not relax even in demonstrably safe environments; his nervous system, he felt, had simply stopped believing in safety as a category. These triggers fed directly into his hypervigilant monitoring, so that the moment something unpredictable occurred, his threat system was already primed and his body locked — he would freeze completely, unable to speak or move, sometimes for a full minute.

Gerald had come to believe that thinking about the explosion would undo him entirely. He was certain that if he allowed the memory full purchase, something in him would simply collapse and not recover. This appraisal — that the event was too extreme to be metabolised — drove him toward a set of strategies that provided momentary relief but slowly narrowed his life. He began sitting with his back against the wall in every room he entered, a habit that began as vigilance and calcified into compulsion. He spent money impulsively: books he would not read, equipment he did not need, online purchases made at two in the morning when the listening for sounds at the door became unbearable. These strategies, however, kept his attention perpetually organised around threat. The very act of scanning the room from his wall-backed position meant he was always looking for what might go wrong, which meant the triggers — a photograph of industrial wreckage in a magazine, an unexpected change in plan — arrived with his nervous system already at full alert.

The memory itself had a quality Gerald described as cinematic and unreal simultaneously: it played on a loop, yet he could barely believe it had happened to him. When it surfaced — and the hypervigilant state reliably surfaced it, as did the chemical taste that occasionally returned when he ate certain preserved foods — he did not feel as though he were remembering; he felt as though he were still inside the moment, still tasting the chemical air, still watching through a cracked viewfinder. The reliving experience in turn deepened his certainty that the event was beyond processing, reinforcing his belief that engagement with the memory would destroy him, which sent him back toward spending, freezing, and wall-sitting — all of which kept the threat system running hot, which kept the memory accessible, which confirmed the appraisal.

Gerald had stopped pitching stories. He had stopped attending the editorial meetings he once led. He described his emotional life as flat and foreign — he was certain he would never feel genuine engagement again, that nothing in his remaining years would carry meaning. It was his editor, a woman who had known him for twenty years, who told him plainly that she was frightened for him. That conversation, and the quiet shame of recognising how much had been lost, finally brought him to seek help. What he feared most was that the clinician would confirm what he already suspected: that he had waited too long, and that the man who had once run toward disaster to bear witness was now simply one of its casualties.

# Vignette: Luka, Age 24

Luka grew up in a close-knit Samoan family in South Auckland, the eldest of four siblings, and the first in his family to complete a university degree. He finished his pharmacy qualifications at twenty-two, proud and quietly relieved that he could finally give something back to his parents, who had sacrificed so much to get him there. For a while, life felt like it was moving in the right direction.

Fourteen months ago, Luka's younger brother Sione, then seventeen, was struck by a car while crossing a road near their home on a Friday evening. Luka was the one who received the phone call. He arrived at the scene before the ambulance did. He remembers the way the streetlight caught the wet road, and the sound his mother made when she pulled up seconds after him. He held Sione's hand and spoke to him, not knowing whether his brother could hear him, watching his chest rise and fall in a way that looked wrong. Sione survived but sustained a severe traumatic brain injury. He spent three months in hospital and was discharged to home care requiring daily support for basic tasks he once did without thinking. The Sione who came home is, in Luka's words, "the same face, but someone different inside."

In the weeks after the accident, Luka returned to work at the community pharmacy where he had been building his career. He told himself that staying busy was the right thing to do. His colleagues noticed he was quieter than usual but said nothing. Luka found himself reading medication labels three and four times before dispensing, terrified of making an error, convinced that one small mistake would destroy someone else's life the way one inattentive driver had altered his family's. The confidence he had felt in his clinical judgment had simply vanished.

At night, Luka lies awake replaying the scene at the roadside. He does not choose to think about it — it arrives on its own, vivid and physical, as though he is kneeling on that wet asphalt again. He wakes from sleep with his heart pounding, sometimes unsure for a moment where he is. He has stopped driving past that intersection entirely, adding fifteen minutes to his commute each day without explaining why to anyone. He avoids the hospital where Sione was treated, even when visiting Sione would require passing through that part of the building.

What troubles Luka most, and what he finds hardest to say aloud, is the guilt. He was the eldest. He was the one who was supposed to protect the family. Rationally, he knows he was not there when the accident happened and could not have prevented it. But rationality does not seem to reach whatever part of him has decided otherwise. He finds himself unable to feel much pleasure in things he once loved — rugby on the weekend, cooking with his mother, the easy banter with his workmates. He describes feeling like he is watching his own life through glass.

Luka lives at home, which means he sees Sione every day. He helps with his brother's care on weekends, feeding him, sitting with him, sometimes reading to him. He says this feels like the only thing that makes sense right now, the only place his guilt has somewhere to go. But it also means he cannot step back from the trauma, cannot let the acute edge of it soften even slightly. His mother worries about him. He tells her he is fine.

He came to therapy at the suggestion of his GP, who noticed during a routine appointment that Luka had lost weight and was not sleeping. Luka sat down in the first session, folded his hands in his lap, and said, with the careful composure of someone who has been holding it together for a very long time: *"I just need to be able to do my job properly again."*

He is 63, a married North American man who has spent most of his adult life practicing medicine, and he carries himself with the careful composure of someone accustomed to being needed. When he first speaks about the event, he does so in the same measured tone he might use with a colleague, as if precision can keep the memory contained. But as the story unfolds, it becomes clear that the attack he survived has not stayed in the past. It continues to arrive in fragments, intruding into ordinary moments and altering the way he moves through the world.

The terrorist attack happens while he is traveling for a medical conference in a large city. He remembers the weather, the crowded streets, the ordinary feeling of walking between commitments with a half-finished cup of coffee in hand. Then the blast comes, abrupt and senseless, followed by screaming, smoke, and a violence so immediate that his mind struggles to organize it. He drops to the ground without thinking, instinct taking over before thought can catch up. In the minutes afterward, he is not a doctor but a body trying to survive. He sees shoes scattered on the pavement, notices a shoe with no person attached, and later cannot shake that image. He helps a wounded stranger with pressure on a bleeding wound, but his own hands shake so badly that he doubts whether he is helping at all. He is aware, with a sickening clarity, that this is the kind of scene he has only ever encountered in the abstract, in war reports and emergency planning discussions, not in his own life.

In the days after, he returns home physically intact but altered in ways his family can see before he can name them. He does not sleep. When he does drift off, he wakes with his heart pounding and his body drenched in sweat, certain for a few seconds that another explosion has occurred. He becomes preoccupied with entrances, exits, and the sound of engines idling outside the house. In the clinic, he keeps his manner steady with patients, but his concentration slips. He finds himself rereading charts, losing his place in conversations, and needing to excuse himself to the restroom when a hallway door slams too hard. He hates how quickly his body reacts, how it betrays him with a surge of adrenaline before he has even understood what he is hearing.

He begins avoiding news coverage, crowds, unfamiliar cities, even family outings that might involve long lines or packed public spaces. He offers practical reasons at first—he is busy, tired, behind on work—but his wife notices that his refusals come too quickly, with a flatness that feels different from mere preference. He stops sitting near windows in restaurants. He chooses seats that allow him to see the room. He scans people’s hands, their bags, the spaces around parked vehicles. These habits come so automatically that he only realizes how tense he has become when his shoulders ache at the end of the day.

What unsettles him most is the way his mind returns to the dead and injured. He thinks about the strangers he saw on the pavement and about whether he did enough in those first chaotic minutes. As a physician, he has spent his life acting decisively in crisis, and he cannot reconcile that identity with the helplessness he felt there. He replays the scene while driving, while shaving, while trying to listen at dinner. Sometimes a siren in the distance or the smell of diesel can pull him back so suddenly that he has to stop and orient himself, embarrassed by the force of it. He does not cry easily, but he becomes more irritable, more impatient, and more withdrawn. His wife says he seems present and absent at the same time.

Over time, he continues working, though not without strain. He remains committed to his patients, and his professionalism is intact, but it costs him more energy than it used to. He arrives early, checks locks without thinking, and sits with his back to the wall in meeting rooms. He is aware that he is bracing for something he cannot predict. At home, he tries to be reassuring, but his family has learned to read the brief tightening around his mouth when a loud sound startles him or when a televised blast scene appears without warning.

He speaks less about vulnerability than he once did, but beneath his restraint is a grief he is still trying to understand: grief for the people who died, for the world that had seemed orderly, and for the version of himself who believed that clinical knowledge offered some protection from randomness. He knows the event happened in a matter of seconds, yet its echo has stretched across months, shaping the way he sleeps, works, and moves through ordinary life with a quiet, constant vigilance.

Kaelen had always found the world a place of vibrant, chaotic beauty, something to be captured on canvas. At 71, he still spent his days painting, his hands steady, his eye for color as keen as ever. That all changed nine months ago. He was at an outdoor art fair, his own stall filled with landscapes of the Pacific islands of his youth, when the first explosion tore through the cheerful chatter of the crowd. He was knocked from his stool by the panicked surge of people, the smell of cordite and fear instantly overwhelming the scent of oil paints and popcorn. He remembers the rough scrape of the cobblestones against his cheek and the sight of an overturned fruit cart, its contents staining the ground a terrible red. He lay there, curled into himself, for what felt like an eternity, listening to the screams and the sirens that followed.

In the months since, the memory of that day has refused to fade. It is not a hazy recollection but a series of vivid, high-definition snapshots that force their way into his mind without warning. The memory is not just mental; it is physical. When an image of the chaos surfaces, Kaelen feels his body involuntarily reenact the trauma, his shoulders hunching as if to protect his head, his muscles tensing into the same tight crouch he held on the ground. These sensory-rich intrusions have profoundly reshaped his understanding of the world. The memory of utter helplessness and the sight of people running for their own lives has convinced him that he cannot rely on other people in a crisis. More fundamentally, the raw violence of the memory has taught him that the world is a deeply dangerous place, and that his own aging body is no defense against it; he feels he can no longer rely on himself.

This new set of beliefs—that the world is hostile and he is defenseless—has dictated his every action. The conviction that he is unsafe has led him to retreat from the very life that once sustained him. He no longer goes out. The bustling streets he once loved to sketch now seem filled with hidden threats. His downtown studio, once a sanctuary, sits unused. He has his groceries and art supplies delivered, the brief interaction with the delivery person his only contact with the outside world for days at a time. Internally, he works tirelessly to maintain a state of detached calm, believing that any strong emotion is a sign of weakness, a crack in his fragile defenses. This constant effort to control his emotions is exhausting. He also calls his niece, Leilani, three or four times a day, asking the same questions: Had she heard any news? Was everything alright? He is seeking a reassurance that he is okay, a confirmation of safety that evaporates almost as soon as the call ends.

These strategies, meant to keep him safe, have only served to imprison him further. By staying inside, he never has the chance to see that the world can be ordinary, even boring. His self-imposed isolation gives the intrusive memories more space to bloom. The immense effort he pours into suppressing his feelings often backfires, making the memories burst through with even greater force, as if a dam has broken. This failure to control his mind only reinforces his belief that he can't rely on himself, that he is fundamentally broken by what happened. Each time he calls Leilani for reassurance, the fleeting relief is followed by a wave of shame at his own dependency, further cementing the painful appraisal of his own inadequacy. His world has shrunk to the size of his apartment, a feedback loop where the memories prove the world is dangerous, his avoidance confirms this belief, and the resulting isolation makes the memories more potent.

It was Leilani who finally insisted he seek help. During their last call, her voice was strained with a mixture of love and exhaustion. "Uncle," she had said gently, "you can't live like this. Your paintings are gathering dust. You are gathering dust." Kaelen knows she is right. The canvases in his apartment stand blank, and his once-vibrant palette of colors has been replaced by the gray walls of his self-made prison. He has come to therapy not with a grand hope of reclaiming his old life, but with a small, specific prayer: to one day feel safe enough to walk to the art supply store, to feel the sun on his face, and to choose a new tube of cadmium yellow without his body preparing for a disaster that has already passed.

James was only a child when he witnessed his father's violent outbursts against his mother. The memories of those terrifying moments were etched into his mind with vivid detail. He remembered the sound of breaking glass and the way his mother's voice would tremble as she tried to calm his father down. One particular night stood out: his father had thrown a vase across the room, and it shattered against the wall just inches from where James was hiding under the kitchen table. The silence that followed was even more chilling, making him feel like something worse was about to happen. As he grew older, these memories didn't fade; instead, they became more potent triggers for his discomfort. Unexpected touches, especially in crowded places, would send a jolt of panic through him. He often felt uncomfortable around people who seemed suspicious or unpredictable, as if they might suddenly turn violent. This discomfort was not just an isolated feeling but one that frequently brought back the snapshots of those traumatic moments. Each time he remembered, his body would tense up, mimicking the positions he had taken to protect himself during the abuse. James's fear of going crazy began to take hold when he noticed how his reactions were becoming more intense and unpredictable. He often found himself avoiding unfamiliar places, where he couldn't assess the danger or control the environment. In these settings, unusual silence made him feel on edge, as if it signaled an impending threat. His hyper-vigilance extended to noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects in any room, a habit that had become ingrained over time. These negative appraisals of himself and his situation deepened his sense of helplessness. He felt like he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him, just as he had been unable to protect his mother during those violent episodes. This helplessness fueled his fear of going crazy, making him doubt his own sanity and reliability. Every time a memory surfaced, it reinforced these negative beliefs. The overwhelming grief that accompanied the memories made him feel like he was losing control, further solidifying his belief that he couldn't rely on himself. The cycle of triggers, threats, and negative appraisals became self-reinforcing. When James felt threatened by silence or potential weapons, it triggered more memories of the abuse, which in turn heightened his sense of threat. These moments were not just fleeting; they built into a persistent pattern that began to affect his daily life. As a police officer, he found himself constantly on edge, always scanning for signs of danger. This hyper-vigilance made it difficult for him to trust his colleagues or relax during off-duty hours. The memories and the threats they brought with them also led James to avoid social interactions. He became isolated, preferring to stay in familiar environments where he felt a sense of control. However, this isolation only reinforced his negative appraisals, making him feel more helpless and out of touch with reality. The grief that came with each memory further compounded his fear of losing his mind. Despite his efforts to manage these symptoms, the strain became too much. James's performance at work began to suffer, and he received a warning from his supervisor about his increasingly erratic behavior. What frightened him most was the realization that he might not be able to protect others if he couldn't even protect himself. This fear, along with the overwhelming grief and helplessness, finally brought him to seek help. When James first walked into the therapist's office, he was filled with a mix of hope and dread. He hoped that therapy could provide some relief from the constant cycle of triggers, threats, and negative appraisals. But he was also afraid that it might confirm his worst fears—that he was indeed going crazy and that there was no way to escape the memories that haunted him. Despite these fears, James was determined to find a way forward, to break the cycle and regain control over his life.

At 33, he is a married African man who works as a social media manager, someone who once prided himself on being able to shape chaotic events into clear, calm messages. Before the trauma, that skill felt meaningful. He had joined a humanitarian organization during a period when conflict was escalating, helping coordinate communications for relief efforts in a war zone. At first, he tells the story as if he was “only online,” posting updates, answering inquiries, translating urgency into language donors and families could understand. But over time the work pulled him closer to the ground. Internet outages, staff shortages, and the pace of displacement meant that he was no longer simply scheduling posts from a safe distance. He traveled with field teams, documented aid deliveries, interviewed families for public updates, and learned how quickly a road, a market, or a school could become a place of blood and screaming.

The event he returns to most often happened during what was supposed to be a routine delivery of food and medical supplies. He remembers the heat first, and the dust that clung to his clothes and phone screen. He had been filming short clips for the organization’s channels, trying to show that supplies were reaching people. Then there was shelling. He does not describe it dramatically. He says there was “sound, then confusion, then too many people on the ground.” He remembers diving behind a vehicle, his ears ringing, his chest squeezed so tightly he thought he would faint. When he lifted his head, one of the drivers he had joked with that morning was motionless beside torn bags of grain. A mother who had been holding a child was screaming for help. He remembers trying to use his phone and realizing his hands were shaking so hard he could not unlock it. Even now, recounting it, he stares at the floor as if he can still see the dust turning muddy under spilled water and blood.

After that day, he keeps working because everyone keeps working. In the war zone, he says, stopping feels like a luxury. He posts updates about resilience and urgent needs while sleeping lightly, if at all. Every bang sends his heart racing. He begins scanning rooftops and roads without meaning to, calculating where he would run, where he would hide. At night he sees the driver’s body again. Sometimes the dream changes and it is his own wife lying there, or a future child he does not yet have. He wakes drenched in sweat, already alert, unable to return to sleep. During the day he feels ashamed that he is alive and able to write carefully worded statements while others are buried without names.

When he eventually returns home, people expect relief. His wife is grateful he is back and tries to make their apartment feel quiet and welcoming, but he does not settle. He startles at the slam of a neighbor’s door and drops to a crouch before he knows where he is. Fireworks, motorcycle backfires, even a heavy object falling in the office send a jolt through him so fierce it leaves him trembling. He begins avoiding news footage from the region, then avoiding calls from former colleagues, then avoiding the parts of the city where crowds gather. At church he sits near the exit. At restaurants he insists on facing the door. His wife notices that he rarely laughs the way he used to. When she reaches for him in bed after he wakes from a nightmare, he sometimes pulls away before recognizing her touch.

His work as a social media manager becomes tangled with the trauma. He spends his days monitoring feeds, images, breaking stories, and public responses. The scroll of content feels like a trap: one clip of rubble or a child crying can pull him straight back into the convoy. He lingers over posts from the war zone compulsively, then feels sick with himself for looking. He drafts polished captions about solidarity while his jaw is clenched so tightly it aches. He misses deadlines because he keeps rereading simple messages, unable to concentrate. Colleagues notice he is irritable in meetings and unusually harsh about minor mistakes. He tells himself he should be stronger; after all, this is just a desk job now. Yet by afternoon he is exhausted from the effort of appearing normal.

At home, his world has narrowed. He sleeps poorly, checks locks repeatedly, and keeps his phone charged and within reach at all times. He avoids talking in detail about what happened because he fears that if he starts, he will not be able to stop. Still, memories break through when he is washing dishes, sitting in traffic, or hearing a child cry in a supermarket. He feels detached from people he loves, as though some part of him is still crouched behind that vehicle, waiting for the next blast. He tells his wife he wants to be the man who came home, but some days he is not sure that man exists anymore.

Kai Nakamura was seventy-seven years old, a retired firefighter in a small Midwestern city, but the war that had ended half a century ago still owned him. In the spring of 1975, as a young man in a coastal village in southeastern Asia, he had been a civilian in a war zone. He remembered the morning his neighbor’s house took a direct hit from an aerial bomb. The blast had thrown him against a wall, and for a long moment the world had been nothing but pressure and a high, ringing silence. When his hearing returned, he heard a woman—Mrs. Tran from two houses down—screaming her children’s names over and over. *Minh! Anh!* He never found out if they had survived. He had fled the village that same night, walked for three days, and eventually made his way to a refugee camp, then to America.

The memory had never faded. It arrived without warning—a vivid, full-color replay of the explosion, the screams, the smell of burning wood and flesh. And yet, when Kai tried to hold it in his own hands, it felt foreign, as though it belonged to a different man entirely, someone else’s history playing behind his eyes. He had learned to avoid the memory altogether, because he was certain that if he let himself think about it, he would come apart. So he did not think about it. He kept moving, working, scanning.

For decades, being a firefighter had suited him. The job gave him a reason to stay alert. Even after a long shift, when he came home to his wife, Mayumi, he found himself checking the shadows in the backyard, the corners of the living room, the parking lot outside the grocery store. He did not call it hypervigilance; he called it being careful. But there was a darker current, too. Late at night, when sleep refused to come, Kai would lie still in the dark and imagine the people responsible for the bombing—the pilots, the commanders, whoever had given the order. He pictured them suffering, pictured himself making them suffer. The fantasies were vivid and detailed, and each time they left him feeling hollow, as if he had ceased to be a person and become only a container for rage.

The triggers had become harder to avoid as he aged. Hearing certain Vietnamese names in conversation—even just on television or in a store—would send him spinning back to that morning, Mrs. Tran’s voice piercing through the ringing in his ears. Ambulance sirens were even worse. They had never bothered him on the job; he had ridden in plenty. But now, in retirement, the high-low wail passing his house made his chest lock. And bangs—a car backfiring, a door slammed too hard, a child’s balloon popping—these sounds produced a physical response he could not control: a flinch, a cold sweat, a need to drop to the floor.

Sleep had become the enemy. Kai could not lie in the dark without the memories forcing their way in. So he stayed up until exhaustion overwhelmed him, usually in the armchair with the television on and all the lights blazing. Mayumi had tried to coax him into bed, but he had snapped at her more than once, and the guilt afterward was a separate weight. He told himself that someone else—a stronger man, a soldier, a real survivor—would never have let himself get trapped in that situation in the first place. He had been a civilian, unarmed, helpless. That thought corroded him.

What finally brought Kai to a therapist’s office was not his own decision. Mayumi had found him in the garage an hour after an ambulance tore past their house at 3 a.m., sitting on a crate with his hands over his ears, rocking. She had not threatened or begged; she had simply asked him, “What are you so afraid of?” and he had not been able to answer. Now, as he sat in the waiting room, he was terrified of what he might uncover if he spoke about the memory at all. But he was also tired—so tired of being a man who could not lie down, who checked door frames for threats in his own home, who clung to revenge fantasies like they were the only proof he was still alive.

Three years ago, Maren found herself in a remote region marked by sharp ethnic and geographic tension. She was visiting a cluster of Arab villages when the atmosphere fractured. She watched structures ignite, felt the heat of the flames, and stood powerless as the situation spiraled into chaos. The stress of those hours, the sight of fire, and the specific geography of the place etched themselves into her awareness. Since that night, her life has unfolded alongside a collection of experiences that no longer feel separate from what she witnessed. Her memories arrive without warning. A passing scent, a shadow, or a familiar sound instantly pulls the full recollection forward, vivid and unmediated. When the memories surface, she sometimes hears the exact noises she registered during the frightening event, clear and unbroken. The recollections feel more real and tangible than her everyday life, outshining ordinary conversations or routine moments. In those seconds, she feels and acts as if the stressful experience is actually happening again, her posture tightening, her breathing shifting to match the past. Strangers walking toward her on a sidewalk trigger a cold sense of alarm, as if their proximity carries an immediate charge. She has developed a strict evening ritual of checking that the doors and windows are locked, repeating the test multiple times, certain that a single lapse would undo her safety. What frightened her most was the way these experiences occupy her attention. She had come to believe that staying busy is the only way to navigate the days, so she throws herself into datasets and coding tasks, working excessively to avoid being alone with her thoughts. At work, where she spends her days as a data scientist, moments of acute stress are met with deeper immersion in models and dashboards. Yet the office environment also holds moments that cut through her focus; a sudden flare from a colleague’s lighter or a raised voice during a deployment can mirror the past so precisely that the present dissolves. She goes over and over why the event happened to her, tracing the same questions day after day. She should have protected others and she failed, a conviction that sits beside the daily routines of locking doors and typing lines of code. She was certain that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, and she keeps that certainty close to her chest. She is not sure her life is worth living anymore. These patterns have settled into long-standing habits. The overwork has stretched her weeks into uninterrupted blocks of screen time, and the evening lock checks have kept her husband awake with the quiet clicking of bolts and the distant, unfocused way she meets his questions. They have learned to navigate around each other’s routines, a quiet distance forming in their shared home. Maren finally stepped into this office after a routine evening when a nearby street vendor’s grill flared up, sending a wave of familiar dread through her chest that made her step back and question her own footing. She came to this room because she is exhausted from moving through her days on high alert, because she hopes to find a way to sit with the memories without letting them dictate her posture, and because she fears that if the hollow question of her worth continues to weigh on her, she will lose the ability to stay engaged with the life she has built.

Thirty years earlier, the pediatric intensive care unit had held a sharp, unyielding scent of antiseptic, a smell that would forever anchor Layla to the night her son’s breathing failed. She had watched nurses thread IV drips into his fragile arms, the glint of needles and the rhythmic beaming of monitors becoming inseparable from the moment his life hung in the balance. Now, at eighty, the same clinical odor drifting from a community center’s cleaning cart, or the sight of a physical therapist’s tubing, instantly pulled the old emergency forward in her mind. Rather than a coherent scene, the recollection arrived as a suffocating wave of emotion without a clear image, uncontrolled access that flooded her chest before she could even brace herself. The sensory cue did not merely remind her of the past; it actively forced the memory forward, stripping her of the present moment and leaving her breathless in the middle of a mundane afternoon. As the unbidden recollection rose, Layla’s own narrative quickly shaped it into evidence of her unraveling. The sudden appearance of loss themes in a neighbor’s quiet conversation did not just stir sadness; it activated her core belief that she was permanently changed for the worse, stripped of the capable woman she once knew. She recognized this pattern well: the sensory intrusion first delivered the raw emotional recall, and that same recall then cemented her judgment that she had violated her deepest values by failing to shield her child. Every time the memory surfaced, it did not simply exist alongside her; it actively reinforced the conviction that she was fundamentally altered and powerless to prevent catastrophe. The appraisal did not linger in isolation; it directly fed back into her nervous system, ensuring that each future encounter with medical equipment or hospital-adjacent spaces felt dangerously immediate. Convinced that she was broken and helpless to halt life’s sudden blows, Layla began to construct a careful perimeter around her daily existence. The conviction that she had acted against her own moral compass did not sit quietly; it directly dictated her retreat from going out and her steadfast refusal to enter hospitals, ambulances, or even routine physical examinations. When the overwhelming grief on recall became too heavy, she learned to push the thoughts out of her mind, not because they faded, but because she could no longer tolerate the weight of feeling them. This thought suppression, paired with her physical withdrawal, gave her a temporary sense of control, yet each avoided doctor’s visit and each time she turned away from stepping outside served not as relief, but as active fuel for her self-judgment. The more she insulated herself, the more her professional identity as a social worker faded into the background, replaced by a quiet, persistent dread of the very environments she once navigated with ease. Her belief in her own permanent damage did not remain abstract; it actively shaped how the past returned, ensuring that each recollection arrived stripped of context and loaded with the same suffocating dread. Layla began to notice how the appraisal of her own powerlessness actively recalibrated her perception of the present, transforming routine hospital odors and passing conversations about loss into immediate threats. The memory’s sudden intrusion did not stay contained; it directly amplified her physiological response to needles and clinical spaces, making each visual cue feel dangerously familiar. These sharpened triggers then reached back to hijack her recall, delivering that same emotion without image, which in turn magnified the grief on recall. The cycle tightened over the years: each suppressed thought and each retreated room reinforced the appraisal, which birthed new triggers, which fed the memory, which justified further avoidance. Now, at eighty, widowed and living alone, Layla found herself standing outside her primary care clinic, her hand gripping a paper cup of cold tea as the antiseptic scent from the adjacent pharmacy window caught her breath. A recent fall had forced her into physical examinations she had spent decades avoiding, and the uncontrolled access of her son’s final days would surface so violently that she could no longer pretend to hold it back. What frightened her most was not the memories themselves, but the certainty that she had permanently damaged her capacity to live, that she had violated the values of care she once taught others. She had finally come to the intake room hoping for a way to step outside without feeling the floor give way, desperately seeking a path back to the life she had convinced herself she could no longer inhabit.

Margot Vance had not expected the afternoon to unravel so completely. At sixty-three, she still remembered the weight of the stone floor, the sudden pressure, and the way the officer’s pen scratched against his pad while he asked questions she could not answer without shaking. He had called it a rape, but the language felt thin. When she recounted it now, weeks later, she did not speak of statistics or diagnoses. She spoke of the siren that wailed past her window the night it happened, the unfamiliar hands that did not let go when they should have, and the quiet collapse of everything she had trusted to keep her protected. She had come to believe that the world held a steady threat, one that could arrive without warning in the spaces she had once considered ordinary. Her PCL-5 score of 78 mirrored the quiet intensity of her days. In the months that followed, Margot’s routine became a careful navigation of boundaries. Her studio, a converted warehouse with north-facing windows and a heavy iron door, sat at the center of her world. She moved between her kitchen and the workspace, rarely venturing beyond the familiar brick walkway. She only felt safe in that very limited number of places, and when she did step outside, she kept her shoulders tight, listening for the sudden cry of emergency vehicles. A siren would cut through the afternoon, and her breath would catch; her body would answer before her mind could explain it. She was certain that the sound carried the same urgency as that night, and it pulled her attention toward the door. Known people brought their own weight. Her husband’s sisters, who visited on Sundays, carried conversations that tugged at old threads, and Margot found herself retreating to the drafting table, not from dislike, but from a quiet need to preserve her composure. Her work as a sculptor provided both structure and unexpected encounters. While shaping wet clay on the wheel, Margot noticed how easily the material could yield, how a sudden shift could alter an hour’s labor. Comments about sexual violence, sometimes offered casually by suppliers or gallery visitors, landed heavily on her. She would feel a wave of fear and horror rise in her chest, followed swiftly by anger, guilt, and a sharp, familiar shame. When a friend’s young cousin visited the studio, bouncing a rubber ball against the plaster wall, Margot flinched as the ball struck the wood with an unexpected movement. She reacted as if she were in danger, though she knew logically the child meant no harm. She had acted in ways that did not sit well with how she understood herself. During the weeks after the assault, she had not fought as fiercely as she thought she should have, and she had not sought help quickly enough. The institution that had received her report had folded the paperwork, offered polite assurances, and moved on. The people who should have protected her had let her down, and she carried that disappointment like a stone in her pocket. Slowly, the days began to lose their texture. Her sculptures sat half-finished on the table, and she often found herself staring at them without knowing why she had started them. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore; the routines remained, but the substance had drained from them. What finally brought her to seek help was not a single breaking point, but the steady accumulation of days that felt like waiting. Her husband had noticed how she hesitated before stepping into the garden, how she paused at the sound of a passing car, how she sometimes sat perfectly still while strong negative feelings flickered across her face. He had asked her to come, and she had agreed, hoping that someone might help her understand why the world still felt so close to the edge. She was most afraid of being caught off guard again, of losing the careful boundaries she had built, but she also hoped that the quiet rhythm of her studio and the steady presence of those who stayed might remind her of what remained intact.

Kofi had always been a private person, but after the stalking incident, he became consumed by an unshakeable sense that the world was a perilous place. It started with small things – constantly looking over his shoulder on the bus ride to work, avoiding certain streets at night, and being extra cautious when meeting new people online for freelance UX design projects. As time passed, this hypervigilance seeped into every aspect of his life. He found himself wondering if he was being watched even in the safety of his own apartment, and the mere sound of footsteps outside his door made him jump. The incident itself still felt like a blur. Kofi had met someone on a dating app, and what initially seemed like a harmless connection quickly escalated into an obsession. The person would show up at his workplace, send him endless messages, and even appear at his favorite coffee shop. Kofi tried to brush it off as an overzealous admirer, but deep down, he knew something was seriously wrong. When the stalker finally disappeared, Kofi was left with a lingering sense of guilt – if only he had been more careful, more discerning, maybe this wouldn't have happened. As a UX designer, Kofi's work required him to be attuned to human behavior and psychological patterns. But now, his professional curiosity felt tainted by an insatiable need for self-protection. He started to see potential threats everywhere – in the way people interacted with each other online, in the design of public spaces, even in the algorithms that governed social media platforms. His once-thriving freelance business began to suffer as he became increasingly withdrawn, turning down projects and avoiding networking events. Kofi's friends and family grew concerned about his growing isolation, but he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was just one misstep away from disaster. He started to doubt his own judgment, wondering if he had inadvertently invited this kind of attention into his life. His usual optimism was replaced by a nagging sense of self-doubt – maybe he wasn't as careful, as aware, or as in control as he thought. As the months went by, Kofi's world shrunk further and further. He stopped attending design meetups, quit his favorite hobby (photography), and even avoided social gatherings with close friends. It was as if he had lost faith in his own ability to navigate the world safely. His online presence, once a source of creative expression, became a liability – every post, every comment, felt like an invitation for potential predators. Kofi's decision to seek help came when he realized that his fear had become all-consuming. He couldn't bear the thought of living in this state of constant vigilance forever, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. As he sat in his dimly lit apartment, surrounded by the familiar comforts of his design work, Kofi finally acknowledged that something needed to change – not just his environment, but his own perception of himself and the world around him.

Leilani was twenty-one, a nurse, and she had been home from her deployment for eleven months when the sirens started following her. The first time was on a Tuesday afternoon, driving home from the hospital; an ambulance passed her on the highway, and she was suddenly back in the forward operating base, the air-raid warning screaming overhead. Her heart slammed against her ribs, and her hands locked on the steering wheel so hard that her knuckles went white. She had to pull over. She sat there shaking, the sound of the siren fading into the distance, but the feeling of it—the certainty that something was about to explode—stayed with her for hours.

The memory of that day in the combat zone came back not as a story she could tell, but as a wave of rage and overwhelm that rose up without warning. She had been on a routine supply run when the mortar hit. The blast, the dust, the screaming. She remembered the medic beside her, the way his face went slack. She remembered the rage. It was a hot, helpless fury at the enemy, at the command who had sent them through that corridor, at herself for not seeing it coming. When the memory returned, she felt so overwhelmed by emotion that she had to stop whatever she was doing. She knew what had happened, but she could not find the words to describe it. The words simply were not there.

The rage was the hardest part. It did not stay in the past. It leaked into the present. A loud noise—a car backfiring, a door slamming—and she would be on her feet, fists clenched, ready to fight someone who was not there. Her boyfriend, Marcus, learned not to startle her. He learned to announce himself before entering a room. Even so, there were evenings when she snapped at him for no reason, her voice sharp and cruel, and she saw the hurt in his face before she could take it back. She hated that. She hated herself for it. But the scanning for danger was constant now, and it wore her out. She could not stop checking her surroundings, could not stop watching the faces of strangers in the parking lot, could not stop listening for the wrong sound in the silence.

She began to avoid things that might make her feel happy or hopeful. It was not a conscious decision at first, but she noticed that whenever she let herself relax—a movie with Marcus, a walk in the park—the crash afterward was worse. The happiness felt like a trap. So she stopped. She stopped making plans. She stopped saying yes to invitations. She also stopped exercising, even though she had been a runner before the deployment. The first time she tried to jog after coming home, her heart started pounding, and the pounding felt exactly like the seconds before the mortar hit. She could not separate the sensation from the memory. So she stopped running.

The scanning for danger made everything worse. Every time she caught herself checking a room, every time she flinched at a siren, the memory of the attack came back stronger. It was as if the hypervigilance itself was the trigger, a feedback loop that tightened with each rotation. The more she scanned, the more she remembered. The more she remembered, the more she scanned. She could not break it. The rage and the overwhelm fed on each other, and the scanning fed on both. She started to believe that if she stopped watching, something terrible would happen. That she would be caught off guard again. That the next explosion would not miss.

The sirens were everywhere. She worked at a hospital in the city, and ambulances came and went all day. Every siren was a hook that pulled her out of the present and dropped her back into the dust and the noise. She began to dread her shifts. She avoided the emergency department entrance. She took the long way around the building, even though it made her late. She could not explain it to her supervisor. She could not explain it to anyone. She just knew that the sound undid her, and that the undoing was getting faster, not slower.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the break room. A coworker dropped a metal tray, and Leilani was on the floor, her back against the wall, her hands over her ears, her heart pounding so hard she thought she might die. She did not remember getting there. She did not remember the seconds in between. She only knew that she could not keep living this way—that the rage and the fear and the scanning and the memory had become a cage she could not find the door to. She was terrified that she was losing herself. She was terrified that Marcus would leave. She was terrified that the next time a siren went off, she would not come back.

# Amara's Vigilance

Amara was seventy-eight when the car hit her. She had been crossing the street in downtown Lagos—she was visiting family, as she did every other year—when a delivery truck ran a red light and struck her broadside. The impact threw her against a storefront window; she remembered the sound of the glass, the sensation of her ribs compressing, and then the high-pitched wail of the ambulance siren that seemed to go on forever as they loaded her into it. The driver had been texting. She had done nothing wrong. But in the months after returning to her home in Atlanta, after the surgery and the physical therapy, Amara had come to believe that someone more careful, more aware, would never have been in that spot at that moment. She replayed the crossing a thousand times, searching for the split-second decision that would have kept her safe—a different route, a moment's hesitation, anything that would have meant she was not there when the truck came through. The belief that she had failed to protect herself, that her body was no longer trustworthy, had settled into her bones alongside the chronic pain that never fully left.

Two years had passed since the accident, and Amara was now eighty. She had returned to her work as a midwife at Grady Memorial Hospital, a position she had held for forty-three years, but the hospital had become a landscape of invisible traps. The ambulance bay doors opened and closed with a sound that made her flinch—not quite a siren, but close enough to trigger the flooding sensation of helplessness that came with the memory of that wail. When the emergency alert system tested its sirens on the first Tuesday of the month, Amara would find herself gripping the edge of whatever surface was nearest, her heart accelerating into her throat. The sound did not simply startle her; it pulled her backward into the moment of impact, and in that moment she was certain that her body—already damaged, already fragile—would not survive another collision. Each siren reinforced what she had come to know as absolute truth: that she was vulnerable in ways other people were not, that her life as she had known it was finished.

At home, her husband James had noticed that she no longer slept through the night. She would lie awake beside him, listening to the street sounds outside their window, tensing at every car that passed. When he touched her in the dark, she sometimes startled so violently that he withdrew, hurt and confused. She had taken to sleeping in the guest room, telling him it was so she would not disturb his rest, but the truth was that she could not bear the vulnerability of sleeping beside another person. She was always watching, always listening, her body coiled even in rest. The sleep deprivation accumulated—nights of two or three hours, her mind cycling through catastrophes, her vigilance never resting even when her body briefly did.

The locked examination rooms at the hospital had become unbearable. When she entered one to check on a laboring patient, the moment the door clicked shut behind her, Amara's breathing would shallow. She was trapped. If something happened—a complication, an emergency—she would not be able to move freely. The claustrophobia was new; she had never experienced it before the accident. But now, enclosed in that small room with its single door, she felt the same helplessness that had seized her in the moment the truck hit her, the same certainty that her body could not protect itself. She had begun to make excuses to stay out of the locked rooms, asking younger staff to handle those patients, and her supervisor had begun to notice. This was not the Amara who had trained a generation of nurses, who had delivered three thousand babies with steady hands and an unshakeable presence.

The threat monitoring never stopped. At traffic lights, she watched the cross-traffic obsessively, her foot hovering over the accelerator, ready to flee. When other cars came too close, she felt certain they would hit her—not might, but would. Her body was permanently damaged; she had felt the break in her ribs, the way her left shoulder had never quite regained its full range of motion. If she was hit again, she would not survive it. This conviction, born from the accident but now fused with every moment of hypervigilance, every startle, every sleepless night, had become the lens through which she saw the world. Amara had finally called her daughter last month and admitted that she could not manage alone anymore, that something had to change. She was ready to seek help, though part of her believed that no amount of therapy could undo what the accident had done—that her life, as she had lived it, was truly gone.

Boon-Nam Srisawat is a 66-year-old Thai-American man who has worked as a roofer for nearly four decades, a trade he learned shortly after immigrating and one that gave him a quiet, durable pride in his own capability. He came to the clinic accompanied by his wife, speaking carefully through a mixture of English and pauses, and what emerged over the intake and first two sessions was a picture of a man who had once known himself well and now felt like a stranger to himself.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Boon-Nam was contracted to re-seal a flat commercial roof. The job required working with a solvent-based coating compound in conditions with inadequate ventilation — a detail that was not communicated to him beforehand. Within the first hour, he began to feel a burning in his throat and chest. By the time he understood what was happening, he had inhaled a substantial quantity of chemical fumes and collapsed near the roofline. He was found by a coworker and taken by ambulance to the hospital, where he spent three days in a respiratory unit. He remembers the antiseptic smell of the ward with terrible clarity — the way it mixed with the residual chemical taste still sitting in his lungs — and he remembers waking repeatedly in the darkened room, disoriented, unable to locate himself in time or place, certain at several moments that he was dying.

In the months that followed, those sensory details did not recede. The smell of antiseptic — encountered now whenever he drives past the hospital on the way to job sites, or catches a cleaning product in a hardware store — hits him before conscious recognition arrives, and in those moments the memories return with a vividness that feels less like recollection and less like imagination and more like the event simply continuing. His memories of the roof, the collapse, and the ward are clear and detailed in a way that ordinary memories are not: he can describe the exact quality of the light, the sound of the monitors, the weight of the oxygen mask. Sometimes, without any image arriving at all, he is flooded with the fear of those three days — a full-bodied dread with no picture attached, which he finds even more disorienting than the visual replays. These intrusive memories have quietly hardened his belief that he cannot rely on himself — that a man who did not notice the danger until it felled him is not a man who can be trusted to assess risk — and from that conviction has grown a broader, darker certainty: that the world is dangerous in ways that cannot be predicted, and that he, specifically, has no reliable future. He has come to believe that his body was permanently changed by what happened, that his lungs are compromised in ways the doctors have not fully disclosed, and that the life he imagined for his remaining years is simply no longer available to him.

These appraisals have made the triggers more potent, not less. Because he is certain the world is dangerous and that he cannot trust his own judgment, he is hypervigilant to anything that might signal exposure — smells especially, but also darkness, which carries the memory of waking in the hospital ward not knowing where he was. Nighttime has become a sustained ordeal; he wakes repeatedly, and the dark room is enough to pull the whole sensory experience back. The threat he feels is constant and does not respond to reassurance. Even at home, in a space he has lived in for twenty years, he cannot fully relax. He has difficulty concentrating on conversations, on paperwork, on the small tasks of daily life. He avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot quickly scan them for chemical hazards or exits, and he has quietly stopped accepting jobs at sites he has not worked before — a significant professional contraction for a man who once took pride in his adaptability.

Rather than speaking about any of this, Boon-Nam has tried to manage it alone. He suppresses thoughts of the event deliberately, pushing them down when they surface, which leaves him exhausted and, paradoxically, more vulnerable to intrusion. He dwells on the man he was before — the roofer who climbed without hesitation, the husband who did not flinch — and the distance between that self and his current one confirms, again and again, that he cannot rely on himself. He never disagrees with his wife or his coworkers, never asserts a preference or raises a concern, because conflict feels like one more thing his system cannot absorb. But the suppression and the passivity together have kept him from processing what happened, and the memories return with full force each time the strategies fail, which tightens the sense of threat and confirms the appraisals all over again.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a conversation with his wife, who told him she was frightened — not of him, but for him. What he most fears is that nothing will change. What he most hopes, though he said it quietly and only once, is that he might be able to sleep through the dark again.

Riya is 22 years old, a delivery driver in a bustling city, navigating through crowded streets and alleyways. She wears her headphones to drown out the chaos of honking horns and hurried pedestrians. While she enjoys the independence her job provides, it has taken on a different hue since the night of the mugging, a night that has replayed in her mind like a haunting echo.

It was a Friday evening, the sun dipping below the horizon, casting long shadows as she parked her bike in front of a restaurant for a pick-up. The streets were busy, the air filled with the enticing smells of street food and laughter echoing from nearby cafes. Riya felt a rush of excitement; it was a typical night, one where she could earn good tips and meet interesting people. She remembers reaching for her phone to check the next order when suddenly, a man appeared beside her, his face obscured by a hoodie. In an instant, her heart races, a primal fear surging through her veins. 

“Give me your phone,” he demanded, his voice low and threatening. Riya froze, feeling as if time had slowed. The world around her faded, and all she could hear was the pounding of her heart. She remembers thinking, *This can’t be happening to me.* Instinctively, she clutched her phone tighter, a split-second decision that would change everything. The man’s hand shot out, grabbing her wrist, and Riya felt a sharp pain as he pulled her toward him. Her mind screamed at her to fight, to flee, but her body betrayed her, paralyzed by fear. 

In the struggle, she lost her grip, and he snatched the phone from her hand, disappearing into the night as quickly as he had come. Riya stood there, trembling, her breath coming in short gasps. The vibrant city around her felt surreal, the colors muted, as if someone had turned down the brightness of her reality. She was shaken, terrified, but also angry at herself for not acting faster. 

In the days that followed, Riya’s world begins to close in around her. The once lively streets now feel ominous and unwelcoming. She avoids certain areas, taking longer routes to avoid the place where it happened. She finds herself checking over her shoulder constantly, her heart racing at the slightest sound. The laughter of friends rings in her ears, but it feels distant, like a memory she can’t quite grasp. 

At work, her deliveries become increasingly difficult. The thrill of the job is overshadowed by a persistent anxiety that creeps in whenever she nears a busy street or dark alley. Each delivery feels like a gamble, a test of her resilience. She worries about her safety, her hands trembling as she grips the handlebars of her bike. The fear lingers like a shadow, a reminder of what she has lost—her sense of safety and control. 

Riya’s friends notice her growing distance. Once the life of the party, she now struggles to engage in conversations, her smile a mere shadow of its former self. She finds herself isolating, preferring to scroll through her phone at home rather than meet friends for dinner. When they invite her out, she often declines, feeling a wave of guilt wash over her as she imagines them having fun without her. 

At night, the memories invade her dreams, replaying the mugging in vivid detail. Riya wakes up drenched in sweat, her heart racing, the sheets tangled around her legs. She tries to shake off the panic, but it lingers like an unwelcome guest. The noise of her surroundings becomes overwhelming, and she often finds herself retreating to her room, where she feels a fleeting sense of safety. 

Riya’s laughter is rare these days, the weight of her experience heavy on her shoulders. She longs for the carefree days before the mugging, when she rode her bike under the sun, feeling invincible. Now, each day is a battle against the chains of fear that bind her, a struggle to reclaim her life from the grip of trauma. 

As she sits in therapy, she grapples with the remnants of that night, searching for a way to breathe again, to find peace in a world that has shifted beneath her feet. Riya knows she must confront the darkness, but for now, she is still finding her way back into the light.

Aisha, a respected city councilwoman at 77, carried the weight of a past that had irrevocably shaped her present. Decades ago, in a relationship she had once cherished, an argument with her partner escalated violently. His voice, usually a comforting presence, had risen in a furious crescendo, his face contorting with an anger she’d never seen directed at her. He struck her, and as she fell, hitting her head, the sight of her own blood on the floor became a stark, terrifying image, forever etched in her mind alongside his sudden, terrifying proximity.

In the aftermath, Aisha found herself grappling with a profound internal struggle. When she tried to piece together the event, she was met with an **incomplete picture**; significant parts of what happened felt frustratingly missing, obscured by a mental fog. This fractured recall often brought with it an intense wave of **guilt on recall**, a tormenting question of whether she could have prevented it, or if she was somehow to blame. More often than not, she found herself **pushing the memory away before she could fully recall it**, a desperate attempt to escape the overwhelming emotional pain. This inability to form a coherent narrative, coupled with the guilt, solidified her conviction that **she had permanently changed for the worse**, believing the vibrant woman she once was had been irrevocably broken. She was certain she would **never be able to feel normal emotions again**, convinced that joy and peace were now beyond her grasp, and this deep-seated belief made recalling the event even more painful, often leading her to block the memory before she could fully process it.

These deeply ingrained **negative appraisals** permeated every aspect of her life. Her pervasive **mistrust** of others, a direct consequence of her shattered faith in a loved one, meant she was constantly on guard, fueling an intense **night vigilance** where she found it much harder to feel safe after dark than during the day. This constant sense of being unsafe, evident in her sleepless nights and her tendency to scan her surroundings, cemented her appraisal that people couldn't be trusted. Believing that people couldn't be trusted, Aisha found herself hyper-attuned to potential threats, making even calm expressions of anger or physical proximity feel like potent **triggers**.

In her demanding role as a city councilwoman, Aisha’s work often placed her in crowded public spaces, bringing her into close **physical proximity** with constituents and colleagues. These moments, particularly in bustling committee rooms or during town halls, would send a jolt through her, activating an exaggerated **startle response** to sudden noises or movements. A firm but calm **expression of anger** from a frustrated citizen or a rival politician, even if not directed at her, would immediately bring fragments of the traumatic evening rushing back, though always incomplete, further solidifying her sense of an **incomplete picture**. The mere sight of **blood** on the news, a campaign poster, or even a minor cut on her own finger, reinforced her deep-seated belief that she had permanently changed for the worse, a powerful **trigger** that intensified her **negative appraisals**.

Her constant feeling of being on edge and easily startled meant that her system was primed, making even mild expressions of anger or close proximity register as overwhelming **triggers**. This constant state of hypervigilance made it difficult to process her memories, often blocking them before she could fully recall the event. The incomplete and guilt-laden memories, when they did surface, would plunge her into a state of acute anxiety, manifesting as an intense **startle response** to sudden sounds, and she found herself **frequently looking behind her to check if someone was following her** as she walked through the corridors of City Hall. Each time she wrestled with the blocked memory, the images that did surface made her even more sensitive to potential threats, turning innocuous physical proximity into a potent **trigger**.

This relentless cycle had begun to take a toll on Aisha's public life. She found herself increasingly retreating from public engagements, delegating tasks that required face-to-face interaction, and struggling to connect with her constituents, who perceived her as distant. Exhausted by her **night vigilance** and the constant need to check her surroundings, she found it difficult to concentrate during important council meetings. What frightened her most was the growing realization that her life was shrinking, consumed by a fear she couldn't outrun. It was this creeping isolation, and the fear that she was losing herself completely, that finally led Aisha to seek help, hoping to reclaim some semblance of the person she once was.

Cody Marsh is a 39-year-old divorced construction worker who presented for an initial psychological assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 73, indicating severe post-traumatic stress. He is broad-shouldered and quietly spoken, choosing his words with the careful economy of a man who has learned that saying too much costs something. He was referred through his union's employee assistance program after a supervisor noticed a pattern of absences and what colleagues described as episodes of "zoning out" on the worksite.

Approximately fourteen months before this intake, Cody was working a commercial renovation job when a co-worker and friend of seven years, a man named Dale, fell from unsecured scaffolding three floors above street level. Cody was directly below, mixing compound, when the structure gave way. He watched Dale fall and land on the concrete a few metres away. What followed — the sound, the smell of blood and dust and something he has never been able to name, the acrid taste that coated his mouth in the moments he knelt beside Dale screaming for help — became the sensory architecture of a memory that has refused to stay in the past. Dale survived but sustained catastrophic injuries. Cody walked away without a scratch, a fact that has never felt like luck to him.

In the weeks after the accident, Cody found that the memory returned not as a narrative he could recount but as a cascade of images — a freeze-frame of Dale's body mid-fall, the colour of the concrete, the particular angle of light that afternoon. These pictures arrived without warning, and with them came the smell, something metallic and chemical that he cannot always locate in the external world but that arrives with full conviction. More disturbing still, there are moments when he can taste what he tasted that day — a specific, visceral sensation that arrives in his mouth and makes him feel that the afternoon on the scaffold is happening now rather than a year ago.

Cody had come to believe, in the months that followed, that the world he thought he understood — one in which a man who works carefully and looks out for his crew can keep the people around him safe — no longer existed. He was certain that bad things would continue to happen regardless of anything he did or did not do, and he had arrived at a quiet, settled conviction that he was inadequate: not merely that he had failed Dale in that specific moment, but that inadequacy was something constitutive of him, a fixed feature rather than a circumstance.

What frightened him most was the anger. In the days after the accident Cody had felt a rage so large it seemed dangerous to him, and he made a decision — not quite conscious, but firm — that he would never allow himself to feel or express it. He became, by his own account, very still. Colleagues noticed he no longer argued on the site, no longer pushed back when work was unsafe. The man who had once been the loudest voice in a safety meeting now signed off on conditions he would previously have refused. This change had a concrete professional consequence: three months ago, a junior worker on his crew was injured when Cody failed to flag a hazard he had seen and said nothing about.

In the evenings, Cody drove to a casino forty minutes from his apartment. He was clear-eyed about what he was doing there — it was not about winning. The noise and the lights and the specific quality of suspense at the table gave him something to feel that was not the images and not the stillness. On the nights he could not bring himself to drive, he found ways to go somewhere else internally, to blank out, to leave his body sitting in the chair while he went somewhere that had no sensory texture at all.

His divorce had been finalised six months before the accident, and he now lived alone. There was no one at home to notice when he returned at two in the morning, and no one to remark on the money disappearing from his account. What finally brought him in was the incident with the junior worker — not guilt exactly, but a recognition that something was happening to him that he could no longer manage alone. He arrived at the intake hoping, with considerable scepticism, that someone might be able to tell him whether the person he used to be was recoverable, or whether that man had also fallen that afternoon on the scaffold.

Miguel is a 67-year-old physician who came to treatment months after his adult son’s life-threatening illness, speaking about it in fragments and then apologizing for “not saying it right.” He lives alone and has spent most of his life in medicine, a setting that once gave him a sense of competence and steadiness. The event that now intrudes on him happened when his son was admitted in critical condition. Miguel remembers the speed of it first: the phone call, the rush to the hospital, the abrupt transition from being a doctor who understood emergencies to being a father watching his child’s life hang in the balance. What stays with him are not smooth memories but disconnected pieces that arrive with force—the sight of his son in the hospital bed, the machinery around him, the atmosphere of urgency in the room, the sense that he might lose him. When he tries to describe the worst part, he stalls. He says he knows exactly what happened and at the same time cannot find words for it. He can give isolated images, but not a full account. Even privately, he cannot make it into a story that runs from beginning to end.

In the weeks after the hospitalization, Miguel returned to work, but his days changed in ways that were obvious to him even if he tried to conceal them from colleagues. He kept himself constantly occupied, filling every empty moment with charting, extra reading, calls, errands, anything that would stop his mind from drifting back to the hospital. At home, he left the television on, sorted papers he did not need to sort, and found reasons to stay busy late into the night. He tried hard not to think about what had happened to his son. If an image began to come up, he would interrupt it immediately, turning his attention to something concrete in front of him. He had come to dread the internal shift that happened when his mind slowed down, because that was when the memory fragments pressed in.

At the hospital where he works, the strain is sharpest. A sudden deterioration in a patient, the sound of urgent movement in a corridor, or seeing a worried parent at a bedside can bring on a moment in which he no longer feels fully anchored in the present. For a few seconds he feels as if he is back in that earlier crisis, not as a physician but as the terrified father who could do nothing except watch. During these moments his body reacts before he can reason with himself. He becomes acutely watchful, scanning faces, monitors, doorways, tone of voice. He notices every shift in the room and cannot relax his attention. What frightens him most is how suddenly this happens. He knows where he is, yet part of him feels pulled into the past so vividly that he later struggles to explain it.

Miguel is also burdened by intense emotions that do not settle. Fear remains close to the surface, especially when his son does not answer a call right away or when any family medical issue is mentioned. Alongside the fear is guilt and shame that he finds particularly hard to bear as a doctor.
