He does not elaborate these feelings easily, but they appear in the way he judges himself for not having been able to protect his son and in how harshly he speaks to himself for still reacting so strongly. He is embarrassed by the fact that he cannot simply “put it in order,” especially given his profession and age. He believes he should be able to speak about a medical crisis clearly and calmly, yet when this event is his own, the words disappear.

Over time, his efforts to push the experience away have narrowed his life. Conversations with family stay on practical topics because he avoids any discussion of the illness. If someone begins to revisit that period, he redirects or excuses himself. At work, he remains capable, but he has become more guarded and tense, and there are moments when he lingers outside certain rooms before entering, collecting himself. Colleagues have noticed that he seems perpetually on alert. Miguel himself knows that he is exhausted from maintaining that level of watchfulness and from trying to outrun his own mind.

He finally sought help after a recent episode at the hospital in which a child’s medical emergency brought back the sense, all at once, that his son was again in danger. For the rest of the day he felt shaken and ashamed, unable to explain to himself why the memory still arrived in pieces and with such force. In coming to treatment, Miguel says he wants to be able to remember what happened without feeling as if he is inside it again. What he fears most is that if he stops holding the memory back, it will overwhelm him completely; what he hopes is that he might one day be able to speak about his son’s illness in a way that feels whole, and survive the telling.

Rabbi Benjamin, a 63-year-old North American man, came to therapy after a long history of trauma that began decades ago when he was forced to flee his homeland as a refugee. The traumatic experience left deep scars that have persisted into his current life and work. Benjamin recounts the harrowing journey of escaping violence, where sudden touches from people in chaotic crowds often led to physical confrontations. This fear has translated into an intense aversion to unexpected touch today, which is particularly challenging given his role as a community leader where people often reach out for support or comfort unexpectedly. The memory of weapons and shouting during those turbulent days also remains vivid; these triggers are reactivated whenever he sees similar objects or hears loud voices in the synagogue or community center. Since then, Benjamin has employed various maladaptive strategies to cope with his overwhelming distress. When confronted by a trigger, such as an unexpected touch or seeing a weapon-like object, he often tells himself that he deserves this suffering because of what happened back then, believing that he must atone for not being able to prevent the violence. This punishment thinking has also led him to engage in distraction techniques, where he immerses himself in work or other activities to avoid confronting his painful memories. The negative appraisals that Benjamin holds about himself and others have significantly impacted his ability to feel safe and secure. He believes that his body is constantly on high alert, reacting as if the danger from his past still lurks around every corner. This sense of being in constant peril has made it difficult for him to concentrate on daily tasks, such as leading services or counseling community members. Benjamin's feelings of self-doubt and inadequacy have only intensified his fear. He often thinks that he cannot rely on himself to protect himself from future harm and believes that someone else could have prevented the traumatic events from happening. These thoughts have led him to engage in safe-seeking behaviors, such as always choosing a seat where he can see all entrances or staying within a very limited set of familiar places where he feels protected. The interplay between his triggers and maladaptive strategies is evident in how quickly these mechanisms kick into gear when he encounters something that reminds him of the past. For instance, if he hears shouting during a heated debate in the synagogue, he immediately starts to distract himself by focusing on administrative tasks or telling himself that he deserves this discomfort as part of his penance. Benjamin's negative appraisals have also created a feedback loop where they perpetuate both his threat perceptions and his triggers. His belief that his body is an enemy constantly reacting in danger mode has led him to feel anxious even in safe environments, further reinforcing his sense of vulnerability. Additionally, the notion that he cannot rely on himself has made it challenging for him to trust others emotionally, leading him to avoid intimacy and emotional closeness with both his partner and congregants. Over time, these maladaptive strategies have had significant consequences on Benjamin’s personal and professional life. His work as a rabbi requires him to be present and engaged with the community, but his concentration difficulties and avoidance behaviors have led to missed opportunities for deep connections and support within the synagogue. He has become increasingly isolated, both personally and professionally. What finally brought Benjamin to seek help was a series of recent incidents where his maladaptive coping mechanisms failed him, leaving him feeling even more vulnerable and distressed. His partner had noticed his increasing withdrawal and urged him to find professional support. Although he is afraid that therapy might bring up too many painful memories, he hopes for a way to regain control over his life and feel safe again within the community he has dedicated himself to serve. In summary, Benjamin's traumatic history has left deep psychological scars that manifest through specific triggers, maladaptive coping strategies, persistent threat perceptions, and negative appraisals. His belief in his own inadequacy and fear of re-experiencing past trauma have led him to a cycle of heightened anxiety, avoidance behaviors, and self-doubt. Seeking therapy now represents both a moment of vulnerability and hope for Benjamin as he grapples with the long-lasting effects of his traumatic experiences.

For forty-two years, Leilani had worn her police uniform as a second skin, a symbol of her role as a protector in her community. At seventy-one, she was the veteran everyone looked up to, steady and unflappable. That persona shattered six months ago, on a warm Saturday evening at a family barbeque in her own backyard. Her grandson, celebrating a new job, had had too much to drink. Leilani smelled the beer on his breath when he came to hug her goodbye and told him not to drive. They argued, his youthful pride clashing with her authority, and he had stormed off to his car. She was still standing on the porch, frozen between her roles as grandmother and officer, when she heard the screech of tires and the sickening, final sound of impact just two blocks away.

The memory of that night never comes to her as a linear story. Instead, it lives in her as a collection of sensory fragments. Her memories are overwhelmingly visual—brutal, high-definition snapshots of the crumpled driver-side door, the shattered glass glittering on the asphalt under the streetlights. These images are so clear and detailed that she can recall the specific pattern of the crack in the windshield. Sometimes, when the house is quiet, the memory is auditory; she hears the percussive crunch of metal, a sound that seems to vibrate deep in her chest, followed by her own raw scream. Because these fragments are so vivid and intrusive, her mind has learned to treat the world as a minefield of potential reminders. The sight or sound of anything that echoes that night has become an immediate and potent trigger for her distress.

This hypervigilance has made her job, once a source of pride, a source of constant torment. Responding to a routine traffic accident is now unbearable. The sight of any car hit in an accident, even a minor fender-bender, doesn't just remind her of the event; it activates a cascade of crushing self-blame. As she looks at the damaged vehicles, the thought is immediate and absolute: *The event happened because of the way I acted. I should have physically stopped him.* This conviction that she failed in her duty to protect her own family has become a central belief. The smell of alcohol, once just a common scent in her line of work, is now a direct indictment. Catching a whiff from a driver at a traffic stop sends a jolt through her, instantly reinforcing the appraisal that she is fundamentally helpless, unable to stop bad things from happening to the people she loves most.

Over the past few months, these connections have forged a debilitating cycle. She started finding reasons to stay at the desk, avoiding patrol calls that might involve a collision. When her colleagues talk about accidents, particularly DUIs, she has to physically leave the room. The conversation itself acts as a trigger, bringing forth the images and sounds, which in turn feed her certainty that she is to blame. She had come to believe that she not only failed her grandson but that she is a fraud as an officer, a protector who cannot protect. Her marriage has grown strained under the weight of her silence and withdrawal. She feels she can no longer be the strong matriarch of her family, convinced she has forfeited that right.

Leilani has sought therapy because she received a formal warning about her performance at work, and she knows she cannot continue this way. She is terrified of being forced into retirement, not because she wants to keep working, but because leaving the force would feel like a final admission of her failure. More than anything, she is desperate for a way to quiet the images and sounds in her head, to stop the relentless loop of self-blame that begins the moment she encounters any reminder of the night she believes she lost not only her grandson, but herself.

She is nineteen, a contemporary dancer who has spent most of her adolescence inside studios—counting beats under her breath, stretching before dawn, measuring herself against mirrors. Before the trauma, her life feels narrow in a way she likes: class, rehearsal, performances, part-time work at the front desk of the dance school, then home with sore muscles and the private satisfaction of getting stronger. She is single, living with her mother, and already imagines a future organized around companies, auditions, and touring. Her body is not just hers; it is her instrument, her discipline, and the way she understands herself.

The event happens at an indoor arts complex where she is attending a weekend workshop. It is crowded with students, teachers, parents, and performers moving between rehearsal rooms and a small theater. She remembers standing near a vending machine in her warm-up clothes, checking the time and rubbing resin off the bottom of one shoe. Then there is a blast—violent, metallic, and wrong. For a moment she does not understand it as an explosion, only as a force that throws sound and heat through the corridor and folds everyone into chaos. The lights go out. Fire alarms begin. People scream in different directions. Later she learns it is an intentional bombing, a man-made attack that tears through the lobby just as participants are changing rooms.

What she remembers most is not a clear sequence but fragments: the sting of dust in her eyes, someone falling against her shoulder, the smell of smoke and chemicals, a girl from another studio crying for her mother. She drops to the floor because others are dropping. She crawls, her palms sliding over broken glass and something wet she does not let herself identify. A teacher grabs the back of her sweatshirt and drags her toward an exit. Outside, in the cold air, she realizes she is barefoot. Sirens layer over each other. She keeps patting her own arms and legs, checking whether they are still there. Her left calf is cut, and her ears ring so loudly she cannot hear questions. She sees stretchers. She sees a man covered in dust standing perfectly still, as if he has forgotten how to move. For weeks afterward, that image returns to her with a force stronger than memory.

At first everyone tells her she is lucky. She is not killed. Her injuries are minor. She even returns to dance after a few weeks, though the cut on her calf pulls when she points her foot. She tries to believe she can step back into the life she had. Instead, the studio becomes unpredictable terrain. The slam of a heavy door makes her drop into a crouch before she can stop herself. During music changes, if the speakers crackle, her chest locks and she cannot catch her breath. She begins scanning every room for exits before she notices the choreography. In rehearsal, she loses counts she has known for years because part of her attention is always somewhere else, listening for danger.

Sleep changes next. She dreads it. When she does drift off, she wakes soaked in sweat, heart racing, the explosion happening again before she fully opens her eyes. Sometimes the dream is exact; sometimes it is only noise, smoke, and the certainty that she will die. She starts avoiding sleepovers, early train rides to auditions, crowded cafés after class. Her friends text and invite her out, but she leaves messages unanswered because she does not know how to explain why a busy room now feels unbearable. If someone comes up behind her unexpectedly, she spins around with her hands up, ashamed before she even understands what she is doing.

Dance, once the place where she feels most fluent, becomes tangled with fear and grief. She stares at herself in the mirror and feels estranged from her own body. The same body that used to feel precise and disciplined now feels jumpy, unreliable, too full of adrenaline. She grows angry when instructors tell her to “relax into the movement,” as if she is choosing this stiffness. On certain combinations involving floor work, she freezes. Being low to the ground brings back the corridor, the broken glass, the pressure to keep crawling. She tells people her calf still hurts, which is sometimes true, but not the whole truth.

At home, her mother notices she keeps the television volume low and checks the locks repeatedly at night. She sits with her back to walls in restaurants. She studies strangers’ hands, bags, shoes, as though clues might announce who is dangerous. News reports about attacks in other cities pull her in and repel her at the same time; she cannot stop reading them, then feels sick and shaky afterward. She is harder on herself than anyone else is. Nineteen feels, to her, too young to be this afraid and too old to need comforting.

Now, months later, she still speaks about life as divided into before and after. She goes to class, marks combinations, and sometimes even performs, but she moves through the day braced for another rupture. She wants the old certainty back—the simple trust that a building is just a building, that music will stay music, that her body belongs to dance and not to fear. Instead she lives with the sense that disaster can enter anywhere, at any time, and that some part of her is still in that corridor, barefoot in smoke, trying to find the exit.

Lila had always prided herself on her resilience and problem-solving skills. As a network engineer, she thrived in high-pressure environments where quick thinking was essential. But nothing could have prepared her for the day her daughter, Aria, fell ill with a rare and life-threatening condition. The diagnosis felt like a punch to the gut, followed by weeks of hospital visits, endless medical procedures, and the constant fear that each moment might be their last. The memory of those days remained vivid in Lila’s mind. She could still hear the sterile beeps of the heart monitor and the sharp scent of antiseptic. The sight of Aria hooked up to tubes and machines, her small body barely visible beneath the hospital blankets, haunted her. It was during one particularly harrowing procedure that Lila felt a surge of helplessness and terror, a feeling she could not shake off even after Aria's condition stabilized. Months passed, but the echoes of those traumatic moments persisted. Lila found herself on high alert at home, always scanning her surroundings for any sign of danger. The slightest unexpected movement—Aria darting across the room or a sudden creak in the floorboards—triggered an immediate fight-or-flight response. Her body would tense, her heart race, and she would feel a wave of panic wash over her. Even when Aria was safely at school, Lila remained vigilant, unable to fully relax. The constant state of hypervigilance made it difficult for Lila to function. Simple arguments with friends or family members, which had once been manageable, now sent her into a spiral of anxiety and defensiveness. The familiar patterns of conflict—raised voices, tense faces—became triggers that reminded her of the helplessness she felt during Aria’s illness. Each argument reinforced her sense of threat, making it harder to let go and move on. This heightened state of alertness also extended to medical settings. Even routine check-ups or minor procedures for herself or Aria left Lila feeling overwhelmed and on edge. The sterile environment, the white coats, and the clinical questions all served as potent reminders of the traumatic event. Each visit rekindled the fear that something could go wrong again, making it nearly impossible for her to feel safe in these environments. Lila’s job as a network engineer became increasingly challenging. Her mind was often preoccupied with thoughts of Aria and the potential dangers lurking around every corner. She found herself avoiding social interactions at work, preferring to isolate herself during breaks and lunch hours. Colleagues noticed her withdrawal and began to distance themselves, leading to a sense of isolation that only compounded her anxiety. The cycle of triggers and threat responses became a self-reinforcing loop. Every time Lila encountered a trigger—whether it was an argument, a medical procedure, or an unexpected movement—her body reacted with intense physical and emotional distress. These reactions, in turn, heightened her sense of threat, making her more susceptible to future triggers. It was a vicious cycle that seemed impossible to break. Despite her best efforts to cope, Lila’s daily life became increasingly strained. Her relationship with Aria's father, already tenuous after their divorce, deteriorated further as he struggled to understand and support her. The lack of emotional connection left Lila feeling alone and overwhelmed. It was this sense of isolation, combined with the realization that she could no longer function effectively at work or home, that finally prompted her to seek help. When Lila walked into the therapist’s office, she carried a heavy burden of fear and uncertainty. What frightened her most was the thought that she might never be able to shake off this constant state of hypervigilance and return to a semblance of normalcy. She hoped that therapy would provide the tools and support she needed to break the cycle of triggers and threat, allowing her to feel safe once again in her own home and with her daughter.

Bao, a thirty-one-year-old carpenter, had always prided himself on his steady hands and sharp eye, skills that had served him well in his workshop. But for the past year, a tremor had settled deep within him, a constant hum of unease that no amount of sawdust or familiar tools could quiet. It began late one evening, driving home after delivering a custom cabinet. He had been pulled over, the flashing lights startling him, and before he could fully process the situation, the interaction with the officers had escalated violently. He remembered the confusion, the sudden force, the feeling of being pressed against the cold asphalt, unable to see what was coming from behind him, unable to understand why this was happening or what might come next. The memory was fragmented, but the feeling of utter powerlessness, the fear of the unknown, remained chillingly vivid.

In the weeks and months that followed, Bao found himself repeatedly blaming himself for what happened. He replayed the incident countless times in his mind, searching for a different action he could have taken, a word he could have left unsaid, convinced that if only he had acted differently, the outcome would have been less brutal. This relentless self-recrimination was exhausting, and he desperately tried to avoid thinking about the event altogether. He would fill his days with work, then his evenings with distractions, anything to push the intrusive images and the shame away. Yet, the harder he tried to suppress them, the more they seemed to resurface.

Sleep offered little respite, and even when he was home with his wife, in the safety of their familiar apartment, Bao was unable to relax. He felt a persistent tension, a readiness for something awful to happen. He had come to believe that the world was inherently unpredictable and dangerous, a lesson brutally imprinted on him that night. This hypervigilance manifested in subtle, unsettling ways. In his workshop, he found himself constantly aware of his surroundings, repositioning his workbench or even himself during breaks so that he felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the entire room, his eyes scanning the entrance. This made certain tasks difficult, especially when he needed to focus on intricate details with his back to the open floor.

The uncertainty of the traumatic event also left him with a gnawing anxiety around delays. When a supplier was late delivering materials, or his wife took longer than expected to reply to a text, he immediately assumed something bad was happening. His mind would conjure worst-case scenarios, a rapid spiral of catastrophic thoughts that left him breathless and irritable. To cope with this pervasive unease and the relentless self-blame, Bao began to take drugs. What started as an occasional escape slowly became a daily ritual, a numb haze that offered temporary relief from the mental torment but left him feeling increasingly disconnected from his life and his wife.

The accumulated strain began to show. His usually meticulous carpentry work suffered as his focus wavered, and the constant need to be aware of his surroundings made him less efficient. His wife, noticing his withdrawal, his irritability, and the increasing distance between them, had gently but firmly urged him to seek help. He knew she was right, that the drugs were no longer working, and that the fear that something terrible was always just around the corner was slowly consuming him. What frightened him most now was not just the memory of the past, but the certainty that he could never truly be safe, and the despair that he might never find peace again. It was this creeping despair, and the quiet desperation to reclaim some semblance of his former self, that finally brought Bao to therapy.

# Karim's Vigil

Karim was thirty-eight when his younger brother Samir was hit by a delivery truck outside their family's grocery store in Dearborn. The impact happened in an instant—Samir stepping into the street, the sound Karim could never quite describe, the way his brother's body moved in a way bodies should not move. By the time Karim reached him, Samir's left leg was bent at an angle that made Karim's mind refuse to process what he was seeing. The blood pooled on the asphalt, and there was a smell—not quite copper, not quite anything Karim had encountered in his fourteen years as a paramedic. It was the smell of exposure, of something interior made suddenly exterior. He had worked the code himself, his hands performing the motions while his mind fractured into two parts: the paramedic who knew the protocols, and the brother who was losing Samir.

Samir survived, but barely. He spent six weeks in the hospital, and those weeks became the architecture of Karim's new life. He visited every shift he could, and the hospital smell—that particular blend of bleach and something medicinal that Karim had never noticed before—began to live in his nostrils. It followed him home. It was in his clothes, in his hair, in the fabric of his car. Two years later, he still caught it sometimes when he walked past a pharmacy, and his chest would tighten as if the truck were coming again.

Work became impossible and indispensable at once. Karim would volunteer for extra shifts, telling his wife Leila that the overtime was for Samir's ongoing physical therapy bills, though the medical debt had long since been managed. The truth was that sitting at home meant thinking, and thinking meant the memory would arrive whole and complete—not just the visual of Samir's leg, but the smell, the particular quality of the sunlight that afternoon, the sound of someone screaming, though he could not now remember if that someone was himself. When the memory came, it came with a terror so immediate and so total that Karim's body would respond as though the truck were hitting Samir again in that very moment. His hands would shake. His breath would come in short bursts. He would have to leave the room, leave the house sometimes, just to escape the sensation that he was standing on that street again.

The work itself had become different. A month ago, Karim responded to a call for a construction accident—a man with a visible laceration on his forearm, nothing severe by any measure. The moment Karim saw the wound, something in his vision narrowed. He could not look at it directly. He found himself assigning the bandaging to his junior partner, something he had never done in fourteen years. His partner had noticed. So had his supervisor. There had been conversations about "fitness for duty," words that made Karim feel as though he were failing at the one thing he had always been competent at.

At home, Leila had learned not to touch him without warning. Two months ago, she had placed her hand on his shoulder while he sat at the kitchen table, and he had flinched so violently that he knocked over his coffee. The shame of that moment—of his wife having to apologize for touching him—had lodged somewhere in his chest. He had come to believe that something fundamental in him had broken that day on the street, that he was no longer the man Leila had married, no longer someone she could rely on. He would sit in the living room and choose his seat based on what he could see, where his back was protected, which exit was closest. He was aware of how this looked, how paranoid it seemed, and yet he could not stop doing it.

He could not remember the exact moment the truck hit—there was a gap there, a blank space his mind refused to fill. But he remembered everything else with a clarity that felt like torture. He had tried, for months, to suppress the thoughts, to push them away through sheer force of will, but they would return unbidden, complete and overwhelming. Last week, his supervisor had suggested he take medical leave. Karim had finally agreed. He was sitting in his living room, in his chosen safe seat, when he called to make an appointment with a therapist. What he wanted most was to stop being afraid. What he feared most was that the person he had been before that day was simply gone.

Ravi is an 18-year-old photographer with strikingly expressive eyes that seem to capture not just images but fragments of his soul. He has always found solace behind his camera lens, but recently, the world he used to see through it has become distorted and shrouded in shadows. Growing up in a bustling city in Southeast Asia, Ravi has always been passionate about capturing the vibrancy of life around him. His camera became an extension of himself, allowing him to translate unspoken emotions into visual narratives.

However, everything changed when he enlisted to serve in the military. Ravi wanted to make a difference, to protect his homeland, and perhaps, to escape the mundane routine of everyday life. As he stepped into the role of a combat photographer, he felt a thrill that quickly morphed into a haunting nightmare. During his deployment, he witnessed horrors that would forever alter his perception of reality. One fateful day, while documenting the aftermath of a skirmish, a nearby explosion sent him sprawling to the ground. The air filled with dust and the acrid scent of smoke, mingling with the cries of the wounded. In that moment, time felt suspended, and he became acutely aware of the fragility of life. 

Now, months after returning home, Ravi feels like a ghost wandering through a world that no longer feels like his own. Each time he picks up his camera, memories flood back—images of blood-soaked earth, faces twisted in agony, and the deafening roar of chaos. He tries to focus on the beauty of his surroundings, hoping to recapture the joy he once found in photography, but the lens often captures only the pain he carries within. The vibrant colors of the market he used to photograph seem muted, overshadowed by the gray of his memories. 

Ravi struggles with sleep, often waking in a cold sweat, heart racing as he relives the moments of terror. The quiet of his bedroom is often pierced by phantom sounds—gunfire, screams, the explosion that changed everything. He throws the sheets off and stares at the ceiling, feeling trapped in a cycle of dread. Each day feels like a battle, and he feels unarmed.

His relationships have frayed; friends reach out, but he finds himself withdrawing. Conversations feel superficial, and he can’t bear to share what he experienced. The weight of his trauma is isolating; he feels as though no one could possibly understand the depths of his pain. When they ask about his time in the military, he offers vague responses, masking the turmoil that churns within. He fears that revealing the truth will push them away. 

In his attempts to cope, Ravi immerses himself in photography, hoping to document healing and beauty. He finds himself wandering through the streets, capturing the laughter of children, the serenity of nature, and the warmth of community. Yet, even in these moments, he feels a cloud of despair looming over him. The feelings of guilt are pervasive; he questions why he survived when others did not. He often wonders if he is deserving of joy when so many others are still suffering.

The smells of the market, once intoxicating, now trigger a visceral response. He recoils at the scent of spices, which transports him back to the chaos of war. Ravi avoids crowded places, feeling trapped and exposed, as if the world is a battleground once more. His heart races, and he feels a tightening in his chest when people brush against him on the street. He finds himself retreating to quieter corners, seeking solace in solitude.

Occasionally, Ravi tries to talk to his mother about his experiences, but the words get stuck in his throat. He watches her face contort with worry, and he feels the urge to shield her from his darkness. He wants to be the son she remembers, the joyful boy who brought home snapshots of life. Instead, he feels like a stranger in his own skin, grappling with an invisible weight that seems to grow heavier with each passing day.

As he navigates this tumultuous journey, Ravi clings to his camera, hoping that one day, he could find a way to tell his story—not just the one of trauma, but one of resilience and healing. For now, he wanders through the world as a silent observer, searching for a glimpse of light in the shadows that loom over him.

Eleanor had always prided herself on order. For twenty-five years as a civil servant, her life had been a study in predictability, a world of clear regulations and defined outcomes. That world dissolved nine months ago at a regional planning conference. She remembers the moment not as a clear sequence, but as a collage of terrifying sensations. A muffled boom from the hotel’s service wing, followed by a strange, acrid smell that caught in her throat. Then came the alarms, a piercing shriek that seemed to vibrate in her bones. The grand ballroom descended into chaos. People were shouting, but their words were a meaningless, overlapping roar, a tide of noise that pulled her under. She was pushed from all sides, a stranger’s hand grabbing her arm so hard it left a bruise. All she could think was that she couldn't breathe, that the air itself had become poison. When the paramedics arrived, their questions were just more incomprehensible chatter, their touch just another violation.

In the months that followed, Eleanor found that the chaos of that day had seeped into every corner of her life. She returned to her job at the municipal building, but the familiar environment now felt like a minefield. The open-plan office, once a space of quiet industry, was now a source of constant threat. The low, indistinct murmur of her colleagues talking on the phone or to each other felt exactly like the panicked roar in the ballroom, and she would find her heart pounding, her breath growing shallow. She began to feel a spike of pure fear whenever a stranger, even a colleague from another department, approached her desk unannounced. She was certain they meant to harm her, to trap her. To manage this, she started preparing for every possible conversation, sitting at her desk in the morning and mentally rehearsing scripts for phone calls or potential questions from her supervisor. This need for control bled into her home life. Her husband’s casual touch, once a comfort, now made her flinch and pull away. She couldn’t explain why, only that any physical contact felt like being grabbed in the crowd again, a prelude to being crushed.

Her world has shrunk to a handful of predictable spaces: her car, her small cubicle at work, and the spare bedroom at home which she has converted into a study. Only in these places does the relentless feeling of being on guard ease slightly. Outside, every unexpected sound—a siren in the distance, a car door slamming—sends a jolt of terror through her. She avoids all medical settings, cancelling her annual physical and refusing to even drive past the local hospital. The sight of an ambulance is enough to make her pull over, shaking. The memory of the event itself remains stubbornly out of reach. When her husband encourages her to talk about it, the words simply won't form. She starts to explain, then loses the thread, trailing off mid-sentence. It’s not a story in her mind; it’s a physical state. She can feel the tightness in her chest, recall the metallic taste in her mouth, but she cannot arrange it into a coherent narrative. Trying to deliberately recall the sequence of events is like trying to grasp smoke.

It was a letter from Human Resources that finally prompted her to seek help. Her avoidance of a mandatory health screening had been flagged, and her position was now under review. The life she had so carefully managed was beginning to fracture under the strain of her vigilance. She sits in the therapy office, rigid and alert, having rehearsed what she would say for three days straight. What frightens her most is the belief that she has been permanently broken, that the feeling of safety is a luxury she will never know again. Her hope is a small, fragile thing: to one day sit in her own living room with her husband and not feel the need to bolt when he reaches for her hand.

Mary, a 75-year-old Oceania woman and an auditor by profession, has been struggling with the aftermath of her experiences during a civilian stint in a war-torn region. Her life was turned upside down when she witnessed the chaos and destruction firsthand, events that continue to haunt her deeply. The traumatic incident occurred several years ago when Mary found herself caught in the crossfire while visiting family members who lived in a conflict zone. The sounds of gunfire and explosions mixed with the acrid scent of smoke and sweat still linger vividly in her mind. She remembers the overwhelming fear as she tried desperately to find shelter, only to realize that there was nowhere truly safe amidst the chaos. Since then, Mary has experienced intense reactions whenever she encounters triggers that remind her of those harrowing days. The smell of sweat or body odor instantly transports her back to that terrifying moment, triggering a visceral response of panic and anxiety. Even the mere sensation of feeling happy or relaxed can suddenly make her feel uneasy and on edge, as if her peace is an invitation for danger. Mary’s workplace has also become a source of distress. The structured environment and the demands of auditing have begun to trigger memories that she cannot escape. She spends much of her time there ruminating about how the event could have been prevented or questioning why it happened to her. This rumination often leads her into a cycle of negative thoughts, making it increasingly difficult for her to focus on her work. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, Mary has developed several maladaptive strategies. She frequently rehearses what she will say in any given interaction, trying to anticipate and prepare for potential threats or misunderstandings. This heightened state of vigilance also manifests in her daily life, where she feels unsafe unless her back is against a wall, allowing her to monitor the room at all times. Mary has noticed herself taking risks that could potentially cause harm, as if she is subconsciously seeking some form of control over her fate. She frequently looks behind her, checking if someone is following her, a constant reminder of the vulnerability she experienced during the traumatic event. Her memory of the incident remains vivid and detailed, akin to looking at photographs in her mind’s eye. However, when trying to articulate these memories, she finds herself unable to find the words to describe what happened, leading to feelings of frustration and isolation. Olfactory recall is another aspect that plagues her; the smell of sweat or smoke can instantly bring back those traumatic moments. Mary has come to believe that others can see what happened to her just by looking at her, a deep sense of exposure that leaves her feeling vulnerable and exposed. These negative appraisals have left her questioning whether life is even worth living anymore. She fears she will never be able to feel normal emotions again, leading her to withdraw from activities and relationships that once brought her joy. The cumulative effects of these symptoms have taken a toll on Mary’s daily functioning. Her work performance has declined, and she finds it increasingly difficult to engage with colleagues without feeling anxious or hypervigilant. The strain in her marriage has also increased, as her husband struggles to understand the depth of her distress and feels helpless in his attempts to support her. It was a particularly intense episode at work that finally pushed Mary to seek help. She realized that she could no longer manage these overwhelming feelings on her own and feared that her life would continue to deteriorate without intervention. As she contemplates this decision, what frightens her most is the possibility of never being able to reclaim her sense of peace or normalcy. However, there is also a glimmer of hope that through therapy, she might be able to find some relief from the constant burden of her memories and fears.

David had been 63 for several years when he finally decided that what he had carried for most of his adult life had become too heavy to keep arranging around himself. He was a North American Jewish rabbi, in a long-term relationship, and outwardly his days were orderly: services, pastoral visits, meetings, study, and the ordinary routines of a life built in safety far from the place where it had begun. But the safety of his present life had never erased what had happened when he was a refugee. He had fled as a younger man from a country where armed men had appeared suddenly, where shouting meant danger before anyone had even understood the words, and where weapons were not abstract symbols but the visible edge of control. He remembered the chaos of being moved along by force, the hard certainty that if he did not stay alert he could be hurt, and the humiliation of realizing that his own judgment had not protected him.

In the years after that escape, David learned to move through the world as if danger might still be waiting just outside the frame. At first he told himself he was simply careful, but over time he noticed how often he scanned for exits and settled into seats that let him see the room clearly. In restaurants, in synagogues, at family gatherings, and even in meeting rooms at work, he chose the place that felt most protected, usually with a wall behind him or a clear line to the door. If he arrived somewhere and the only available seat felt exposed, he could remain tense through the entire meal or meeting, aware that his body was braced before his mind had caught up. He found that he felt safe only in a very limited number of places, and he organized his life accordingly. When he had to concentrate on a sermon, a text, or a pastoral conversation, he could be pulled off track by the smallest hint of raised voices from another room, and he would lose his place or have to re-read the same lines several times before they made sense.

Certain moments still arrived in his body before he could prepare for them. Unexpected touch could jolt him sharply, especially if someone came up behind him in the synagogue hallway and put a hand on his shoulder without warning. He would flinch, his whole frame tightening before he could turn and reassure himself it was only a friend or congregant. Shouting had the same effect. A burst of loud voices on the street, or an argument breaking out nearby, could make him go still and hyperalert, his attention narrowing to where the sound was coming from and what it meant. Weapons, or even ordinary objects used as weapons in film, in news footage, or in a person’s hand in an agitated moment, drew his attention with a fast, grim recognition. He did not need to see much to feel his stomach tighten and to know that his mind had already moved back toward danger.

David had also become accustomed to speaking to himself harshly about the past. There were moments when he told himself that he deserved to suffer because of what had happened, as if endurance itself were a form of moral accounting. At other times, more quietly but just as painfully, he was certain that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening. He returned to that thought often, imagining that a stronger, wiser, or quicker man would have done something different and prevented the worst of it. When he saw his own hands shaking or felt his pulse race in a harmless setting, he interpreted it as proof that his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe. That experience was deeply frustrating to him because, by temperament and profession, he believed in steadiness and self-command. Instead, he found himself thinking that he could not rely on himself, not when his body seemed to betray him so readily.

As the years passed, David developed habits that helped him get through the day but narrowed his world. He distracted himself whenever painful memories pressed close, shifting into work, reading, or practical tasks rather than staying with what he felt. He also kept emotional distance where he could. Even in his relationship, where there was warmth and loyalty, he often held back from being fully intimate, not because he lacked feeling but because closeness made him vulnerable in ways he found hard to bear. He worried that if he allowed himself to be fully seen, the old fear and shame would show too plainly. His partner noticed that he could be present and loving, yet sometimes abruptly inward, as though he had stepped behind an invisible curtain.

By the time he sought help, David was no longer pretending these reactions were minor inconveniences. He had begun to worry that the circle of places and situations that felt safe had become too small, and that the effort of arranging his chair, monitoring voices, and suppressing the memory of his body’s alarm was leaving him exhausted. He came to treatment wanting relief from the constant tension of waiting for the next jolt, and hoping to understand why a man who had built a meaningful life as a rabbi could still feel, in his own words, as if some part of him had never come home. What frightened him most was the prospect that he would continue living by avoidance and self-reproach, and what he most hoped for was the chance to sit, listen, and touch the present without being pulled so quickly back into the danger of the past.

Nina was twenty-five and lived in a small, bustling town where the memories of a traumatic day still loomed large. Just over a year ago, she had been involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that changed her life in an instant. It was a rainy afternoon, and she was driving home from work when another car, traveling at high speed, collided with hers. The sound of metal crunching and the shattering of glass echoed in her mind. She remembered the jarring impact, the sensation of helplessness as her car spun out of control. Although she survived, the aftermath haunted her, and it was this experience that drove her to seek help.

In the months that followed the accident, Nina found herself increasingly anxious and withdrawn. Simple sounds became triggers; hearing names like "Crash" or "Accident" sent her heart racing. Even casual conversations could lead to discussions about cars or driving, which she instinctively tried to avoid. Arguments with her husband, Sam, became particularly difficult for her, as they often reminded her of the chaos and fear she experienced that day. The slightest disagreement could send her spiraling into a state of panic, where her mind raced with thoughts of the collision. She would often find herself questioning her decisions that day, convinced that her actions had somehow led to the accident. "If only I had left work earlier," she would tell herself, her mind filled with self-blame and guilt over something she felt she could have prevented.

The weight of these thoughts became unbearable, and Nina began to reframe her relationships with friends and family. She avoided social gatherings, fearing that unexpected conversations would trigger memories she was desperate to suppress. Each missed invitation piled on the guilt; she felt as though she was pushing away the very people who cared for her. Her friends reached out, concerned about her absence, but she couldn't muster the strength to face them. Instead, she found herself retreating deeper into solitude, a cycle that fed her sense of mistrust. “They can’t possibly understand what I’ve been through,” she thought, convinced that no one could comprehend her pain.

At work, Nina’s role as a database administrator required her to focus intently on complex problems, but even that became an ordeal. The pressure of deadlines heightened her anxiety, and physical stressors, such as long hours at the computer, became unbearable. She avoided any situation that could lead to physical discomfort, opting instead to remain in her safe space, her desk cluttered with papers she often glanced at but never touched. The tension in her body mirrored the turmoil within her mind, and when the stress became too much, she resorted to self-harm—a way to distract herself from the haunting memories. It was a desperate measure, a harmful attempt to regain control over her chaotic thoughts.

As the months passed, Nina felt increasingly trapped in her own life. The guilt of not doing more to prevent the accident became an ever-present shadow, one that whispered to her in moments of quiet. “I will never forgive myself,” she would think, replaying the events over and over in her mind, searching for a different outcome. She felt paralyzed, unable to take action in her life, convinced that she was stuck in a cycle of blame and regret. The thought of reaching out for help was daunting; what if no one could help her? What if she was destined to live like this forever?

It was during a quiet evening, after a particularly overwhelming day, that Nina finally decided she couldn't continue on this path. She sat on the couch beside Sam, who had been patient but increasingly worried about her well-being. As she watched him scrolling through videos on his phone, she realized that she was tired of feeling alone in her suffering. The thought of seeking help terrified her; she feared opening up about her experiences and the depth of her pain. Yet, she also felt a flicker of hope—a desire to reclaim her life, to find a way to move past the trauma that had consumed her.

With a heavy heart but a sense of determination, Nina made the decision to seek help. She understood that it wouldn’t be easy and that she would have to confront the very memories she had been trying to avoid. But deep down, she hoped that with the right support, she could learn to navigate her fears, rebuild her trust in others, and, perhaps one day, forgive herself for the past.

Arthur had driven the same municipal routes for thirty-two years, until the Tuesday evening drop-off behind a vacant industrial park changed everything. He had just stepped out of his van with a cardboard carton when a man emerged from the shadows, demanding a package Arthur didn’t have. What followed was a sudden, crushing shoving match against a stack of metal pallets. Arthur’s knees buckled, his breath vanished, and the attacker’s weight pinned him to the cold concrete while threats were spat inches from his face. The violence was not just physical; it was absolute, stripping away his usual calm and leaving him trembling in the sudden quiet after the man fled. In the months since, Arthur found that specific sounds and spaces instantly triggered that same visceral paralysis. Last Thursday, when a neighbor’s delivery truck backed into his driveway with a loud reversing beep, Arthur dropped his coffee mug and pressed his back against the wall, his breath shortening until the sound matched the exact noise of the attacker’s footsteps that night. Gradually, the attack dismantled his internal compass. Arthur had come to believe he could not trust that he would do the right thing if confronted again, questioning every instinct that had kept him safe on the road for decades. The orderly logic he had relied on felt completely destroyed, replaced by a sense that danger could materialize without warning. Alongside this collapse came a paralyzing conviction: if he thought about the event, he would not be able to handle it. The memories felt too sharp, and he was certain that giving them any mental space would cause him to fracture. Because he was certain that dwelling on the memories would leave him emotionally ruined, Arthur worked hard at keeping busy with other things, treating stillness like a physical threat. He began taking on extra municipal zones, washing his van until the paint faded, and reorganizing the garage twice a week, using relentless motion to outrun the quiet hours at home. The same conviction that his own judgment was fundamentally broken pushed him to eat excessively to manage the distress that spilled over, going through jars of crackers and bags of chips in a steady, numbing rhythm. He also tried hard not to think about the trauma, deliberately steering his van away from the intersection where the attack occurred and forcing his mind to recite route numbers whenever his peripheral vision caught a shadow. These habits slowly narrowed his world. His wife, Clara, noticed how he flinched at the doorbell and stopped answering calls after six. The dispatcher began flagging his refusal of afternoon routes as a reliability issue, and Arthur’s hands shook during a recent inspection, threatening his livelihood. The exhaustion of this vigilance became impossible to ignore. After a routine drop-off triggered a panic attack in his driveway, Arthur finally called for an evaluation. He walks into the clinic hoping someone can help him stop running from his own thoughts, terrified that without intervention, the world will continue to feel like an inescapable trap.

Keanu, a 48-year-old roofer with a sturdy build and a quiet demeanor, presented for therapy after months of internal struggle that had begun to fray the edges of his life and his marriage. He carried the weight of a sexual assault that had occurred several years prior, an event that had fundamentally reshaped his experience of himself and the world around him. He recalled it with a clarity that felt unnerving, more vivid and present than any other memory, as if it had happened yesterday. It was late, after a long day’s work, and he had been walking home when a man, reeking of stale alcohol and the exhaust of a powerful motorcycle, had cornered him in an alley. The memory of the assault itself was often fragmented, but the overwhelming sense of being trapped, the visceral fear, and the pervasive smell of alcohol lingered with a chilling intensity.

In the years that followed, Keanu had developed a series of coping mechanisms, attempting to regain a sense of safety and control that had been violently stripped away. The smell of alcohol, even a distant whiff from a passing stranger or a spilled drink in a restaurant, could instantly plunge him into a state of profound emotional distress. He would feel the full terror and humiliation of that night, a powerful surge of emotion that sometimes arrived without any accompanying image or clear memory of the event itself, leaving him disoriented and panicked. Similarly, the roar of a motorcycle engine, particularly one accelerating hard, would make him flinch and his heart pound. He worked on roofs daily, and the sound of a bike on the street below could trigger a sudden wave of dizziness, making him clutch at the nearest support beam, certain he was about to lose his footing. He had come to believe that any situation that put his body under physical stress was inherently dangerous, a direct echo of the vulnerability he had experienced during the assault. This made his work increasingly challenging; he found himself avoiding heavy lifting, delegating tasks he once performed effortlessly, and even turning down jobs that seemed too physically demanding, a significant shift for a man who had always prided himself on his strength and capability.

To counteract this pervasive feeling of helplessness, Keanu had developed a strict regimen. He worked hard at keeping busy, often taking on extra hours, meticulously cleaning the house, or throwing himself into home improvement projects. He rarely allowed himself moments of quiet reflection, fearing what thoughts might surface. This constant activity, he felt, kept the darkness at bay. He also began to control his eating strictly, meticulously planning meals and limiting his intake, a ritual that provided him with a fragile sense of mastery over his own body. He believed that if he could control this one aspect of his existence, he might prevent further harm. Yet, when a news report came on, even vaguely related to an assault or a violent crime, Keanu would immediately change the channel or leave the room. He was certain that engaging with such content would overwhelm him, bringing back the vividness of his own trauma, and when he did inadvertently recall the event, an overwhelming grief would wash over him, a profound sorrow that was difficult to bear.

His wife, Elena, had recently expressed growing concern. His endless busyness left little room for shared moments, and his avoidance of physical exertion had started to impact their finances and his reputation among his peers. The constant anxiety, the sudden shifts in his mood when a trigger appeared, and the quiet despair he carried had become undeniable. Keanu finally sought help, driven by a deep fear that he was losing himself, that the assault had irrevocably broken him. He desperately wanted to feel safe in his own skin again, to reclaim the man he was before, but he was terrified that acknowledging the full scope of his pain would only make it more real, more impossible to escape.

Linh was fifty-two years old, a Vietnamese-American librarian at a public library in a small coastal town, when Hurricane Nadia made landfall three years ago. She and her husband, Sopheap, had decided to ride out the storm at home, a decision she would later replay hundreds of times. The storm surge came fast, pushing water through the ground floor while they climbed to the attic. For hours they listened to the wind scream and the house groan, and then—suddenly, impossibly—silence. The eye. That stillness, the absence of any sound, was the most terrifying moment of her life. She knew the storm would return, and when it did, the noise was even worse, but it was the silence that stayed with her. In the aftermath, they were rescued by neighbours from two houses down, the Parkers, who had a boat. Linh never saw the bodies of the two people who drowned on her street, but she could not stop imagining it. And every time she saw Mr. Parker in the grocery store or Mrs. Parker at the post office, her chest tightened and she felt the same helpless numbness she had felt in the attic. She started crossing the street to avoid them, even though they had saved her life. She told herself it was because she didn’t want to talk about the storm, but the truth was that their faces yanked her straight back into that moment—the cold water, the splintering wood, the awful silence.

In the weeks that followed, Linh tried to return to her normal routines, but the world felt different. She found herself watching the edges of every room, scanning the corners of the stacks at the library, making sure no one was too close. She began choosing her seat in the staff break room with her back to the wall, and at home she insisted on sitting in the chair that faced the front door. Sopheap asked her about it once; she said she just felt safer that way. She did not tell him that she was constantly alert, that her heart jumped every time the silence of a reading room settled around her. At work, she would sometimes find herself holding her breath, listening for something she could not name. One afternoon a patron who resembled Mrs. Parker—same grey hair, same way of standing—approached the reference desk, and Linh felt her vision narrow. She excused herself and went to the staff room, shaking. She could not explain why. She only knew she had to get away.

Nighttime became difficult. Linh began leaving a lamp on in the bedroom, and she woke several times a night, disoriented and afraid, convinced the dark was pressing in. She avoided walking outside after sunset. More troubling, she started to lose attention during conversations. When a patron or a colleague spoke, she would feel herself pulling away, deliberately trying to leave her body, to blank out the moment. It worked, briefly, but then she would come back feeling hollow. She stopped going to the small gym near her home because the exertion made her heart pound and she could not calm down afterward. She told Sopheap she was just tired from work.

But the worst moments came without warning. She could be shelving books in a quiet aisle—the library was always quiet, that was the problem—and suddenly she would be back in the attic, the smell of wet wood in her nostrils, her throat tight. The memory forced its way into her mind, and along with it came an overwhelming wave of grief, so heavy she had to lean against the shelves. She was not just remembering the hurricane; she was mourning the woman she had been before, the one who walked into the dark without a second thought. She began to avoid certain sections of the library—disaster preparedness, weather, anything related to water—and she asked a colleague to cover the evening shifts. She said she needed to be home earlier. She did not explain that being in the dark, even on her own street, made her feel like she was drowning again. The Parkers called once, to check on her, and she let the call go to voicemail. She never called them back. She could not bear to hear their voices, because their voices reminded her of the boat ride through the flooded street, the wreckage, the uncertainty of who had survived.

The consequences accumulated. Her supervisor noted she seemed distracted, and a patron complained that Linh had given a curt answer when asked about a book on hurricanes. Linh withdrew from the small circle of friends she and Sopheap had maintained. She stopped attending the book club she had led for years, claiming scheduling conflicts. In truth, she could not bear the silences that fell between sentences, the way a pause in conversation could send her back to that moment of absolute stillness. She felt trapped between two worlds: the one she lived in, where her body was present, and the one she kept revisiting, where she was powerless.

Linh came to therapy because Sopheap had begged her. He found her one morning standing in the kitchen at three a.m., staring at the wall, having dissociated for so long she did not remember walking there. She agreed to come because she was terrified that she was losing her mind, and more afraid that she would lose her marriage. In the first session, she sat in the chair closest to the door, her back to the wall, her eyes scanning the room twice before she spoke. She said she wanted to stop feeling like a disaster survivor and start feeling like herself again, but she could not imagine how silence would ever feel safe—or how she could ever look Mr. Parker in the eye again without falling apart.

Michael, a 37-year-old North American man who worked as a database administrator, described his life as having divided cleanly into “before” and “after” the illness that nearly killed him. Before that time, he had been recently divorced and living alone, keeping a careful routine that made work and home feel manageable. The illness began abruptly enough that, when he tried to explain it, he still sounded unsettled by how ordinary the day had seemed at first. What had started with breathlessness became a medical emergency, and he remembered the frightening loss of control in stark, physical fragments: struggling to get air, being rushed through examinations, and seeing needles, tubing, and other medical equipment moving in and out of his body while he was too frightened and too weak to do anything but endure it. Those images stayed vivid for him, and even now he could recall the feel of shortness of breath as the moment his mind linked his own body with danger.

In the weeks that followed, Michael found himself responding intensely to anything that resembled that period. He noticed that if he became winded climbing stairs, on a brisk walk, or even after hurrying across the parking lot to the office, he would suddenly feel a wave of alarm. The sensation of not getting enough air was not just uncomfortable to him; it had the quality of a warning that something terrible was about to happen again. He also became uneasy in medical settings and had a strong urge to avoid hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations whenever possible. Even seeing medical equipment was enough to unsettle him. Needles, IV drips, and the sight of carts or tools in a clinic waiting room could make him tense up before anyone had touched him. He found procedures especially difficult, because they placed him back in the role he had most dreaded during the illness: lying still while others examined him, with no clear sense that he could protect himself.

As the months passed, Michael developed a set of habits meant to help him feel more in control. He began restricting his eating strictly, telling himself that if he could keep his intake tightly regulated, at least one part of his life would feel orderly and contained. He also started avoiding exercise. He had once tried to keep himself healthy through regular physical activity, but now exertion had become linked in his mind with breathlessness, and breathlessness with emergency. Even minor workouts felt risky to him, so he drifted away from them entirely. At work, this showed up in small but important ways: he would choose routes that kept him away from the hospital building near his office, and he became reluctant to schedule routine checkups, even when he knew he probably should. The avoidance was not dramatic, but it slowly narrowed his world and made ordinary errands feel more complicated than they used to be.

What Michael spoke about most readily in the sessions was the way his body stayed on guard. He said he felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, as if some part of him were still waiting for the illness to return. He would notice his muscles braced before he even understood what had set him off. When something reminded him of the original experience, his body could react strongly and suddenly. A sensation of tightness in his chest, an unexpected shortness of breath, or the sight of medical gear could send him into a state of immediate physical alarm, and he described these moments with frustration because they seemed to happen before he had time to think. Alongside that, he was aware of intense negative feelings that he found difficult to sit with: fear, horror, anger at how vulnerable he had been, and shame that his body had become so unreliable to him. He did not present these feelings as abstract emotions but as a daily burden he carried in silence, especially since his divorce had left him with less immediate support at home.

Recently, Michael sought help after realizing how much energy he was spending organizing his life around the possibility of another medical crisis. He had delayed appointments, avoided exercise, and monitored his body closely, yet still felt he could never fully relax. What finally pushed him to come in was the sense that he was living as though his body were always one step away from failing him again. He said he wanted to understand why a breathless moment or a medical setting could still make him feel so physically overwhelmed, and he was most afraid that he would be caught unprepared if his body signaled danger again. At the same time, he hoped that treatment might help him move through ordinary life without feeling forced to brace himself for another emergency every time he became short of breath or saw the equipment of medicine.

Malia was a veterinarian on a humanitarian mission in a conflict zone, treating livestock and working animals in villages caught between shifting frontlines. She had been there for three months, and the work felt meaningful. Then came the mortar attack on the market town where she and two colleagues were running a mobile clinic. She remembered the first explosion—a deafening crack that seemed to come from inside her skull—and then the chaos of people and animals screaming. She was thrown to the ground, and someone grabbed her arm, yanking her toward a truck. She could not recall the evacuation clearly; the memories came in disconnected pieces: the feel of a rough hand on her wrist, the smell of smoke, a fragment of a prayer, the sight of one of her colleagues lying still on the ground. She was certain she had done nothing useful. She had frozen. When she later learned that her colleague had died, she felt a shame so deep it seemed to live in her bones. Nothing about that day had been fair—she had gone to help, and instead she had been helpless, and no one had ever been held accountable for the attack.

Back home in the United States, Malia tried to resume her life as a veterinarian in a suburban animal hospital. She was married to a quiet, patient man named Tui, and they had a comfortable house. But within weeks, the symptoms took hold. The loud, sudden bark of a large dog in the exam room would send her heart racing and her vision tunneling, and she would have to excuse herself to the bathroom to breathe. She began to flinch when clients or staff touched her unexpectedly—a hand on the shoulder, a tap on the arm. She could not bear to have Tui drive her anywhere; the sight of his hands on the wheel, the motion of the car, the feeling of being a passenger without control, brought back the jostling ride in the evacuation truck. So she drove herself everywhere, gripping the wheel too tightly, scanning every intersection and pedestrian. At night, she lay rigid in bed, alert to every creak and whisper, unable to let herself fall deeply asleep because she needed to be ready. Even when she knew the house was locked and safe, her muscles would not relax.

The memories came like a film that played over and over, but the film had missing frames. She could not piece together the moments between the second explosion and the truck ride. What she did recall—the shame of her inaction, the feeling of being grabbed, the sound—felt more vivid and more real than the present. She began to believe she could not rely on herself. If she had failed then, what was to stop her from failing again? She could not stop bad things from happening, no matter how carefully she prepared.

At work, she avoided procedures that required her to be in close, sustained physical contact with large animals—she asked her colleagues to handle the horses and cattle, saying she had a sore back. She started leaving the exam room door open so she could hear anyone approaching from behind. Her husband grew worried when she stopped wanting to go out to dinner with friends; the noise of the restaurant, the possibility of someone brushing past her chair, was too much. He asked what was wrong, and she could not explain it in a way that made sense. She began to feel that she was disappearing into her own vigilance, that the world had become a series of threats she had to monitor.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was a moment in the surgery suite during a routine spay. The autoclave released a high-pressure hiss, and she dropped her scalpel and backed into the wall, shaking. Her surgical nurse looked at her with alarm. Malia knew then that she could no longer keep her fear separate from her work. She made an appointment with a psychologist who specialized in trauma, and she sat in the waiting room with her hands clasped, scanning the room for exits. She was afraid of what the therapy might stir up—afraid of the shame, afraid of the helplessness. But she was more afraid of losing the life she had rebuilt: her marriage, her profession, her sense of who she was before she became someone who could not be touched, who could not rest, who could not trust herself.

Layla was thirty-eight, a school principal in a suburban district, divorced, and living alone. Six years earlier she had been a combat medic in Afghanistan, part of a supply convoy that rolled into an ambush in a narrow valley. The IED took out the lead vehicle; then the small-arms fire came from both sides. She remembered the sound of rounds striking metal, the screaming of the soldier beside her, and the confusion of trying to drag him to cover while the world dissolved into smoke and noise. She could not put those minutes in the right order—the scream came before or after the second blast? The memory arrived as a jumble of sounds: the sickening thud of bullets hitting flesh, the radio chatter, her own shouting. And then, even now, the rage. When the memory surfaced, she felt a hot, focused fury at the men who had done it, at the army for sending them into that valley, at herself for not saving the soldier.

That rage fed something darker. Each time she recalled the ambush, she found herself concluding that people could not be trusted. The enemy had been hiding, waiting. The trust she once placed in others felt like a dangerous naivety. After the divorce, she had told herself it was her fault—her reactions since the event proved she was a lousy coper. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore; she did her job, but it was hollow. These appraisals did not stay inside her head. They made her body ready. She became watchful even inside her own home, checking the locks twice, sitting with her back to the wall. She always identified escape routes before she felt comfortable anywhere—a habit she brought into her school every morning.

Being a principal meant endless meetings, but Layla could not focus. While a teacher presented a lesson plan, her eyes tracked the exits, the window, the distance to the parking lot. That hypervigilance, in turn, summoned the memories. During a sudden fire drill last semester, the alarm blared and for a moment she was back in the valley, hearing the scream. The memory was fragmented, but the rage came instantly, and then the self-blame—see, you are still a bad coper, you cannot even handle a drill.

The loop tightened. Because she believed she was a lousy coper, she stayed on guard constantly, which triggered more intrusive memories, which reinforced her sense that nothing mattered and people were dangerous. At school, she began avoiding staff gatherings, telling herself it was safer to eat lunch alone in her office. She had become distant from her assistant principal, a woman she used to confide in. Her life shrank to work and her empty house. 

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at a school assembly. A student dropped a metal chair, and the sound sent Layla into a flashback she could not control—she found herself crouched behind the podium, shaking with rage and fear. A teacher had to guide her out. The next day, Layla sat in a therapist’s office, her hands gripping the armrests. She was most afraid that nothing could change, that she would always be this coiled, angry woman who could not trust anyone, not even herself. But beneath that, what she hoped for was a single thread of meaning, a way to believe that her life was not over because of a few minutes in a valley six years ago.

Mārama grew up with a father whose anger arrived without warning—a raised voice, a slammed fist, and then the physical blow. She remembers some moments with startling clarity: the way his shadow fell across the kitchen floor, the smell of his sweat. But other parts are gone entirely, like a film with missing reels. What remains feels as though it happened to a different child, not to her. Now thirty, married, working as a plumber, she has built a life far from that house. Yet the past intrudes in ways she cannot control. A customer shouting across a job site, a supervisor’s calmly expressed frustration, even the sensation of being watched while she works under a sink—these moments trigger a cascade she barely understands. Her body tightens, her heart pounds, and she finds herself gasping at an unexpected footstep nearby. Her mind, she says, “goes somewhere else,” and the fragmented memories surface like shards of glass. Once those memories break through, she cannot shake the feeling that danger is right behind her—that the threat has followed her into the present. The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next. She has learned to cope by pushing those thoughts away, by keeping her mind occupied with constant mental tasks, and by skipping meals—she lost eight pounds in the past two months. The restriction gives her a sense of control, but it also leaves her lightheaded and more vulnerable to the startle reflex that follows any sudden movement.

The causal loops are tight and self-reinforcing. When a colleague expresses even calm anger, Mārama’s body goes on alert, her concentration dissolves, and the alien, incomplete memories press closer. That immediate threat response makes her even more vigilant for the next angry tone, and the more she tries to suppress the memories, the more fragmented they become—and the more dangerous her environment feels. She often lies in bed after work, muscles still rigid, trying to distract herself with a podcast, but the effort of constant mental vigilance exhausts her, which in turn amplifies her sense of bodily tension. She has also noticed that the harder she avoids thinking about the trauma, the more likely she is to be startled by a sudden sound at the shop, as if her mind is scanning for threats even as it tries to look away. The undereating, she believes, helps her feel less—less emotion, less memory—but the physical weakness only makes her feel watched and exposed. Her husband has begun to worry; he sees her flinch when he enters a room quietly. Mārama came to therapy after a client’s angry outburst made her freeze under a bathroom sink for twenty minutes, unable to move or speak. What frightens her most is the sense that she is losing her grip on the present, that the past is not staying where it belongs. She hopes the therapy can help her feel safe in her own body again—and perhaps finally fill in the gaps that feel like they belong to someone else.

Marianne, a 79-year-old European American widow who had spent most of her life working as a tailor, came to treatment after years of trying to keep her world small. Her wartime trauma had happened when she was young and working near a military site during a period of upheaval: she had seen blood, heard men shouting, and been caught in a scene so frightening that even now she could not place it in order. When she tried to tell it, the pieces came out broken and out of sequence, and she would stop in frustration, saying she could not put the event into words. What remained most vivid was the surge of rage she felt whenever she remembered it, as if the anger were still alive in her body. Marianne said that when unwanted thoughts forced their way in, or when a conversation turned to war, soldiers, or old losses, the event would return with a force that made her feel that her life had been ruined. Blood was especially potent for her; even a glimpse of it in her sewing work, or on a television scene in the background, could make her recoil and think, with a heaviness she found hard to shake, that she used to be a happy person but was now always miserable. Once those reminders took hold, they did not stay as simple shocks; they quickly became proof to her that the world could turn cruel without warning and that she would never be able to keep herself steady. Each cue seemed to confirm, with a private certainty she could not talk herself out of, that she had been permanently changed and could not trust her own judgment to keep danger out.

Those moments did not just upset Marianne; they shaped the way she understood herself and her future. When the memories broke in, disordered and wordless, she was left with the sense that something in her had been damaged beyond repair. She would sit afterward feeling dead inside, and from that numbness she would conclude that nothing good could happen to her anymore. That conviction did not leave the memory behind; instead, it pulled her back toward it, as if she had to keep returning to the scene to prove to herself how badly she had been ruined. The more certain she became that she was broken and helpless, the more the original event filled out again in her mind, vivid and immediate, with her own helplessness at the center of it.
