She believed there was no point in hoping, because whenever she tried to picture a better future, the old fear came back with the memory and crushed it. The more often her mind went to the event, the more certain she became that her life had not only changed but had lost all possibility of happiness.

To manage this, Marianne began keeping away from almost everything that might stir either memory or feeling. She avoided friends, turning down visits and letting phone calls go unanswered, because social gatherings could drift into the very kinds of conversation that brought the war back to mind. In her home and in her small tailoring routine, she also avoided situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful. Birthdays, family celebrations, even small pleasures such as a good meal or a kind remark felt unsafe to her, because positive feeling seemed to invite disappointment and make the later fall worse. When she noticed herself softening or enjoying something, she pushed the feeling away, bracing herself against it before it could take hold. The more Marianne lived with the belief that she was unsafe and that good feeling would only set her up for a harder fall, the more ordinary things around her began to stand out as reminders. A raised voice outside the shop, a customer mentioning a cousin in the service, or the sight of blood on a pin could all suddenly seem loaded with threat, because her own fearful conclusions taught her to scan for signs that the old danger was still near. In the short term this kept the memories at bay, but over months it deepened her conviction that she was cut off from ordinary life and had little left inside except misery and emptiness.

At work, Marianne remained skilled with her hands, but the shop had become narrower than it once was. A customer mentioning wartime relatives, a television program in the background, or a pinprick of blood from a needle could set off unwanted thoughts that followed her for the rest of the day. Each time the memory arrived, the confusion of its sequence and her inability to tell it clearly left her feeling even more helpless, and the helplessness fed her belief that she had become someone who could only endure rather than live. The more she kept people away and the more she pushed down anything hopeful, the more isolated and numb she felt, which in turn confirmed her sense that nothing good lay ahead. What had begun as an effort to survive the recall of one terrifying event had, over time, settled into a life organized around avoiding reminders, avoiding comfort, and avoiding the risk of feeling alive.

By the time she sought help, Marianne was exhausted by the constant vigilance and the bleakness that had taken hold of her days. She was frightened that the unwanted thoughts would keep returning, that one stray conversation or one glimpse of blood would pull her back into the same rage and misery, and that if she allowed herself to hope or to see friends again, the loss would hurt even more. Still, she hoped that treatment might help her make sense of the memory she could never quite order or say aloud, and that if it could be faced in a safer way, she might not have to live as though nothing good could happen to her anymore.

Evelyn, a 37‑year‑old violinist from Detroit, remembers the night of the bombing as if the concert hall had never been a safe place. The city’s grand theater was packed with families and friends for the premiere of a new concerto. She was onstage, bow poised, her heart racing with anticipation. Suddenly, a deafening explosion tore through the foyer. Light flashed, a plume of smoke filled the air, and the sound of shattered glass drowned out the music. In that instant she felt herself fall from the stage, her breath caught, and the world turned into a storm of noise and fear. When the police arrived, the chaos was still palpable; the scent of burning plastic clung to the air like a second skin. Evelyn’s voice onstage was replaced by the roar of her own pulse. The event left a scar that would follow her wherever she played. The first time Evelyn realized how the memory haunted her was during a rehearsal a week later. She was trying to master a difficult passage, but every time she placed her fingers on the correct string, a flash of the explosion’s light rushed into her mind. Her mind would then cut back to the stage, her breathing shallow, the taste of burnt plastic and coffee that had been in her hand during the blast. “When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once,” she told me, her voice trembling. The threat of being surrounded by a crowded hall—loud applause, the murmur of a crowd, even the simple sound of a microphone—was enough to bring her back to the front row, feeling the ground shift beneath her. This threat‑driven flashback disrupted her concentration, leaving her unable to focus on the notes she had practiced for weeks. The irritability that followed her onstage during that evening was not merely frustration; it was a protective reaction to the sudden feeling that the world had shifted to a place where danger lurked behind every curtain. The vivid, sensory‑rich memories of the terror, however, did more than just cause flashbacks. The clarity and detail of the images—“My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed” – amplified the sense that the event was not merely a past occurrence, but a persistent threat. The taste she could summon each time she recalled the explosion made the memory feel as fresh as that night. Evelyn’s thoughts swirled, “I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns,” and the taste was a reminder that the danger was not over. This relentless recollection fed her negative appraisals. She came to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere, that people are not what they seem, and that she has no future. Each recollection reinforced the idea that she was unsafe and that the world had turned against her. Conversely, her negative appraisals fueled the intensity of the memories. As Evelyn began to see her colleagues as unreliable, as audiences as potentially hostile, the context in which she imagined the concert hall changed. The very act of believing that people are not what they seem cast the memory of the bombing into a darker light. The fear that she would be judged or betrayed made the memory more urgent, making the taste of burnt plastic feel even more urgent and real. In this way, the negative appraisal loop tightened the grasp of the traumatic memory, and the memory further entrenched those negative beliefs. For months, the cycle of threat, memory, and negative appraisal continued to erode Evelyn’s ability to perform. The same sounds that once exhilarated her now triggered the flashback, and her frustration led to angry outbursts that left her colleagues wary. Her relationship with her partner suffered because the partner’s supportive words were often dismissed as “not what they seem,” a product of her distrust. Evelyn’s concentration suffered so badly that she missed a rehearsal entirely and almost lost her next performance slot. She finally sought help after a rehearsal in which, in the middle of a passage, she felt herself freeze and taste the metallic tang of fear so strongly that she could not finish the bow. She realized that her life as a musician, the place where she felt she belonged, had become a battlefield. Evelyn came to the clinic clutching her score, her fingers trembling on the strings. She was most afraid that the memories would continue to strip her of her career and her sense of place, and she hoped to regain control over her concentration and her relationships. The next session, she described her fear that she would no longer belong anywhere, and she asked for help to break the cycle that had turned the memory of a single night into an all‑encompassing threat.

**Vignette: Amara**

Amara is an eighty-year-old Congolese woman who has been married to her husband Emmanuel for over fifty years. She serves as a pastor in a small Pentecostal congregation in the city where she resettled nearly two decades ago, and on most Sunday mornings she stands at the pulpit with a steadiness that few in her congregation would question. What they do not see is what happens when she sits alone in the church after everyone has gone home.

She was in her early sixties when the violence came to her village. She had lived through political unrest before — her whole life had been shaped by it — but nothing had prepared her for the morning armed men moved through her community with a purposefulness that left no room for negotiation. She and Emmanuel fled with two of their grandchildren, walking for days through bush and across borders, sleeping in fields, eating almost nothing. One of her daughters did not make it out. Amara does not speak of her daughter by name in sessions, referring to her only as "the one we left." Whether she means left behind in the village or left behind in death is something she has never clarified, and her face closes in a particular way whenever the subject approaches, like a door swinging shut.

The years in the refugee camp were long. She was a pastor there too, holding services in a canvas tent, praying over the sick and the grieving, holding other women's hands through losses that mirrored her own. She learned to be a container for other people's suffering, which meant she had little practice acknowledging her own. By the time she was resettled and her congregation grew and Emmanuel's health began to decline, her own interior life had become a place she rarely visited.

Now, at eighty, she finds herself visited instead. Sleep comes reluctantly and leaves early. In the hours before dawn she lies in the bed she shares with Emmanuel and watches the ceiling, her mind returning without her permission to the road out of the village — the sound of her own breathing, the weight of a grandchild on her back, the smoke behind her. She does not call these memories. She experiences them as a kind of presence, as though the past has not passed at all but is simply waiting in the dark room with her.

During the day she manages. She visits congregation members, she prepares her sermons, she counsels young couples and grieving families. But certain things undo her without warning. A car backfiring on the street outside the church sends her heart into a kind of frenzy she finds shameful. The smell of woodsmoke from a neighbor's fireplace in winter can stop her completely in the middle of a sentence. She has learned to excuse herself quickly in those moments, to step outside or into a bathroom, to press her hands flat against a wall until the feeling passes. She tells no one.

She came to therapy not for herself, she explained in the first session, but because Emmanuel had noticed she was not sleeping and had asked her to come. She sat with her handbag in her lap and her back very straight and said she understood that what happened to her family was God's will, and she meant it, and she also could not stop seeing the road.

There is a particular grief she carries that she has only recently begun to name: the sense that she has spent twenty years helping her congregation survive their losses while her own loss has gone unwitnessed. She built a life of extraordinary purpose in the aftermath of trauma, and she does not regret a moment of it. But some part of her is still walking out of that village, still carrying the child, still not yet allowed to stop and sit down and say: *this happened to me, and it was unbearable, and I am still here.*

Emma, a 66-year-old divorced woman of Oceania descent, has been working as a Curriculum Designer for over four decades. Her life took an unexpected turn when she was deployed to a combat zone during her military service years ago. The trauma from that experience continues to shape her daily life and interactions. The traumatic event itself unfolded with shocking suddenness. Emma had been tasked with setting up a safe communication channel in a remote area when the base came under heavy fire. As chaos erupted, she watched helplessly as comrades were injured or killed around her. A helicopter made several low passes overhead, dropping supplies and medevac teams, but the noise of its rotors only added to the overwhelming cacophony of gunfire and explosions. Since then, Emma’s world has been punctuated by sudden intrusions from that day. At home, in her quiet suburb, she would be out for a walk when a distant drone of an aircraft overhead would trigger a flood of memories. The sound of rotors spinning would plunge her back into the fear and helplessness she felt during those moments under fire. Emma had come to believe she was powerless in such situations, leading her to avoid places where she might encounter similar auditory triggers. She found herself increasingly isolated from others due to these avoidance behaviors; instead of attending social gatherings or going out for errands, she stayed home as much as possible. Even at work, Emma made a point to remain close to the exit during meetings, feeling a constant need to be ready to escape if something similar happened again. In her role as a Curriculum Designer, Emma’s daily environment became another source of distress. She worked in an open office space, and the sounds of colleagues’ conversations or the hum of machines often reminded her of the combat zone she had escaped. Her tendency to avoid feelings intensified at work; when faced with deadlines or challenging tasks that required emotional investment, she would retreat into a detached state, finding it difficult to fully engage with her job. Emma’s memories of the event were fragmented and surreal. She knew what happened but found herself unable to articulate the sequence of events clearly. The memory was so extreme it felt almost unbelievable, as if it had been something that happened to someone else. This fragmentation made it even harder for her to process or integrate the experience into a coherent narrative. The weight of these experiences led Emma to develop strong negative appraisals about herself and her surroundings. She harbored deep self-doubt, questioning whether she could make the right decisions in critical situations. Her isolation only grew as she felt increasingly set apart from others who didn’t understand or share her intense fears and memories. It was during a particularly overwhelming episode at work that Emma realized she needed help. A distant helicopter sound had triggered a panic attack while she was in a meeting, leading to a series of distressing flashbacks. She found herself unable to focus on anything else until she left the office abruptly. This incident, along with growing concerns about her declining performance and increasing isolation from colleagues, finally pushed Emma to seek professional assistance. What frightened her most was the prospect of never feeling safe again, always living in a state of hypervigilance where every sound or situation could trigger memories of that day. Yet, she was also hoping for a chance to reclaim her life, to find ways to manage and cope with these intrusive thoughts and feelings so that she could reconnect with others and regain control over her daily experiences. Emma’s journey toward recovery is marked by the hope that through therapy, she can begin to rebuild her sense of self and trust in her ability to navigate the world without being consumed by the lingering echoes of her traumatic past.

Rohan is a 20-year-old South Asian American writer who presented for treatment approximately seven months after the sudden death of his younger brother, Arjun, who collapsed without warning from an undetected cardiac arrhythmia during a family gathering. Arjun was seventeen. There had been no illness, no warning, no moment in which the family could have prepared themselves. One moment Arjun was laughing at the dinner table; the next, Rohan was on the floor beside him, calling his name while their mother screamed for someone to dial 911. Rohan held his brother's hand until the paramedics arrived. Arjun was pronounced dead at the hospital that evening.

In the weeks that followed, Rohan described feeling as though the architecture of his understanding of the world had simply collapsed. He had grown up believing, in the way that most young people do without examining it, that catastrophe announces itself — that there are signs, that youth is a kind of protection, that the people sitting across from you at dinner will still be there tomorrow. Arjun's death had not simply taken his brother; it had dismantled every quiet assumption Rohan had ever made about how life worked. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt less like a thought and more like a physical fact, that the world was genuinely and randomly dangerous — that safety was an illusion people told themselves because they had not yet seen what he had seen. When friends described feeling safe or content, he found their confidence bewildering, almost naïve.

Rohan had always identified as a warm, curious, and essentially happy person. Writing had come easily to him; he had been working on a novel and contributing essays to a small literary magazine. In the months after Arjun's death, he found himself certain that the person who had written those pages no longer existed. He did not experience this as grief in any form he recognized — he experienced it as a permanent alteration, a before and after with no bridge between them. He was not sad in a way that felt temporary. He was miserable in a way that felt like the truth about him now.

His sleep had deteriorated significantly. He lay awake for hours, and when he did sleep, he woke easily. Ordinary sounds — a door closing in another room, a notification chime from his phone, a car backfiring outside his apartment building — would jolt him upright, his heart pounding, his body certain something had gone wrong. He was unable to settle even in environments he knew to be safe. Sitting at his writing desk, which had once been a place of absorption and pleasure, he found himself scanning, waiting, unable to release the vigilance that had taken up residence in him since the night he knelt on the floor beside his brother.

His writing had effectively stopped. He could not make plans — not for the novel, not for submissions, not even for the following week. What frightened him most about planning was the implicit assumption that the future would arrive, that the people he loved would be in it. He had learned, in the most visceral way possible, that this assumption could be shattered in a single moment, and he was not willing to make it again. He had withdrawn from a writing residency he had been accepted to before Arjun's death, citing personal reasons without elaborating. His editor at the literary magazine had stopped reaching out after several unanswered emails.

He had also begun seeking reassurance from his parents and his closest friend with a frequency that had begun to strain those relationships — asking, repeatedly, whether they thought he was handling things normally, whether they believed he would be all right. He avoided anything that carried Arjun's presence: a particular playlist, the restaurant where they used to eat together, the neighborhood where they grew up.

What finally brought Rohan to seek help was a conversation with his mother, who told him quietly that she was worried she was losing him too. He came to the first session saying very little about what he hoped for, except that he wanted to know whether it was possible to live in the world again without being afraid of it.

Valentina Cruz grew up in a modest American home where the living room floor served as both a play space and a battleground. When she was eight, her father would pace the rug during their arguments with her mother, his hands sweeping stacks of mail, mugs, and ceramic figurines from the coffee table. The violence arrived in sharp, physical bursts. Valentina learned to track his shoulders tensing before a throw, to brace herself before the crash. Those mornings carried a sensory imprint that outlasted the shouting: the smell of burnt toast and the fine dust of plaster settling from a dislodged picture frame. Even now, at twenty-one, the memories do not sit neatly in her past. They feel more real than normal, as if the plaster dust still hangs in the air. When a slight breeze or a shift in thought carries that familiar scent, the scene rushes back, complete and immediate, but she often pushes it away before it settles, blocking the full recall before it can fully form. The sensory map of that childhood room persists. A sudden clatter in her apartment sends her shoulders up; a photo on her phone screen showing a raised hand or a scattered table catches her eye and holds her still. She remains hyperalert to the space around her, watching for movement, so that when a coworker suddenly turns near her drafting desk, her body reacts as if danger is already closing in. Her irritability has developed beside this watchfulness. She snaps at small delays, her anger flaring without warning, yet the tension in her chest never quite dissolves. She is certain that even the slightest upset signals something larger going wrong, that she cannot cope with the friction of daily life, and that the people who caused the original harm walked away unscathed, leaving her to bear the weight alone. As an animator working in a bright, open-plan studio, Valentina’s days are structured around digital canvases and stylus movements. Her workspace has become a quiet theater for her habits. When her tablet slips or a colleague drops a sketchpad, she still feels the old sweep of objects mid-air. She has come to believe that bad things happen without warning, that she cannot stop them from landing. To steady herself, she restricts her eating, counting portions and choosing bland, predictable meals. The strict control feels like a bulwark. She also avoids future plans, declining weekend gatherings and delayed trips, since committing to tomorrow feels like leaving herself exposed. At work, she sidesteps anything that reminds her of her father, avoiding the particular cadence of his voice in her head when male supervisors speak, steering clear of the studio’s heavy wooden doors that echo like the living room floor. Her avoidance is a quiet habit that has accumulated over months, narrowing her circle without her noticing. Now, Valentina sits in her therapy office with a folder of animation sketches she has been meaning to finish, but has postponed indefinitely. She has come for help not because something has shattered, but because the quiet accumulation of her habits has begun to feel heavier than her childhood years. She worries that she will never trust the future to be still, that she will remain locked in a perpetual state of bracing. What she hopes for is simple: to sit with a memory long enough to let it pass, to say yes to a plan without feeling the floor give way, and to know that when things do rise and fall, she can stay grounded. She leaves the session carrying the same hyperalert watchfulness, but with a new certainty that she does not have to carry it alone.

He is 64 now, a jeweler with steady hands and tired eyes, and when he talks about his childhood he does it the way he handles a damaged clasp—carefully, indirectly, as if too much force will break something small but essential. He grew up in a crowded apartment above his uncle’s grocery store, the middle of several children, in a home where everyone learned to listen for footsteps. At night he would lie awake and track the sounds that mattered: his father’s key at the door, the scrape of a chair, his mother’s voice turning soft and appeasing. Then, sometimes, the crack of a hand against a wall or a body. He remembers the yellow light over the kitchen table, the smell of beer and fried onions, his mother trying to keep her face still while his father shouted at her for money, for dinner, for looking at him the wrong way. As a boy he never knew what would set it off. He only knew the feeling that came first—that sudden drop in his stomach, the sense that the room had changed temperature.

He never describes himself as a victim. He says, “Nothing happened to me directly.” But he remembers standing in the hallway in his undershirt, hearing his younger sister cry in the bedroom while his father pushed his mother against the sink. He remembers wanting to run in and also being unable to move. Sometimes he would pull his siblings into the room they shared, shut the door, and tell them to stay quiet. Other times he would sit against the door from the inside, as if his weight could keep the violence contained to the kitchen. In the morning the family would behave as though the night had been erased. His mother wore long sleeves. His father drank coffee and read the paper. The children went to school.

As he got older, he learned to live in a state of readiness. He watched faces closely. He noticed changes in tone before anyone else did. Teachers described him as serious, mature, “good in a crisis.” Inside, he was restless and easily startled. If a classmate slammed a desk, his whole body jolted. He was ashamed of that reaction and covered it with a shrug or a joke. By adolescence he spent as little time at home as possible, lingering after school, then apprenticing with a jeweler in his late teens. He says he was drawn to the bench because it was one place where pressure had rules. Metal responded to heat in predictable ways. A stone could be set with patience. Tiny instruments, careful attention, quiet—he built his life around these things.

He marries young and works hard. Customers trust him with engagement rings, family heirlooms, watches engraved with births and anniversaries. He likes repairing what other people are afraid to lose. Yet at home he is not easy. He startles when his children run up behind him. He cannot tolerate yelling, especially between a man and a woman. If his wife raises her voice during an argument, even for ordinary reasons, he feels his chest tighten and his thoughts go blank. He either goes silent for hours or leaves the apartment and walks until he can breathe normally again. He tells himself he is preventing a worse fight, but his distance becomes its own wound in the marriage. His wife says she never knows where he goes emotionally. Eventually they divorce, a loss he speaks about with more regret than anger.

Over the years he becomes known as meticulous, dependable, somewhat formal. He opens his shop before sunrise and keeps the front display immaculate. But he avoids certain jobs, though he does not advertise this to anyone. If a couple comes in bickering sharply over a purchase, he feels his shoulders lock. If a customer pounds the glass case to emphasize a point, he has to steady his hands under the counter before he can pick up a loupe. Loud voices from the street pull him to the window before he even realizes he has moved. He checks the lock several times each night before leaving. At home he sleeps lightly and wakes from dreams he cannot always fully remember—only the feeling of dread, his heart racing, the certainty that something terrible is about to happen in the next room.

He still minimizes what he lived through. He says his father “had a temper,” his mother “put up with a lot.” Yet he tears up when he describes his grandson hiding under a table during a family argument, and how seeing that small curled body made him feel suddenly sick. Since then, memories have come more insistently. He finds himself back in that kitchen hallway, hearing his mother plead in a voice meant not to provoke. He avoids family gatherings where alcohol is flowing because he becomes tense and watchful, unable to relax. He prefers to work alone at the bench, bent over gold and silver, where concentration can narrow the world. Even there, if someone enters too abruptly or raises their voice from the showroom, a flash of fear moves through him before he can name it. He is a man who has spent decades creating beauty and repair with his hands, while carrying a nervous system still organized around the sounds of violence from long ago.

Hinerangi is a 77-year-old New Zealand Māori woman, divorced, who has practiced as a cardiothoracic surgeon for over four decades. She was referred for psychological assessment following a protracted and life-threatening illness — a severe cardiac event that required emergency intervention approximately fourteen months ago. The cruel irony of the referral was not lost on her: she had spent her career on the other side of the sternum, and she arrived at the intake appointment with the particular disorientation of someone who had become, without warning, the patient.

The event itself unfolded in fragments she has never been able to reassemble into a coherent whole. Hinerangi recalls the sudden pressure in her chest during a morning ward round, the ceiling tiles of her own hospital tilting as she lost her footing, and then — nothing. There are hours she simply cannot account for. She knows from colleagues that she was resuscitated in the corridor, that she was intubated, that she spent eleven days in the ICU. But her memory of that period arrives in disconnected pieces that refuse to cohere: a brief, extraordinarily vivid image of a nurse's face close to hers, the sensation of restraints, a fragment of conversation she cannot place. Other stretches are entirely blank, as though excised. Some moments are rendered in near-hallucinatory clarity while adjacent hours have vanished entirely. She describes it as trying to read a document with whole paragraphs burned away.

It is precisely this fractured, unresolvable quality of the memory that has driven Hinerangi toward the coping strategies she now relies upon — strategies that, over the past year, have quietly worsened her position. Unable to construct a coherent narrative of what happened to her, she has turned to relentless meaning-seeking, spending hours in a kind of ruminative loop asking why this happened to her specifically, at this point in her life, after decades of disciplined self-care. This search for causation has found no satisfying answer, and the unanswered question has become a wound she keeps reopening. Alongside this, she has imposed on herself a rigid regime of forced positive thinking — she will not permit herself to acknowledge fear or grief, insisting internally that she is fortunate, that she survived, that she must be grateful. The effect of this suppression is that the fragmented memories are never processed, never contextualised, never allowed to settle into a stable narrative. The gaps remain gaps. The pieces do not fit together any better for being refused.

What has emerged from the interaction of these unresolved memories and the strategies deployed to manage them is a profound and frightening transformation in how Hinerangi understands herself. The person she was — certain, technically gifted, grounded in a vocation she had inhabited since her twenties — is no longer recognisable to her. She had built her identity around competence in the face of mortal crisis, and having been the body in crisis, she no longer knows who she is. She has lost faith not only in the reliability of her own body but in something larger: the sense that life holds a comprehensible order, that decades of service and discipline confer some protection, that the world is fair in any meaningful way. Forced positive reframing, applied as a daily discipline, has not restored this faith — it has, if anything, deepened the sense of inauthenticity, because she knows she does not believe the reassuring thoughts she is manufacturing.

The occupational consequences have been severe. Hinerangi continues to operate, but she now avoids all contact with the medical environment that is not strictly required by her surgical duties. She declines to attend clinical case reviews held in the ICU, refuses her own scheduled physical examinations, and has not set foot in the cardiac ward where she collapsed. Her colleagues have noticed. She has offered no explanation. The avoidance keeps the fragmented memories at a safe distance, but it also keeps her from the very professional context that once anchored her sense of self.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the scrub room three weeks ago when she looked at her own hands preparing for surgery and did not recognise them as belonging to her. She is most afraid that the person she was before is simply gone. What she is hoping for, though she says it with some difficulty, is to understand what happened to her — all of it — and to find out whether there is still someone coherent on the other side.

# Magda's Vigil

Magda was seventy-four when she first walked into the clinic, her posture still upright from decades of physical therapy practice, but her hands trembled slightly as she filled out the intake forms. She had been referred by her primary care physician, who had grown concerned about her drinking and her refusal to leave the house except for essential errands. Her husband, Stefan, sat beside her in the waiting room—they had been married for forty-eight years—and he watched her with the careful attention of someone who had learned to monitor for signs of distress.

The traumatic event had occurred fifty-two years earlier, in 1972, when Magda was a young woman in Prague. She and Stefan had been activists, and on a March evening, Soviet-backed security forces had raided their apartment. The sound of boots on the stairwell, the splintering of the door, the smell of vodka on the breath of the officer who grabbed her—these sensations had been seared into her nervous system with a clarity that had not faded. She had been interrogated for eight hours while Stefan was held separately. The threat had been explicit and physical. By dawn, they had been released, but the message was unmistakable: they were marked. Within weeks, they had fled to America with nothing.

For the first three decades, Magda had built a life. She had retrained as a physical therapist, worked in a busy clinic for thirty-five years, raised two children, and created what appeared to be stability. But five years ago, something had shifted. Stefan had mentioned casually one evening that he had seen a documentary about the Prague Spring on television. Magda had not watched it, but the mere act of him talking about that period—his careful, gentle words about what had happened to them—had triggered something that would not settle. Talking about the event now sent her into a state of agitation that could last for hours. Her breathing would become shallow, her mind would flood with images so vivid that they felt like they were occurring in real time rather than belonging to a past that was decades behind her.

The sensory triggers had become inescapable. The smell of alcohol—particularly vodka, though any strong spirits could do it—would transport her instantly. A client's cologne one afternoon at the clinic had contained a sharp, alcoholic note, and Magda had found herself unable to continue the session. She had excused herself to the bathroom and sat on the closed toilet lid for twenty minutes, her heart racing, her ears straining to hear footsteps in the hallway. The smell of something burnt—toast left too long in the toaster, a neighbor's grill, even the slightly scorched aroma from the clinic's aging HVAC system—would send her into a state of high alert, as if danger were imminent.

Over the past two years, she had begun to drink in the evenings. A glass of wine at first, then two, sometimes three. Stefan had asked her about it gently, but she could not explain it in a way that made sense. The alcohol seemed to dull the constant vigilance, the exhausting work of monitoring her environment for threats. She had come to spend her evenings in the living room with the lights on, a glass in her hand, listening. Always listening. For footsteps on the porch. For the sound of a car slowing in front of the house. For any noise that might signal that someone was trying to enter.

The consequences had accumulated quietly. She had taken early retirement from the clinic six months ago, telling her employer that her knees could no longer handle the physical demands of the work. The truth was that she could no longer tolerate being in a space where strangers approached her, where she could not control the exits, where unexpected sounds echoed off the walls. Her children had stopped calling as frequently because the conversations were strained. When they did call, they could hear the tension in her voice, the way she rushed to end the conversation. She had become someone who dwelt obsessively on how she used to be—confident, capable, present with her clients, able to walk into a room without scanning for threats.

What had finally brought her to seek help was a moment two weeks earlier when a delivery person had knocked on the door. Magda had reacted as if the house were being breached. She had grabbed a kitchen knife and hidden in the bedroom closet, her heart pounding so violently she thought she might be having a cardiac event. Stefan had found her there, shaking, unable to articulate why she had been so terrified of a teenager with a package. That night, he had insisted she call her doctor.

Now, in the clinic, Magda sat with her hands folded in her lap and said quietly, "I don't feel safe anywhere. And the worst part is knowing that I should. That there is no danger. But I can't make myself believe it."

He is a 74-year-old Oceania man who has spent most of his adult life working as an editor, a job that suits the part of him that notices small errors, strained phrases, and the exact place where a sentence stops making sense. He speaks in a careful, measured way, as though he has learned that precision can keep things from falling apart. In sessions, he slowly circles around the events that changed him, returning often to details he can control because the rest still feels too jagged to hold directly.

The violence begins years ago in a romantic relationship that, at first, he remembers as warm, even exciting. His partner is charming in public and volatile in private. The first incidents are easy to minimize: a hand gripped too tightly around his arm, a shove into a wall during an argument, a sudden blow that comes after hours of criticism and taunting. He tells himself it is a bad patch, that if he is patient, if he stops provoking, if he becomes quieter and more agreeable, the relationship will settle. Instead, the abuse becomes a pattern. He learns to read footsteps, slamming doors, the shift in tone that means danger. He starts keeping his body angled away, shoulders slightly hunched, making himself smaller in his own home.

Over time, he becomes isolated. He stops inviting friends over because he does not want to explain the marks on his face or why he seems distracted. As an editor, he remains functional on the surface, but at work he is increasingly unable to tolerate being startled. A dropped book, a colleague approaching from behind, a raised voice in the office can send a surge through him so strong that he has to excuse himself to the restroom and sit with both hands pressed to the sink until his breathing slows. He notices he is reading the same paragraph again and again without taking it in. His work, once a source of pride, becomes a place where he can hide inside other people’s words while his own life becomes unmanageable.

The relationship ends, but the abuse does not feel finished. Long after he is physically safe, his body remains as if it is waiting for the next strike. He wakes in the night with his heart racing, convinced for a moment that someone is in the house. He checks locks repeatedly, then checks them again. He cannot tolerate having his back to a door. He chooses seats in cafés, waiting rooms, and theaters with escape routes in mind. He is embarrassed by how often he scans a room, how quickly he notices exits, corners, and the size of men’s hands. At times he feels ashamed that a voice from the past still seems to have authority over his body.

He is also burdened by memories that arrive without invitation. A smell, a tone of voice, the sight of a clenched jaw can pull him back with such force that the present briefly disappears. He describes it less as remembering than as being pulled under. When this happens, his chest tightens and his hearing seems to narrow. He may find himself standing in the kitchen with no clear sense of how he got there, staring at the counter and trying to reorient. He avoids television scenes with domestic conflict, and he no longer likes unexpected touch, even affectionate touch, because his body cannot always tell the difference soon enough.

The emotional life around the trauma is complicated by grief and self-reproach. He thinks often about how long he stayed, and he speaks with a quiet disgust toward himself that is hard to interrupt. He wonders how he could have misread kindness so completely. Divorce has left him alone, and although he has some contact with adult family members, he keeps much of the worst of it private. He does not want to be seen as fragile. Yet the effort to appear composed costs him. He tires easily, sleeps poorly, and moves through the day with the sense that he is bracing against something only he can see.

Even now, he remains alert to danger in ordinary moments. He flinches at sudden noise. He becomes irritable when interrupted, then feels guilty for snapping. Some mornings he tells himself he is simply old and tired, but the pattern is more than age. He lives in a narrowed world shaped by vigilance, avoidance, and the long afterlife of being hurt by the person who was supposed to love him.

Layla had never thought of herself as someone who could be broken by a single moment. At fifty-two, she had built a life she was proud of—a steady career as a project manager, a marriage that had weathered its share of storms, and a quiet sense of competence that she carried into every room. That was before the bombing at the city plaza, two years ago, when she had been walking back to her office after a lunch meeting. The explosion came from a parked delivery van, and in the seconds that followed, Layla found herself on the ground, her ears ringing, her vision blurred by dust and smoke. She had not been physically injured, not in any way that left a scar, but something inside her had been rearranged in a way she could not undo.

In the weeks that followed, Layla began to notice changes she could not explain to herself. She had always been someone who looked forward to the weekend, who laughed easily with her colleagues, who found pleasure in small routines. Now she woke each morning with a weight in her chest that she could not name. She used to be a happy person, she would think, but now she was always miserable. The thought arrived with a kind of dull certainty, as though happiness had been a coat she had left somewhere and could no longer find. She had also stopped recognizing herself. When she looked in the mirror, she saw a stranger—someone with wary eyes and a rigid posture, someone who flinched at sounds that had never bothered her before. She felt like she didn’t know herself anymore, and that loss was as frightening as the event itself.

The triggers came without warning and without mercy. The first time a police car passed her on the street, she felt her chest tighten and her palms go damp. It made no sense to her—the officers were not a threat—but the sight of an authority presence, the uniform, the vehicle, brought her straight back to the plaza, where she had seen first responders running toward the smoke. Helicopters were worse. The thud of rotors overhead, whether from a news chopper or a medical transport, sent her heart racing and her mind reeling. She would stop mid-sentence, her eyes scanning the sky, her body braced for something she could not name. Violence in any form—a shouting match on the subway, a news report about a fight—made her nauseous. She had begun to avoid crowded public spaces, taking longer routes to work, leaving social gatherings early.

At her job as a project manager, Layla had always been known for her steady hand in high-pressure situations. But now, when a colleague raised their voice in a meeting, she felt her throat close. She had started to suspect that others could see what had happened to her just by looking at her. She was certain that her face betrayed her, that her anxiety was written in the tightness of her jaw, the way she started at sudden noises. She began to avoid eye contact in the hallways, to eat lunch at her desk with the door closed, to decline invitations to team outings. Her husband noticed the distance. He would ask what was wrong, and she would say she was tired, because the truth was too tangled to explain.

What finally brought Layla to seek help was a moment of quiet desperation. She had been sitting in her car in the parking lot of her office building, unable to open the door, because a delivery truck had rumbled past and she had felt the old panic rise. She sat there for twenty minutes, gripping the steering wheel, wondering who she had become. She was afraid that if she did not find a way back to herself, she would lose the life she had spent decades building. She wanted to stop feeling like a stranger in her own skin. She wanted to be able to walk down a street without scanning the rooftops. She wanted to recognize her own face in the mirror again.

Elena Rodriguez remembers the compound walls closing in as the patrols tightened their net. The sharp, familiar tang of aguardiente clung to the border guards as they directed the line of refugees with barked instructions. She watched a man in a crisp olive uniform gesture toward the processing tents, his movements sudden and heavy. Elena had braced herself, expecting another wave of footsteps, another shout that would send her scurrying into the shadows. When the memory surfaces now, it arrives with the same cadence: she hears the guards’ voices echoing in her head, clear and distinct, just as they had been that evening. The details remain locked in place—the cracked pavement, the metallic groan of the gates, the heavy wool of her coat. She does not just recall the event; she relives its texture, and the weight of it often stops her mid-step, leaving her breathless until the moment passes. In the years that followed, Elena had come to believe the world remained as precarious as that night. She was certain that danger could materialize without warning, and she began to distrust the ease of those around her, wondering what motives lay beneath their smiles. What frightened her most was the quiet uncertainty of her own reflection; she looked in the mirror and felt like a stranger wearing her own skin, unsure of who she was or how to act. To steady herself, she developed habits that made sense in their own logic. She dwelled on the night, replaying the decisions she might have made differently, certain that one different choice would have kept her family intact. When the past pressed close, she would fill the silence with loud television or blast her playlist until the sounds from her childhood faded into the background. She learned to position herself carefully, always choosing seats near exits or against solid walls, ensuring she was shielded from whatever might approach. Now, as a prison guard in a sprawling state facility, her daily environment mirrors the landscape of her fear. The corridors echo with the clipped tones of officers, and the scent of alcohol from the break room drifts past her desk, catching her off guard. When a supervisor approaches and issues a direct order, Elena’s shoulders tense, her breath catching as if she is being called to attention once more. She notices the uniforms around her, the structured authority in their posture, and she finds herself stepping back, giving them space rather than meeting them head-on. Unexpected movement near her workspace sends a quick ripple through her; she turns sharply, assessing the threat before she realizes it is only a colleague reaching for a file. She has started to react as though the past is breathing down her neck, even on quiet shifts when the doors are locked and the yard is still. Her careful positioning and heightened alertness have reshaped her workdays, turning routine patrols into moments of sustained vigilance. The quiet accumulation of these patterns has left Elena weary. Her husband notices the distance she keeps, the way she scans the room before sitting down, the way she sometimes stops mid-sentence when a voice from the past rises in her mind. Her PCL5 score reflects the weight of her symptoms, but it is the daily reality that finally brought her to the clinic. She came on a Thursday after a routine head count triggered such a sudden wave of overwhelm that she had to step outside, leaning against the brick wall until her breathing slowed. She no longer wants to live in a state of perpetual readiness. She hopes to understand why the world feels so heavy, and what she might do to stop bracing for a danger that is no longer there.

Michael, a 33-year-old African American tailor, sought help after a series of traumatic events left him feeling lost and constantly on guard. His life had taken an unexpected turn when he witnessed a terrorist attack in his neighborhood last year. The event was so horrifying that he still struggles to remember parts of it. Michael described the scene as chaotic and confusing, with flashes of violence and sudden silence that seemed equally terrifying. Since the incident, Michael found himself spending long hours on his phone or playing games online to avoid thinking about what had happened. He also picked arguments at work, often creating drama just to distract himself from the lingering trauma. The constant need for distraction was a way to cope with the feelings of self-doubt and weakness that plagued him. Michael’s self-doubt intensified as he began to see himself as someone who couldn’t be trusted to make the right decisions. He felt like he no longer belonged anywhere, which led him to avoid making any future plans. This sense of not belonging was deeply tied to his fragmented memories. Sometimes, when he tried to recall what happened during the attack, he would feel completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. Other times, the memories replayed like an endless film, looping through his mind. The memory gaps and emotional numbness only deepened Michael’s feelings of weakness and doubt about himself. He often found himself scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building, feeling unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see everything happening around him. This hypervigilance made it difficult to focus on his work at the tailor shop, leading to several mistakes that further fueled his self-doubt. Michael’s occupation as a tailor provided a backdrop for many of these behaviors and triggers. He would often be distracted by intrusive thoughts while working with fabric or cutting patterns, causing him to lose track of time and make errors in his designs. His colleagues noticed the changes in his behavior but didn't fully understand what was driving them. Over time, Michael’s hypervigilance became a constant presence, and he found himself constantly on edge. This made it nearly impossible for him to engage with others or enjoy his work as he once did. He had come to believe that every unfamiliar sound or movement could signal danger, which only fueled his need to avoid any potential triggers. The culmination of these experiences led Michael to seek help. What frightened him most was the fear that he would never be able to return to a normal life and the constant worry about when the next threat might emerge. He hoped for a way to regain control over his thoughts, emotions, and actions, finding solace in knowing that there were strategies and support systems available to help him navigate through this challenging period. Michael’s journey had been marked by significant challenges, but he was beginning to see a path forward. His hope lay in understanding the connection between his experiences and the symptoms that developed as a result, ultimately aiming for a sense of belonging and self-assurance once more.

# Priya

Priya was sixty-eight when she first understood that the trembling in her hands had nothing to do with age. She had been a photographer for forty-two years—a good one, sought after for wedding portfolios and corporate portraits—but in recent months she found herself unable to steady the camera during shoots. Her hands would shake not from fatigue but from a kind of vigilance that had wound itself so tightly through her body that she could no longer distinguish between alertness and panic. The shaking had begun in earnest two years ago, though she could trace its roots much further back, to a childhood she had spent decades trying not to think about.

Her father had been a man of sudden rages. Priya's mother had died when she was four, and her father's grief had calcified into something cruel. He would strike her without warning—for a mispronounced word, for failing to fold his shirts correctly, for the simple fact of being in his line of sight. The blows had come with accusations: *You're worthless. You'll never amount to anything. You're ungrateful.* By the time she was twelve, Priya had learned to make herself small, to anticipate his moods, to scan his face for the first sign of displeasure. She had also learned something else, something that had never left her: that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that she could never truly trust anyone to protect her.

Now, at seventy, Priya lived alone in a small apartment in Palo Alto. She had been divorced for fifteen years—her husband had wanted children, and she could not bear the thought of bringing a child into her own fractured sense of security. She had no close friends, though she had colleagues who respected her work. What she had instead was a grinding, unrelenting sense that something terrible was always about to happen. Because she was convinced that no one had ever held her father accountable for what he had done—he had died in his sleep at eighty-three, never apologized, never acknowledged the harm he had caused—she had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unjust, that cruelty went unpunished, and that she herself was marked by his violence in a way that could never be erased. This certainty that she belonged nowhere, that she was irrevocably contaminated by what had been done to her, had metastasized into a hypervigilance that governed every moment. She had to be on guard all the time, watching for the next threat, the next person who might hurt her, the next situation that might spiral into violence.

This constant scanning for danger had pushed her toward strategies that felt protective but had become increasingly isolating. She would cover her face with her hands when memories surfaced unbidden—not just the physical blows, but the shame that accompanied them, a shame so intense it felt like a second assault. She tried desperately to control her emotions in public, presenting a composed exterior while internally fracturing. Yet the very vigilance that drove these coping strategies also kept her trapped in a cycle with her memories. Because she was always on guard, always braced for threat, her mind remained hyperactive, alert to any detail that might signal danger. This meant that fragments of the trauma—a loud noise, the sight of an older man's hand raised to adjust his glasses, the smell of her father's cologne on a stranger—would ambush her without warning. When these intrusions came, she would desperately try to suppress them, to push them away, but suppression only made them more vivid. And when she attempted to deliberately recall what had happened, to try to make sense of it in a way that might reduce its power, the memories would scatter like startled birds. She could not access them in a coherent narrative; instead, they came in fragments of sensation and terror, the same terror she had felt as a child, raw and immediate.

She had developed a meaning-seeking ritual, turning the trauma over and over in her mind, asking herself *why* this had happened to her, as though understanding the reason might somehow retroactively make it survivable, might grant it a shape that could be contained. But the question led nowhere. There was no answer that made sense. Her father had simply been broken, and she had been the available target. The injustice of it—that he had lived a full life, that he had never suffered for what he had done, that she alone carried the weight of his violence—had become a kind of obsession.

Two years ago, Priya had stopped accepting new clients. She told people it was retirement, but the truth was that she could no longer manage the unpredictability of other people's needs, the intimacy required to capture someone's best self through a lens. She spent most of her time in her apartment, where the environment was controlled and predictable. She had not been to a restaurant in eighteen months. She had not attended a family gathering—her estranged sister had stopped inviting her after Priya had declined five times in a row. It was only when her optometrist, concerned about her trembling hands during an eye exam, gently suggested that she might benefit from talking to someone, that Priya finally made an appointment. She was afraid of what therapy might ask her to remember, afraid that speaking about the trauma aloud would make it more real. But she was also, at seventy, exhausted by the weight of carrying it alone, and she had begun to wonder if there was any way back to a life where her hands could be steady, where she could walk into a room without scanning for exits and threats.

# Arjun's Story

Arjun Patel was thirty-eight when the men in unmarked vehicles pulled him off a construction site outside Kandahar. He had been working as a civilian contractor, managing logistics for a development project—honest work, he had believed, work that mattered. The soldiers never identified themselves clearly. They moved with the efficiency of men who did not need to explain themselves. Within hours he was in a concrete room with a single window reinforced with steel mesh, and for the next forty-three days, he existed in a state of profound uncertainty. His captors questioned him repeatedly about connections he did not have, affiliations he had never held. They isolated him from other detainees, moved him between locations without warning, and kept him perpetually unsure whether his next meal would come or whether the next sound of boots in the corridor meant interrogation or something worse. When he was finally released—a case of mistaken identity, they said—he was skeletal and disoriented, convinced that his release was a trick, that he would be taken again.

Three years had passed since his return to the United States, and Arjun had rebuilt a life that looked, from the outside, stable. He worked as a park ranger in Colorado, a position that offered solitude and structure. He lived with his partner, Marcus, a man of extraordinary patience who had learned not to ask too many questions about the nights Arjun woke gasping or the meals left half-finished on his plate. But the stability was fragile, held together by habits that had calcified into something closer to ritual than recovery.

The triggers were everywhere, though Arjun had become skilled at naming them only to himself. Any conversation that drifted toward military operations or geopolitics would send him spiraling; he would excuse himself and find a reason to leave the room, his chest tightening with a dread he could not articulate. More insidious was the simple act of being seen—at the ranger station, in a grocery store, anywhere his presence might be noted or his appearance remarked upon. The feeling of eyes on him, of being visible, would resurrect the sensation of being watched through the window of that concrete room, and with it came the old conviction that he was marked, that someone was tracking him. Authority figures triggered the same response, though he had learned to manage it. When a police officer pulled him over for a broken taillight, or when the park superintendent called him into his office, Arjun's body would respond as though he were back in that chair, facing men in uniform who held his fate in their hands.

These triggers did not announce themselves gently. When someone at a dinner party mentioned a news story about military operations in the Middle East, Arjun found himself flooded with fragmented images—the texture of the concrete wall, the sound of a metal door, the particular quality of fear that had no object and no end. The memories came not as coherent narratives but as isolated snapshots, each one searing and complete: the face of one interrogator, frozen mid-sentence; the pattern of light through the mesh window; the sensation of his own heartbeat, which had seemed, in those days, to be the only thing keeping him tethered to existence. When the memories surfaced, they brought with them an echo of physical pain—a tightness in his chest, a phantom ache in his shoulders and wrists—sensations that belonged to that time and that time alone, yet which his body insisted on reliving with perfect fidelity.

What frightened Arjun most was the conviction that had settled into him like a stone: that he was fundamentally different from other men, that someone else would never have allowed themselves to be caught, that his captivity was not simply something that had happened to him but something he had failed to prevent. This sense of humiliation ran deeper than shame; it was a kind of permanent staining. He felt isolated even in Marcus's presence, certain that no one could truly understand what it meant to have been unmade and then reassembled into something that looked like a person but felt hollow inside. These beliefs about himself—that he was weak, that he was marked, that he could not be trusted to keep himself safe—began to reshape how he moved through the world. When he encountered a trigger, the memory would follow, and the memory would confirm what he already believed about himself, and that confirmation would make him more vigilant, more certain that danger was imminent, more convinced that the world was not a place where he could be safe.

Over the months following his return, Arjun had developed strategies to manage the unbearable uncertainty. He began to restrict his eating, counting calories with obsessive precision. The control felt necessary, a way of asserting dominion over at least one domain of his life. If he could master his body, could deny it what it craved, then perhaps he could master the chaos inside his mind. He spent hours constructing elaborate revenge fantasies in which he identified his captors and exacted a precise and terrible justice. These fantasies offered a strange comfort, a sense of agency that his actual life no longer provided. At work and at home, he had become a man of accommodation. When Marcus wanted to go to a restaurant, Arjun agreed, though the prospect of being in a crowded space filled him with dread. When his supervisor asked him to lead a group of tourists through the park, Arjun said yes, though the thought of being observed and evaluated made his skin crawl. He had come to believe that his safety depended on never refusing, never asserting a preference, never drawing attention to himself.

These strategies had consequences that accumulated slowly. His weight had dropped to a point where Marcus expressed concern. His revenge fantasies, once a source of grim satisfaction, had begun to feel hollow and circular, leaving him more depleted than before. The constant accommodation meant that he spent his days performing a version of himself that bore little resemblance to who he had been before captivity. And yet each of these strategies reinforced the very beliefs that had spawned them. When he restricted his eating, he felt the phantom pain in his chest intensify, as though his body were remembering that time when food had been withheld and uncertainty had been total. The pain would trigger a flood of those snapshot memories, which in turn would reinforce his conviction that he was damaged, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that he needed to be even more vigilant, even more controlled. The restriction would tighten. The fantasies would deepen. The accommodation would become more automatic.

At the ranger station, his avoidance had begun to show in his work. He had stopped taking the lead on visitor education programs, claiming he preferred solitary patrols. He had requested a transfer to the graveyard shift, which meant fewer interactions with the public and fewer opportunities to be seen or evaluated. His supervisor had noticed—had asked, gently, whether everything was all right—but Arjun had smiled and assured him that he simply preferred the quiet of the night shift. What he could not say was that the night felt safer, that daylight made him vulnerable, that the prospect of a uniform-wearing officer arriving at the station for any routine matter could send him into a state of hypervigilance that lasted for hours. When unexpected movements occurred near him—a colleague rounding a corner, a tourist approaching from a blind spot—his body would react before his mind could catch up. He would flinch, his muscles would tense, and for a moment he would be certain that danger was imminent, that the reprieve of the past three years had been an illusion, that he was about to be taken again.

The cycle had tightened over months until it felt like the only way he knew how to live. The memories came more frequently now, triggered by the smallest things. The threat felt constant, even when he was alone in his house, even when Marcus was asleep beside him. The conviction that he was fundamentally broken, fundamentally unsafe, had calcified into something that felt like truth. It was only when Marcus, with careful tenderness, had suggested that perhaps he might benefit from talking to someone—a therapist, someone trained in trauma—that Arjun had finally admitted that he could no longer manage alone. He had called the clinic on a Tuesday morning, his voice steady but his hands shaking, and made an appointment. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to articulate it, was the possibility that the man he had been before captivity might still exist somewhere inside him. What he feared most was that he did not.

Margaret, a 58-year-old woman from a small town in North America, had always found solace in the routines of her life, but that sense of normalcy shattered two years ago when she lost her husband, Tom, in a tragic car accident. It was a rainy evening when their lives changed forever. Margaret remembered it vividly—the sound of the rain tapping against the roof, the faint smell of wet asphalt, and the sudden, jarring call from the hospital that altered her world. Tom had been on his way home, rushing to get back to her after forgetting an important anniversary dinner reservation. The memory of the sirens still echoed in her mind, a haunting reminder of the chaos that unfolded that night. 

In the months following Tom's death, Margaret found herself plagued by distressing triggers that seemed to ambush her at every turn. Each anniversary of the accident became a day of dread, a reminder of her profound loss. She could feel the panic rise within her as the date approached, her heart racing like it had that fateful night. The day would come, and she would find herself paralyzed, unable to face the world outside her door. Instead, she would stay home, just as she had done last year, checking the locks on the doors and windows repeatedly, convinced that the outside world was no longer safe. The simple act of ensuring her home was secure had morphed into an obsession, each click of the lock filling her with a fleeting sense of control.

Margaret’s nights grew longer and more restless. Sleep became a cruel joke; she would lie awake, staring at the ceiling while the memories of that night replayed in her mind like a broken record. The sound of an ambulance siren could send her heart racing, her body instinctively tensing as if she were once again caught in the grip of that traumatic moment. It was as if she was trapped in a nightmare, unable to escape the relentless cycle of fear and anxiety. She often woke to find herself breathless, her heart pounding, as her mind raced with thoughts of what could have been done differently, what she could have said to Tom to prevent him from leaving that night. 

Even the mundane elements of her daily life became reminders of her grief. As she walked through town, cars passing by would remind her of the accident, the sight of a vehicle crumpled in an accident flashing before her eyes like a cruel joke. The smell of rain on pavement would transport her back to that dreadful evening, the scent of the wet ground intertwined with the memories she struggled to articulate. When she tried to remember the specifics of Tom's last moments, she found it difficult to access those memories, as if they were hidden behind a wall she couldn’t breach. Instead, they would flood back unexpectedly, leaving her gasping for breath, the weight of loss crashing over her like a tidal wave.

Margaret’s relationship with her friends and family began to suffer as she retreated deeper into her shell, avoiding gatherings that she once cherished, fearing that laughter and happiness would only highlight her own desolation. She had come to believe that her grief was a burden to those around her, so she isolated herself, convinced they would never understand the depths of her sorrow. Losing Tom felt like losing a part of herself, and the thought of sharing her pain felt daunting. 

Despite her overwhelming grief, a sliver of hope flickered within her. It was a quiet moment, an afternoon when she found herself staring at a photo of Tom, a smile frozen in time. Margaret realized she could no longer bear the weight of her anguish alone. The idea of seeking help took root in her mind, but so did fear—the fear that she would have to relive her trauma, that she might not find the solace she so desperately sought. What frightened her most was the idea of confronting the memories she had tried to suppress for so long. Yet, she yearned to reclaim her life, to find a way to honor Tom’s memory without being overwhelmed by the pain of his absence. 

And so, with a heavy heart and trembling hands, Margaret reached out for help, hoping to navigate through the darkness and find a path toward healing. Her journey was just beginning, but the first step was the hardest, a testament to the resilience she had yet to discover within herself.

# Amara's Testimony

Amara had been forty-two years old when she fled Sierra Leone in 2005, and she had been sixty-three for the past eight months. The gap between those two ages—twenty-one years of her life compressed into a series of decisions made under duress, each one stripping away some part of who she believed herself to be—had never fully closed. She lived in that interval still, even now, in a one-bedroom apartment in Atlanta where she had built a careful life as a financial analyst, a profession that rewarded precision, control, and the ability to see patterns in numbers that others missed. Numbers did not betray you. Numbers did not have uniforms or guns or the power to decide whether you lived or died.

The war had come to her village in the Kailahun District in waves, each one preceded by rumors that turned out to be true. When the rebels came through in the spring of 2005, they had separated the men from the women and children, and Amara had watched her husband Kofi being pulled from the group by soldiers whose faces she could no longer quite picture but whose voices—the tone of absolute command—she could still hear in her sleep. She was told to move, to walk, to leave everything behind. When she hesitated for a moment—a single moment—a rifle butt struck her across the shoulders, and she understood then that hesitation itself was a kind of resistance that would not be tolerated. She walked. She was forced to walk for three days through the bush with dozens of other women and children, and when she tried to help an elderly woman who had collapsed, she was struck again and told that mercy was not permitted. That woman did not get up. Amara never knew her name.

She had eventually reached a refugee camp in Guinea, where she remained for four years before an NGO helped her secure passage to the United States. She arrived in 2009 with a work visa, a degree in accounting from Freetown, and a body that had learned to make itself small and compliant. She built her career methodically—her analytical mind was an asset that no one could take from her—and she had made a quiet life. She had few close friends. She had declined several romantic advances, telling herself she was content alone, though the truth was more complicated: she could not bear the thought of depending on someone, of being vulnerable to another person's choices or whims.

But in the past two years, her carefully ordered existence had begun to fracture. It started with her niece Ama, who had moved to Atlanta to attend university. Amara loved her fiercely, and that love had become a kind of torment. She found herself lying awake at night, catastrophizing—imagining Ama in car accidents, attacked on campus, assaulted in her dormitory. Every time Ama was late responding to a text message, Amara's mind spiraled into scenarios of disaster. She would call repeatedly, her voice tight with an anxiety she could not quite explain to her niece, who had begun to withdraw from her, confused by the intensity of Amara's worry.

At work, Amara had become increasingly isolated. She avoided meetings where she might have to disagree with a colleague or assert a different viewpoint. When her manager, a white woman named Patricia, had suggested that Amara's analysis of a client portfolio was incomplete, Amara had felt her throat close. She could not argue back, could not defend her work, could not risk the confrontation. She had simply nodded and redone the analysis, though she believed her original assessment was sound. She began requesting assignments that allowed her to work alone, and her manager had started to pass her over for promotions that required collaboration and visibility.

What had finally broken through her denial was a routine traffic stop three months ago. A police officer had pulled her over for a broken taillight, and when he approached her window, something in her body had simply shut down. She had sat frozen, her hands visible on the steering wheel, barely breathing, while he checked her license and registration. He had been polite, professional, had issued a warning rather than a ticket. But Amara had spent the next week unable to drive, unable to leave her apartment without calculating escape routes, unable to shake the certainty that authority figures of any kind represented an existential threat. She had called in sick to work. She had ignored Ama's messages. She had sat in her apartment and felt the walls of her life contract around her.

It was Ama who finally insisted she seek help, who had researched therapists and made the appointment herself, who had told Amara that she could not live like this anymore—that Amara could not live like this anymore. Amara sits in the waiting room now, her purse held tight against her chest, terrified of what talking about the past might unleash, but more terrified still of the possibility that she might lose her niece, that her fear might push away the one person who still tethered her to a future worth living.

At sixty-six, Elena had always considered her quiet apartment a sanctuary, a place of meticulous order where she could immerse herself in the manuscripts she edited. For the past eight months, however, it had become a cage. The trouble began after her trip to visit her sister in her birth country, a trip meant to celebrate a milestone birthday but which coincided with a sudden, violent political uprising. One afternoon, while buying fruit in a bustling open-air market, a military truck screeched into the square. Soldiers in drab green uniforms spilled out, shouting commands. Elena remembers the chaos, the screams, and then the deafening blast from a car bomb at the far end of the market. In the ringing silence that followed, she found herself face-to-face with a young soldier, his eyes wide with fear and fury, the barrel of his rifle pointed directly at her chest. He didn't shoot, but the image of his face, the cold metal of the gun, and the acrid smell of smoke were seared into her mind.

Since returning to New York, the city has become a landscape of hidden threats. The Fourth of July was unbearable; the percussive boom of fireworks sent her scrambling into her windowless bathroom, hands clamped over her ears, convinced the building was under attack. The rhythmic clang of construction from the building site next door makes it impossible for her to concentrate on her editing work, each metallic bang feeling like a prelude to another explosion. She missed a major deadline last month because she spent three days too agitated to focus, the noise a constant, visceral reminder of the market square. Seeing a police officer on the street or even a uniformed security guard in her lobby sends a jolt of pure terror through her, and she will immediately cross the road or turn back the way she came to avoid them. More than anything, it is the soldier’s face that haunts her. It will flash into her mind without warning—while she’s washing dishes, while she’s reading—and for a moment, he is there in the room with her.

Night is the worst. As soon as darkness falls, a profound sense of vulnerability descends. Elena had come to believe that safety was an illusion, a story people told themselves during the daylight hours. Her daughter calls every evening, her voice full of loving reassurance. "You're safe now, Mom. You're home." But even as Elena agrees, a part of her mind screams that it isn't true, that danger is patient and silent. She finds it impossible to believe she is safe, no matter what anyone says. Sleep offers little escape. She often wakes abruptly in the dead of night, heart hammering against her ribs, straining her ears for any sound from the hallway. Convinced she heard footsteps or the turn of a key, she will creep out of bed to begin her patrol: checking the deadbolt on the front door, ensuring the window latches are secure, peering through the blinds at the empty street below. This ritual can happen two or three times a night, leaving her exhausted and frayed by morning. It was after a week of these broken nights culminated in a tearful, panicked call to her daughter at 3 a.m. that she finally acknowledged she could not endure this alone. She is seeking help not with any grand hope of forgetting, but with the simple, desperate wish to once again feel safe in her own home after the sun goes down.
